entries.content:
本章脉络

第十八章是受难记载的开始，场景快速转换。在园子里被捉拿（1-11节）：耶稣说「我就是」，来捉拿他的人倒退跌倒。在亚那面前与彼得第一次不认主（12-18节）。亚那的审问（19-24节）。彼得第二、三次不认主（25-27节）。在彼拉多面前（28-40节）：「我的国不属这世界」，「真理是什么呢？」，众人选了巴拉巴。

约翰的受难记载有一个鲜明的特色：耶稣始终是掌权的那一位。他主动走出来迎向捉拿他的人，他保护门徒，他在审问中质问审判他的人，他告诉彼拉多权柄从哪里来（约19:11）。表面上是耶稣受审，实际上，在约翰的笔下，被审判的是世界。

深读 18:4-9「我就是」

1. 他主动出来。 「耶稣知道将要临到自己的一切事，就出来对他们说：『你们找谁？』」（约18:4）在约翰福音里，耶稣不是被找到的，而是自己走出来的。这呼应约10:18：「没有人夺我的命去，是我自己舍的。」

2. 「我就是」。 他们说「找拿撒勒人耶稣」，耶稣说：「我就是！」（约18:5）希腊文是 egō eimi。表面上这只是「我就是你们要找的人」，但约翰接着说：「耶稣一说『我就是』，他们就退后倒在地上。」（约18:6）约翰在短短四节之内三次重复这句话（约18:5、6、8）。读过约8:58的读者不会错过它的分量：那里的「就有了我」，原文也是 egō eimi（参第八章）。在被捉拿的那一刻，耶稣仍然是那位「我是」。在旧约里，人在神显现时俯伏在地（结1:28；但10:9）；而诗篇约27:2说，作恶的人前来攻击时「就绊跌仆倒」。

3. 好牧人保护羊。 「你们若找我，就让这些人去吧。」（约18:8）约翰说这是应验耶稣的话：「你所赐给我的人，我没有失落一个。」（约18:9；参约6:39；约17:12）好牧人在狼来的时候不逃走，而是站在羊和狼中间（约10:11-12）。

深读 18:10-11「我父所给我的那杯」

1. 彼得的刀。 彼得拔刀砍下大祭司仆人马勒古的右耳。只有约翰记下了彼得和马勒古的名字。彼得在约13:37说「我愿意为你舍命」，他是真心的，只是用错了方法。

2. 「那杯」。 「收刀入鞘吧，我父所给我的那杯，我岂可不喝呢？」（约18:11）约翰福音没有记载客西马尼园里「把这杯撤去」的祷告，但这一句话里有同样的「杯」。在旧约里，「杯」常象征神的忿怒和审判（诗75:8；赛51:17；耶25:15）。耶稣要喝的，是神对罪的审判；而他是替我们喝的。

深读 18:15-27 炭火旁的「我不是」

1. 交错的两个场景。 约翰把彼得不认主和耶稣受审交错着写：彼得在院子里（约18:15-18），耶稣在亚那面前（约18:19-24），彼得又在院子里（约18:25-27）。读者的视线在两人之间来回。

2. 「我就是」与「我不是」。 使女问：「你不也是这人的门徒吗？」彼得说：「我不是。」（约18:17）希腊文是 ouk eimi。在园子里，耶稣面对兵丁说「我是」（egō eimi）；在院子里，彼得面对一个使女说「我不是」（ouk eimi）。约翰很可能有意形成这个对比：耶稣坦然承认，彼得却否认。

3. 炭火。 「仆人和差役因为天冷，就生了炭火……彼得也同他们站着烤火。」（约18:18）「炭火」（anthrakia）这个字在新约里只出现两次，另一次在约21:9：复活的主在提比哩亚海边生了炭火，在那里三次问彼得「你爱我吗」。彼得在一堆炭火旁三次不认主，又在另一堆炭火旁三次被恢复。

4. 耶稣在审问中。 亚那问耶稣的门徒和教训，耶稣说：「我从来是明明地对世人说话……你为什么问我呢？可以问那听见的人。」（约18:20-21）后来的犹太法典（《密释纳》）要求先传证人，不可要被告自证其罪；这些规定在耶稣时代是否已经通行，学者看法不一，但耶稣的话至少表明：按律法的精神，定罪要凭证人（申19:15）。被差役打了，耶稣说：「我若说的不是，你可以指证那不是；我若说的是，你为什么打我呢？」（约18:23）他没有报复，也没有沉默不言，而是平静地指出不公。

深读 18:28-32 不进衙门，恐怕染了污秽

1. 深刻的讽刺。 「他们自己却不进衙门，恐怕染了污秽，不能吃逾越节的筵席。」（约18:28）他们小心翼翼，不肯进外邦人的房子，免得在礼仪上不洁；同时却在谋害一个无辜的人。这是马太福音约23:24所说的「蠓虫你们就滤出来，骆驼你们倒吞下去」。

2. 「逾越节的筵席」与年代问题。 这一节与第一章讨论过的约19:14相关：如果「吃逾越节的筵席」是指逾越节当晚的晚餐，那么耶稣就是在宰杀逾越节羊羔的那天被钉，比对观福音（记载最后晚餐就是逾越节晚餐）早一天。另一些解经家（如卡森）认为，这里的「逾越节」可以泛指整个节期，包括接下来七天的除酵节筵席，这样就与对观福音一致。两种读法都有福音派学者支持。

3. 「我们没有杀人的权柄」。 「彼拉多说：『你们自己带他去，按着你们的律法审问他吧。』犹太人说：『我们没有杀人的权柄。』」（约18:31）在罗马统治下，犹太公会一般没有执行死刑的权力。约翰说，这是要应验「耶稣所说自己将要怎样死的话」（约18:32）：犹太人的死刑是用石头打死，罗马的死刑是钉十字架，也就是被「举起来」（约12:32-33）。

深读 18:33-38「我的国不属这世界」

1. 「你是犹太人的王吗？」 这是彼拉多最关心的问题：这个人是不是一个政治威胁？

2. 「不属这世界」。 「我的国不属这世界；我的国若属这世界，我的臣仆必要争战。」（约18:36）「属」（ek）的意思是「出于、来自」，不是「不在这世界里」。耶稣的国不是从这世界的权力来源来的，所以不用这世界的方法（刀剑）来推进。这不表示他的国与这世界无关，而是说它的来源和性质不同。

3. 「我为此而生」。 「你说我是王。我为此而生，也为此来到世间，特为给真理作见证。凡属真理的人就听我的话。」（约18:37）「为此而生，也为此来到世间」，两个说法，一个说出生，一个暗示他从别处而来（约3:31「从天上来的」）。「听我的话」呼应约10:3、27：「羊也听他的声音。」

4. 「真理是什么呢？」 彼拉多说了这句话，「又出来到犹太人那里」（约18:38），没有等回答。他问「真理是什么」，而那位说「我就是真理」（约14:6）的，就站在他面前。

深读 18:39-40「不要这人，要巴拉巴！」

「他们又喊着说：『不要这人，要巴拉巴！』这巴拉巴是个强盗。」（约18:40）「强盗」（lēstēs）在当时也用于武装的叛乱分子；马可福音约15:7说他和作乱的人一同捆绑，「他们作乱的时候，曾杀过人」。讽刺的是，耶稣被指控为政治叛乱者，而众人选择释放的，正是一个真正的叛乱者。约翰自己的重点是这个交换：真正的叛乱者得释放，无罪的那一位被定罪，正如该亚法不自觉说出的「一个人替百姓死是有益的」（约18:14；参约11:50）。有人也注意到「巴拉巴」在亚兰文可能是「父的儿子」的意思，但约翰没有点出这一点。

要点：在约翰的受难记载里，耶稣不是命运的受害者。他主动出来，用「我是」使兵丁仆倒，保护门徒，喝下父给他的杯；被审判的那一位，其实是真正的王。
默想

默想： 耶稣说「我就是」，彼得说「我不是」。但耶稣在园子里说「就让这些人去吧」，他喝下那杯，好叫不认他的彼得得释放；巴拉巴得释放，无罪的那一位被定罪。我就是那个被放走的人。今天，当我因害怕而想隐藏自己属于他的时候（在家族聚会、祭祖的场合、同事的饭局上），这个交换能给我什么勇气？彼拉多问「真理是什么」却不等回答。今天我是否愿意停下来，听那位就是真理的主说话？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 18 opens the passion narrative, and the scenes shift quickly. The arrest in the garden (vv. 1–11): Jesus says "I am he," and those who came to seize him draw back and fall. Before Annas, and Peter's first denial (vv. 12–18). Annas questions Jesus (vv. 19–24). Peter's second and third denials (vv. 25–27). Before Pilate (vv. 28–40): "My kingdom is not of this world," "What is truth?", and the crowd chooses Barabbas.

John's passion narrative has a striking feature: Jesus is always the one in control. He steps out to meet those who come to arrest him, he protects his disciples, he questions those who question him, and he tells Pilate where authority comes from (John 19:11). On the surface Jesus is on trial; in John's telling, it is the world that is being judged.

Going Deeper: 18:4–9 "I am he"

1. He comes forward. "Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, 'Whom do you seek?'" (John 18:4). In John, Jesus isn't found; he steps out himself. This echoes John 10:18: "No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord."

2. "I am he." They say, "Jesus of Nazareth," and Jesus says, "I am he" (John 18:5). The Greek is egō eimi. On the surface it simply means "I'm the one you're looking for," but John adds, "When Jesus said to them, 'I am he,' they drew back and fell to the ground" (John 18:6). John repeats the phrase three times in four verses (John 18:5, 6, 8), and readers who remember John 8:58 won't miss its weight: at the very moment of his arrest, Jesus is still the "I am." In the Old Testament people fall on their faces when God appears (Ezek 1:28; Dan 10:9), and Psalm 27:2 says that when evildoers assail, "it is they who stumble and fall."

3. The good shepherd protects his sheep. "If you seek me, let these men go" (John 18:8). John says this fulfilled Jesus' words: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one" (John 18:9; cf. John 6:39; John 17:12). When the wolf comes, the good shepherd doesn't run; he stands between the sheep and the wolf (John 10:11–12).

Going Deeper: 18:10–11 "The cup that the Father has given me"

1. Peter's sword. Peter draws his sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest's servant, Malchus. Only John names Peter and Malchus. Peter said in John 13:37, "I will lay down my life for you." He meant it; he just went about it the wrong way.

2. "The cup." "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" (John 18:11). John doesn't record the Gethsemane prayer, "remove this cup," but the same "cup" is in this sentence. In the Old Testament the "cup" often symbolizes God's wrath and judgment (Ps 75:8; Isa 51:17; Jer 25:15). What Jesus will drink is God's judgment on sin, and he drinks it for us.

Going Deeper: 18:15–27 "I Am Not" by the Charcoal Fire

1. Two interwoven scenes. John weaves Peter's denials together with Jesus' trial: Peter in the courtyard (John 18:15–18), Jesus before Annas (John 18:19–24), Peter in the courtyard again (John 18:25–27). The reader's eye moves back and forth between the two.

2. "I am" and "I am not." The servant girl asks, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" Peter says, "I am not" (John 18:17), in Greek ouk eimi. In the garden Jesus faced soldiers and said "I am" (egō eimi); in the courtyard Peter faced a servant girl and said "I am not" (ouk eimi). John very likely intends the contrast: Jesus openly confesses, while Peter denies.

3. The charcoal fire. "Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them" (John 18:18). "Charcoal fire" (anthrakia) appears only twice in the New Testament, the other time in John 21:9, where the risen Lord makes a charcoal fire by the Sea of Tiberias and there asks Peter three times, "Do you love me?" Beside one charcoal fire Peter denies the Lord three times; beside another he is restored three times.

4. Jesus under questioning. Annas asks Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus says, "I have spoken openly to the world... Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me" (John 18:20–21). Later Jewish law (the Mishnah) required witnesses rather than self-incrimination; whether those rules held in Jesus' day is debated, but Jesus' point stands on the law's own demand for witnesses (Deut 19:15). Struck by an officer, Jesus says, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" (John 18:23). He doesn't retaliate, and he doesn't stay silent; he calmly names the injustice.

Going Deeper: 18:28–32 They Would Not Enter, So as Not to Be Defiled

1. A deep irony. "They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover" (John 18:28). They carefully avoided ritual defilement from entering a Gentile's house while plotting to kill an innocent man. It's what Matthew 23:24 calls "straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel."

2. "Eat the Passover" and the chronology question. This verse connects with John 19:14, discussed in chapter 1. If "eat the Passover" means the Passover meal that evening, Jesus was crucified on the day the Passover lambs were slaughtered, a day earlier than the other Gospels (which present the Last Supper as the Passover meal). Other interpreters (Carson, for example) take "Passover" here more broadly for the whole festival, including the meals of the following seven days of Unleavened Bread, which agrees with the other Gospels. Both readings have evangelical support.

3. "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death." "Pilate said to them, 'Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.' The Jews said to him, 'It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death'" (John 18:31). Under Roman rule the council generally had no power to carry out executions. John says this fulfilled Jesus' words "showing by what kind of death he was going to die" (John 18:32): the Jewish death penalty was stoning, but the Roman one was crucifixion, being "lifted up" (John 12:32–33).

Going Deeper: 18:33–38 "My kingdom is not of this world"

1. "Are you the King of the Jews?" This is Pilate's main concern: is this man a political threat?

2. "Not of this world." "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting" (John 18:36). "Of" (ek) means "from, out of," not "not located in this world." Jesus' kingdom doesn't come from this world's sources of power, so it doesn't advance by this world's methods (the sword). It doesn't mean his kingdom has nothing to do with this world, but that its source and nature are different.

3. "For this purpose I was born." "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world, to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice" (John 18:37). "Born" and "come into the world": one speaks of his birth, the other hints that he came from elsewhere (John 3:31, "he who comes from heaven"). "Listens to my voice" echoes John 10:3, 27: "The sheep hear his voice."

4. "What is truth?" Pilate says this and "went back outside to the Jews" (John 18:38) without waiting for an answer. He asks "What is truth?" while the one who said "I am the truth" (John 14:6) stands in front of him.

Going Deeper: 18:39–40 "Not this man, but Barabbas!"

"They cried out again, 'Not this man, but Barabbas!' Now Barabbas was a robber" (John 18:40). "Robber" (lēstēs) was also used then for armed insurrectionists; Mark 15:7 says he had "committed murder in the insurrection." The irony is that Jesus is accused of political rebellion, and the man the crowd chooses to release is a real rebel. John's own point is the exchange: the real rebel goes free and the innocent one is condemned, just as Caiaphas unwittingly said, "it would be expedient that one man should die for the people" (John 18:14; cf. John 11:50). Some also note that "Barabbas" may mean "son of the father" in Aramaic, though John doesn't draw attention to it.

The point: In John's passion narrative Jesus is no victim of fate. He steps forward, his "I am" sends soldiers to the ground, he protects his disciples and drinks the cup the Father gives him; the one on trial is the true King.
Meditation

Reflect: Jesus said "I am he"; Peter said "I am not." Yet in the garden Jesus said "let these men go," and he drank the cup so that Peter, who denied him, could go free. Barabbas walked out, and the innocent one was condemned. I am the one who was let go. When fear tempts me today to hide that I belong to him, what courage does that exchange give me? Pilate asked "What is truth?" and didn't wait for an answer. Am I willing today to stop and listen to the Lord who is the truth?

entries.verse_text: 耶稣尝了那醋，就说：「成了！」便低下头，将灵魂交付神了。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十九章是全书的中心，也是从约2:4「我的时候还没有到」一路指向的那个「时候」（约12:23；约13:1；约17:1）。鞭打与戏弄（1-7节）：「你们看这个人！」彼拉多与权柄（8-16节）：「除了凯撒，我们没有王。」钉十字架（17-27节）：三种文字的名号，拈阄分衣，耶稣把母亲交托给所爱的门徒。耶稣的死（28-30节）：「我渴了」，「成了！」肋旁的血和水（31-37节）。安葬（38-42节）：两位暗中的门徒走到光中。

约翰在这一章里多次引用经上的话（约19:24、28、36-37）。他要读者看见：十字架不是计划出了差错，而是旧约一路指向的那件事。还有一个反讽贯穿全章：罗马兵丁戏弄耶稣是王，彼拉多写下「犹太人的王」，众人喊「除掉他」，但在约翰的读者眼中，这一切都在宣告同一个真理：他真的是王，而十字架就是他的宝座。

深读 19:1-16「你们看这个人！」与「除了凯撒，我们没有王」

1. 被戏弄的王。 兵丁用荆棘编作冠冕，给他穿上紫袍，说「恭喜，犹太人的王啊！」（约19:2-3）他们以为是在开玩笑，其实说出了真相。

2. 「你们看这个人！」 彼拉多把耶稣带出来说：「你们看这个人！」（约19:5）他可能是想说：看，这个被打得不成人样的人，有什么威胁？希望激起众人的怜悯。但约翰的读者听到的是更深的意思：这就是那个人，道成肉身的那一位（约1:14），完全的人，在这里承受人类的罪。

3. 权柄从哪里来。 彼拉多说：「你岂不知我有权柄释放你，也有权柄把你钉十字架吗？」耶稣回答：「若不是从上头赐给你的，你就毫无权柄办我。」（约19:10-11）「从上头」（anōthen）正是约3:3「重生」的那个字。站着受审的那一位，告诉审判他的人，他的权柄从哪里来。

4. 「除了凯撒，我们没有王」。 彼拉多说：「看哪，这是你们的王！」祭司长回答：「除了凯撒，我们没有王。」（约19:14-15）这是全书最沉重的一句话之一。在旧约里，以色列真正的王是神自己：基甸说「惟有耶和华管理你们」（士8:23），百姓要求立王时，神说「他们不是厌弃你，乃是厌弃我，不要我作他们的王」（撒上8:7）。在逾越节，纪念神从法老手中拯救他们的日子，祭司长宣告他们唯一的王是凯撒。

5. 「约有午正」。 「那日是预备逾越节的日子，约有午正。」（约19:14）马可福音约15:25说钉十字架是在「巳初」（上午九点左右）。解经家提出几种解释：古人计时多是大概的估算，「午正」和「巳初」都只是把上午约略划分；也有人认为约翰用的是不同的计时法。关于「预备逾越节的日子」的年代问题，请参第一章和第十八章的讨论。

深读 19:17-24 三种文字的名号与没有缝儿的里衣

1. 「耶稣背着自己的十字架出来」。 约翰没有提到古利奈人西门（对观福音记载他被强迫替耶稣背十字架），而是强调耶稣「背着自己的十字架」（约19:17）。这不是矛盾，耶稣很可能先自己背，途中才由西门接过去；但约翰的强调与全书一致：耶稣是主动走向十字架的。有人也联想到以撒背着燔祭的柴上山（创22:6）。

2. 三种文字。 名号「是用希伯来、罗马、希腊三样文字写的」（约19:20）：宗教的语言、政治的语言、文化的语言。彼拉多无意中向全世界宣告了耶稣是王。祭司长要他改成「他自己说：我是犹太人的王」，彼拉多说：「我所写的，我已经写上了。」（约19:22）

3. 没有缝儿的里衣。 兵丁分他的衣服，「又拿他的里衣，这件里衣原来没有缝儿，是上下一片织成的」（约19:23）。「上下」原文是「从上头」（ek tōn anōthen），又是anōthen这个字。有解经家指出，犹太史家约瑟夫记载大祭司的长袍也是一片织成、没有缝的，所以约翰也许暗示耶稣是那位真正的大祭司（参第十七章）。约翰没有明说，但这很合乎他的写法。

4. 应验诗篇22篇。 「这要应验经上的话说：他们分了我的外衣，为我的里衣拈阄。」（约19:24；诗22:18）诗篇22篇以「我的神，我的神！为什么离弃我？」开始，是一首受苦义人的诗，后半却转为「列国的万族都要在你面前敬拜」（约22:27），最后一节说「这事是他所行的」（约22:31）。约翰不需要引用整首诗，读者会想起它。

深读 19:25-27「看，你的母亲！」

1. 十字架下的人。 「站在耶稣十字架旁边的，有他母亲与他母亲的姊妹，并革罗罢的妻子马利亚，和抹大拉的马利亚。」（约19:25）门徒大多逃散了，留下来的多是妇女，和耶稣所爱的那门徒。

2. 最后的照顾。 「耶稣见母亲和他所爱的那门徒站在旁边，就对他母亲说：『母亲，看，你的儿子！』又对那门徒说：『看，你的母亲！』从此，那门徒就接她到自己家里去了。」（约19:26-27）在担当世人罪孽的时候，耶稣仍然顾念自己的母亲，尽了儿子的孝道。这里的「母亲」，原文和迦拿婚筵一样是「妇人」（gynai，参第二章）。迦拿时「时候还没有到」，现在时候到了。

3. 新的家。 许多解经家也看见这一幕的象征意义：在十字架下，一个新的家诞生了，属于耶稣的人彼此成为家人。但首先，这是一个儿子对母亲真实的爱。

深读 19:28-30「我渴了」与「成了」

1. 「知道各样的事已经成了」。 「这事以后，耶稣知道各样的事已经成了，为要使经上的话应验，就说：『我渴了。』」（约19:28）道成了肉身（约1:14），而肉身会渴。那位在井旁对撒玛利亚妇人说「人若喝我所赐的水就永远不渴」（约4:14）的主，现在说「我渴了」。诗篇约69:21说：「我渴了，他们拿醋给我喝。」

2. 牛膝草。 「他们就拿海绒蘸满了醋，绑在牛膝草上，送到他口。」（约19:29）牛膝草这种细小的植物，不太适合撑起海绒，所以约翰特别提到它，很可能有用意：在出埃及的那一夜，以色列人正是用牛膝草蘸羊羔的血，涂在门框上（出12:22）。又是一个逾越节的记号。

3. 「成了」。 「耶稣尝了那醋，就说：『成了！』」（约19:30）希腊文只有一个字：tetelestai，完成时，「已经完成，其果效持续」。两节之前，约翰刚用同一个字说耶稣「知道各样的事已经成了」（约19:28）。这也与约13:1「爱他们到底」（eis telos）和约17:4「你所托付我的事，我已成全了」是同一个字根。父所托付他的工作，就是借着他的死成就救恩；这工作已经完成了。有一个流行的说法，认为古代的税单收据上写着这个字，意思是「付清了」。这个说法有些根据，但学者对它的分量有不同看法，不宜太强调。不论如何，这一声不是失败者的叹息，而是得胜者的宣告：他在十字架上替我们死，担当了我们该受的刑罚和神的忿怒（参约18:11「那杯」；赛53:5-6），正如逾越节羊羔的血使审判越过；这就是施洗约翰所说「除去世人罪孽」（约1:29）的方法。罪债已经付清，救恩已经成就，不需要再添加什么。

4. 「将灵魂交付神了」。 「便低下头，将灵魂交付神了。」（约19:30）原文是「交付了灵」（paredōken to pneuma）。他不是被夺去生命，而是主动把生命交出去（约10:18）。有解经家也注意到，「交付」这个字在受难记载里一再出现（和合本多译作「卖」或「交给」）：犹大「交付」他（约18:2），祭司长「交付」他（约18:30），彼拉多「交付」他（约19:16），最后，他自己交付了灵。

要点：「成了」是一个字，却是福音的总结：救恩不是要我们去完成，而是耶稣已经完成了。我们所能做的，就是相信那已经完成的工作。
深读 19:31-37 血和水，与看见的人的见证

1. 骨头没有被打断。 犹太人求彼拉多打断被钉之人的腿，好叫他们快死。兵丁来到耶稣那里，「见他已经死了，就不打断他的腿」（约19:33）。约翰说这应验了「他的骨头一根也不可折断」（约19:36），这是逾越节羊羔的规定（出12:46；民9:12），也呼应诗篇约34:20。第一章施洗约翰所说的「神的羔羊」，在这里完全显明了。

2. 血和水。 「惟有一个兵拿枪扎他的肋旁，随即有血和水流出来。」（约19:34）这首先证明耶稣真的死了。约翰特别强调这件事，可能是为了回应早期教会中一些人（后来被称为「幻影派」）的说法：他们认为耶稣只是看起来有身体，没有真正受苦而死。约翰一书5:6说：「这藉着水和血而来的，就是耶稣基督。」许多解经家也在血和水中看见象征：血是赎罪，水是圣灵所赐的生命（约7:38-39）。

3. 看见的人的见证。 「看见这事的那人就作见证－他的见证也是真的，并且他知道自己所说的是真的－叫你们也可以信。」（约19:35）这是全书中最直接的目击者宣告之一。约翰在这里停下来，直接对读者说话：我亲眼看见了，我说的是真的，好叫你们信。

4. 仰望被扎的。 「经上又有一句说：『他们要仰望自己所扎的人。』」（约19:37；亚12:10）撒迦利亚书12:10说，神要把「那施恩叫人恳求的灵」浇灌下来，「他们必仰望我，就是他们所扎的」：在撒迦利亚书里，被扎的那一位，是耶和华自己。

深读 19:38-42 两位暗中的门徒

1. 亚利马太人约瑟。 「有亚利马太人约瑟，是耶稣的门徒，只因怕犹太人，就暗暗地作门徒。」（约19:38）他去求彼拉多领耶稣的身体，这是公开表明立场的行动。

2. 尼哥德慕。 「又有尼哥德慕，就是先前夜里去见耶稣的，带着没药和沉香约有一百斤前来。」（约19:39）第三章的那个夜访者，在耶稣死后，带着足以安葬君王的香料来了。在耶稣活着的时候，他们没有公开站出来；在耶稣死的时候，在门徒都逃走的时候，他们站了出来。十字架吸引人（约12:32），连最胆怯的人也被吸引了。

3. 园子里的新坟墓。 「在耶稣钉十字架的地方有一个园子，园子里有一座新坟墓。」（约19:41）约翰特别提到「园子」：耶稣在一个园子里被捉拿（约18:1），又葬在一个园子里；到了约20:15，马利亚还以为复活的耶稣是「看园的」。有解经家联想到伊甸园：人在一个园子里堕落，新的创造也在一个园子里开始。

默想

默想： 祭司长说「除了凯撒，我们没有王」。在我的生命中，有没有什么「凯撒」在争夺耶稣作王的位置？约瑟和尼哥德慕在最危险的时刻站了出来，因为十字架吸引了他们。耶稣说「成了」，我是否还在试图为自己的救恩加上什么？今天，我能否单单仰望那被扎的主，在他已经成就的工作里安息、敬拜？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 19 is the center of the whole book and the "hour" anticipated since John 2:4 ("my hour has not yet come") and announced in John 12:23; John 13:1; John 17:1. Flogging and mockery (vv. 1–7): "Behold the man!" Pilate and authority (vv. 8–16): "We have no king but Caesar." The crucifixion (vv. 17–27): the title in three languages, the soldiers casting lots for his clothing, and Jesus entrusting his mother to the disciple he loved. The death of Jesus (vv. 28–30): "I thirst," "It is finished." Blood and water from his side (vv. 31–37). The burial (vv. 38–42): two secret disciples step into the light.

Several times in this chapter John appeals to Scripture (John 19:24, 28, 36–37). He wants readers to see that the cross wasn't a plan gone wrong but the very thing the Old Testament pointed to. An irony also runs through the chapter: soldiers mock Jesus as king, Pilate writes "King of the Jews," the crowd shouts "Away with him," yet to John's readers all of it proclaims the same truth. He really is king, and the cross is his throne.

Going Deeper: 19:1–16 "Behold the man!" and "We have no king but Caesar"

1. The mocked king. The soldiers twist a crown of thorns, put a purple robe on him and say, "Hail, King of the Jews!" (John 19:2–3). They think it's a joke; they're telling the truth.

2. "Behold the man!" Pilate brings Jesus out and says, "Behold the man!" (John 19:5). He may have meant: look at this beaten wreck of a man; what threat is he? hoping to stir the crowd's pity. But John's readers hear more: this is the man, the Word made flesh (John 1:14), fully human, bearing humanity's sin.

3. Where authority comes from. Pilate says, "Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?" Jesus answers, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above" (John 19:10–11). "From above" (anōthen) is the very word of John 3:3, "born again / from above." The man on trial tells his judge where his authority comes from.

4. "We have no king but Caesar." Pilate says, "Behold your King!" The chief priests answer, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:14–15). It's one of the heaviest sentences in the book. In the Old Testament Israel's true king was God himself. Gideon said, "the LORD will rule over you" (Judg 8:23), and when the people demanded a king, God said, "they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them" (1 Sam 8:7). At Passover, the feast remembering God's rescue from Pharaoh, the chief priests declare that their only king is Caesar.

5. "About the sixth hour." "Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour" (John 19:14). Mark 15:25 says the crucifixion was at "the third hour" (about 9 a.m.). Interpreters suggest several explanations: ancient timekeeping was approximate, and both the "third" and the "sixth" hour roughly divide the morning; others think John used a different reckoning. On the chronology of "the day of Preparation of the Passover," see the discussion in chapters 1 and 18.

Going Deeper: 19:17–24 The Title in Three Languages and the Seamless Tunic

1. "Bearing his own cross." John doesn't mention Simon of Cyrene (whom the other Gospels say was forced to carry the cross); he stresses that Jesus went out "bearing his own cross" (John 19:17). There's no contradiction: Jesus likely carried it first, and Simon took it over on the way. But John's emphasis fits the whole book: Jesus goes to the cross of his own accord. Some also recall Isaac carrying the wood for the burnt offering up the mountain (Gen 22:6).

2. Three languages. The title "was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek" (John 19:20): the languages of religion, politics and culture. Pilate unwittingly announced Jesus' kingship to the whole world. When the chief priests asked him to change it to "This man said, I am King of the Jews," Pilate answered, "What I have written I have written" (John 19:22).

3. The seamless tunic. The soldiers divide his garments, "But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom" (John 19:23). "From top" is literally "from above" (ek tōn anōthen), anōthen once again. Some interpreters note that the Jewish historian Josephus describes the high priest's robe as woven in one piece without a seam, so John may be hinting that Jesus is the true high priest (see chapter 17). John doesn't say so, but it fits his way of writing.

4. Psalm 22 fulfilled. "This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, 'They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots'" (John 19:24; Ps 22:18). Psalm 22 begins, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" a psalm of the suffering righteous one, yet it turns to "all the families of the nations shall worship before you" (John 22:27), and its last verse says, "he has done it" (John 22:31). John doesn't need to quote the whole psalm; readers will remember it.

Going Deeper: 19:25–27 "Behold, your mother!"

1. Those at the cross. "Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene" (John 19:25). Most of the disciples had fled; those who remained were mostly women, along with the disciple Jesus loved.

2. His last care. "When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, 'Woman, behold, your son!' Then he said to the disciple, 'Behold, your mother!' And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home" (John 19:26–27). While bearing the world's sin, Jesus still cares for his mother. He addresses her, as at Cana, as "woman" (gynai; see chapter 2). At Cana his hour had not yet come; now it has.

3. A new family. Many interpreters also see the symbolism of this scene: at the cross a new family is born, and those who belong to Jesus become family to one another. But first of all, it is a son's real love for his mother.

Going Deeper: 19:28–30 "I thirst" and "It is finished"

1. "Knowing that all was now finished." "After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), 'I thirst'" (John 19:28). The Word became flesh (John 1:14), and flesh thirsts. The Lord who told the Samaritan woman at the well, "whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty forever" (John 4:14), now says, "I thirst." Psalm 69:21 says, "for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink."

2. Hyssop. "So they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth" (John 19:29). Hyssop is a small plant, not well suited to holding up a sponge, so John's mention of it is probably deliberate: on the night of the exodus, the Israelites used hyssop to dip the lamb's blood and paint it on their doorposts (Ex 12:22). Another Passover sign.

3. "It is finished." "When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, 'It is finished'" (John 19:30). In Greek it is one word, tetelestai, in the perfect tense: "finished, with lasting effect." Two verses earlier John used the same word: Jesus knew "that all was now finished" (John 19:28). It also shares a root with "he loved them to the end" (eis telos, John 13:1) and "having accomplished the work that you gave me to do" (John 17:4). The work the Father gave him, to accomplish salvation by his death, is complete. A popular claim holds that ancient tax receipts bore this word, meaning "paid in full." There's some basis for it, but scholars weigh it differently, so it shouldn't be pressed. Either way, this is no sigh of defeat but a victor's announcement. On the cross he died in our place, bearing the penalty and the wrath of God that we deserved (cf. "the cup," John 18:11; Isa 53:5–6), just as the Passover blood turned judgment away. This is how the Lamb "takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). The debt of sin is paid, salvation is accomplished, and nothing more needs to be added.

4. "Gave up his spirit." "And he bowed his head and gave up his spirit" (John 19:30). Literally he "handed over the spirit" (paredōken to pneuma). His life wasn't taken; he gave it up (John 10:18). Some interpreters also notice that "hand over" recurs through the passion narrative: Judas handed him over (John 18:2), the chief priests handed him over (John 18:30), Pilate handed him over (John 19:16), and finally he handed over his own spirit.

The point: "It is finished" is one word, and it sums up the gospel. Salvation isn't something we must complete; Jesus has completed it. What we can do is believe in the finished work.
Going Deeper: 19:31–37 Blood and Water, and the Eyewitness's Testimony

1. No bone broken. The Jews asked Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken to hasten their deaths. "But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs" (John 19:33). John says this fulfilled "Not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:36), the rule for the Passover lamb (Ex 12:46; Num 9:12), echoed also in Psalm 34:20. The "Lamb of God" John the Baptist announced in chapter 1 is fully revealed here.

2. Blood and water. "But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water" (John 19:34). First, this proves Jesus really died. John may stress it to answer some in the early church (later called Docetists) who taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body and didn't truly suffer and die. First John 5:6 says Jesus "came by water and blood." Many interpreters also see symbolism here: the blood for atonement, the water for the life the Spirit gives (John 7:38–39).

3. The eyewitness's testimony. "He who saw it has borne witness—his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth—that you also may believe" (John 19:35). This is one of the most direct eyewitness claims in the whole book. John stops and speaks straight to the reader: I saw it myself, what I say is true, so that you may believe.

4. Looking on the pierced one. "And again another Scripture says, 'They will look on him whom they have pierced'" (John 19:37; Zech 12:10). Zechariah 12:10 says God will pour out "a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy," and "they look on me, on him whom they have pierced": in Zechariah the one pierced is the LORD himself.

Going Deeper: 19:38–42 Two Secret Disciples

1. Joseph of Arimathea. "Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38). He goes to Pilate to ask for Jesus' body, a public act that declares where he stands.

2. Nicodemus. "Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight" (John 19:39). The night visitor of chapter 3, after Jesus' death, comes with spices enough to bury a king. While Jesus lived, they didn't stand up in public; at his death, when the disciples had fled, they did. The cross draws people (John 12:32), even the most timid.

3. A new tomb in a garden. "Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb" (John 19:41). John mentions gardens: in John 18:1 Jesus was arrested in a garden, here he is buried in one, and in John 20:15 Mary will take the risen Jesus for "the gardener." Some interpreters think of Eden: humanity fell in a garden, and the new creation begins in one.

Meditation

Reflect: The chief priests said, "We have no king but Caesar." Is there some "Caesar" in my life competing with Jesus for the throne? Joseph and Nicodemus stepped forward at the most dangerous moment, because the cross drew them. Jesus said, "It is finished." Am I still trying to add something to my salvation? Today, can I simply look on him whom they pierced, and rest and worship in his finished work?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第二十章是复活的一天，从清早到晚上，再到八天以后。空坟墓（1-10节）：马利亚、彼得和那门徒先后来到坟墓。耶稣向抹大拉的马利亚显现（11-18节）：「马利亚。」「拉波尼！」向门徒显现（19-23节）：「愿你们平安！」「你们受圣灵！」多马（24-29节）：「我的主！我的神！」写这书的目的（30-31节）。

这一章有一个清楚的模式：每一个人都从不信或不明白，走到信。马利亚以为有人把主的身体挪走了，后来认出了他；那门徒「看见就信了」；关着门的门徒从惧怕到喜乐；多马从「我总不信」到全书最高的信心告白。约翰也在结尾转向读者：你们没有看见，却可以信。

深读 20:1-10 空坟墓与留下的布

1. 天还黑的时候。 「七日的第一日清早，天还黑的时候，抹大拉的马利亚来到坟墓那里。」（约20:1）约翰特别写「天还黑」。在这卷书里，黑暗常有象征意义（约1:5；约13:30）。新的一天，新的创造，就在黑暗还没有完全退去的时候开始了。

2. 女人作第一个见证。 在当时的犹太社会，女人的见证在法庭上常不被采信。如果复活的故事是后人编造的，大概不会让妇女成为第一批见证人。四福音都记载，最先发现空坟墓的是妇女，这是复活记载真实性的一个旁证。

3. 细麻布与裹头巾。 彼得进到坟墓里，「就看见细麻布还放在那里，又看见耶稣的裹头巾没有和细麻布放在一处，是另在一处卷着」（约20:6-7）。如果有人偷走了身体，不会花时间把裹尸布解下来、还把头巾卷好放在一旁。这和拉撒路形成对比（约11:44）：拉撒路出来时还被裹着，需要别人解开；耶稣把死亡的裹布留在了身后。

4. 「看见就信了」。 「先到坟墓的那门徒也进去，看见就信了。因为他们还不明白圣经的意思，就是耶稣必要从死里复活。」（约20:8-9）那门徒信了什么？最自然的理解是：他相信耶稣复活了，虽然他还不能从圣经去解释这件事。信有时走在明白的前面。

深读 20:11-18「马利亚」

1. 以为是看园的。 马利亚在坟墓外哭，转过身来，看见耶稣站在那里，却不知道是耶稣，「以为是看园的」（约20:15）。许多读者在这里看见一个反讽：她把他当作园丁，而他正是新创造这座园子的主（参约19:41；创2:8、15）。

2. 一个名字。 「耶稣说：『马利亚。』马利亚就转过来，用希伯来话对他说：『拉波尼！』」（约20:16）她认出他，不是因为看清了他的脸，而是因为他叫了她的名字。这正是约10:3所说的：「羊也听他的声音。他按着名叫自己的羊，把羊领出来。」「希伯来话」在这里指当时犹太人说的亚兰话，英文ESV作「Aramaic」。

3. 「不要摸我」。 「耶稣说：『不要摸我，因我还没有升上去见我的父。』」（约20:17）和合本译作「不要摸我」，但希腊文是现在时的命令（mē mou haptou），意思更接近「不要一直抓住我」、「不要拉着我不放」，英文ESV译作「Do not cling to me」。马利亚想要抓住她刚刚失而复得的主，好像要回到从前的关系。耶稣说：一种新的关系要开始了，不是靠肉身的抓住，而是借着他升天以后赐下的圣灵。

4. 「我的父，也是你们的父」。 「你往我弟兄那里去，告诉他们说，我要升上去见我的父，也是你们的父，见我的神，也是你们的神。」（约20:17）在约翰福音中，这是耶稣第一次称门徒为「我弟兄」。借着十字架和复活，他的父成了他们的父。但他没有说「我们的父」，而是「我的父，也是你们的父」：他本是神的独生子，他们则是借着他成为神的儿女（约1:12）。

5. 第一个传复活信息的人。 「抹大拉的马利亚就去告诉门徒说：『我已经看见了主。』」（约20:18）她成了第一个宣告复活的人。

深读 20:19-23「父怎样差遣了我，我也照样差遣你们」

1. 关着的门。 「那日晚上，门徒所在的地方，因怕犹太人，门都关了。耶稣来，站在当中。」（约20:19）复活的身体是真实的身体（他给他们看手和肋旁），却不再受原有的限制。

2. 「愿你们平安」。 耶稣两次说「愿你们平安」（约20:19、21）。这是平常的问候（shalom），但在这个时刻，它带着全新的分量：约14:27所应许的平安，借着十字架成就了。他给他们看手和肋旁，平安是建立在那些伤痕上的：他在十字架上担当了我们的罪，所以能把平安赐给我们。

3. 差遣。 「父怎样差遣了我，我也照样差遣你们。」（约20:21）约翰福音一再称父为「差我来的」。现在，被差的那一位，差遣他的门徒。门徒的使命，是延续耶稣的使命（参约17:18）。

4. 吹一口气。 「说了这话，就向他们吹一口气，说：『你们受圣灵！』」（约20:22）「吹气」（emphysaō）在新约里只出现在这里。七十士译本在创世记约2:7用这个字描写神「将生气吹在他鼻孔里」，以西结书37:9也用它（「气息啊……吹在这些被杀的人身上，使他们活了」）。约翰似乎在说：复活的主正在开始一个新的创造。

5. 这与五旬节有什么关系？ 解经家有几种看法：有人认为这就是约翰版的五旬节；有人认为这是圣灵初步的赐予，五旬节是更完全的浇灌；也有人（如卡森）认为这是一个预表性的举动，预告即将在五旬节发生的事。这个问题也要和约7:39、约16:7以及使徒行传1:4-5一并考虑（圣灵要在耶稣得荣耀、离去之后才赐下，门徒要在耶路撒冷等候），因此多数福音派学者倾向后两种看法。

6. 赦罪的权柄。 「你们赦免谁的罪，谁的罪就赦免了；你们留下谁的罪，谁的罪就留下了。」（约20:23）这里的「你们」是复数，是对聚集的门徒说的。这不是说门徒自己有赦罪的能力。在福音派的理解中，这是指教会借着宣讲福音所带有的权柄：凡因所传的福音而信的，可以确知罪已赦免；凡拒绝的，罪就仍在（参约3:18、36）。

深读 20:24-29「我的主！我的神！」

1. 多马的条件。 「我非看见他手上的钉痕，用指头探入那钉痕，又用手探入他的肋旁，我总不信。」（约20:25）多马要的证据非常具体，而且是关于伤痕的。他要确认，复活的这一位，就是那位被钉的。

2. 耶稣知道他说的话。 八天以后，耶稣再来，直接对多马说：「伸过你的指头来，摸我的手；伸出你的手来，探入我的肋旁。不要疑惑，总要信！」（约20:27）耶稣用多马自己的话回应他，温和地责备，却先满足了他的需要。「不要疑惑，总要信」，直译是「不要成为不信的，要成为信的」。

3. 全书的高峰。 「多马说：『我的主！我的神！』」（约20:28）经文没有说多马真的伸手去摸。看见就够了。他的告白是全书的高峰：序言以「道就是神」（约1:1）开始，这里以一个门徒称耶稣为「我的神」结束，前后呼应。希腊文是 ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou，原文说「多马对他说」，所以这不是一句惊叹，而是向耶稣说的告白。有学者指出，当时的罗马皇帝多米田曾以「我们的主和神」自称（他的官方书信用这个称号），约翰的读者若在多米田的时代读到这句话，会明白这个告白的分量：真正配得这称呼的，不是凯撒，而是复活的耶稣。

4. 没有看见就信的有福了。 「耶稣对他说：『你因看见了我才信；那没有看见就信的有福了。』」（约20:29）这句话是对多马说的，更是对后来所有的读者说的。我们没有像多马那样看见，但我们并不因此吃亏：没有看见而信的人，耶稣称为有福。

要点：约翰福音从「道就是神」开始，在多马「我的主！我的神！」达到高峰。整卷书要读者走的路，就是多马走的路：从疑惑到敬拜。
深读 20:30-31 写这书的目的

「耶稣在门徒面前另外行了许多神迹，没有记在这书上。但记这些事要叫你们信耶稣是基督，是神的儿子，并且叫你们信了他，就可以因他的名得生命。」（约20:30-31）多马的告白之后，约翰立刻转向读者，说明全书的目的。导读里讨论过这节的细节：「信」可能是「开始相信」，也可能是「继续相信」；卡森认为这句话应当读成「叫你们信基督、神的儿子，就是耶稣」。不论哪一种，约翰在多马之后这样说，是在邀请我们：多马因为看见而信，你们可以因为这本书所记的见证而信。

默想

默想： 复活的主按着名叫马利亚，又带着伤痕来回应多马的疑问。我心里有什么疑惑，可以像多马一样诚实地带到他面前？耶稣对马利亚说不要拉着他不放，我是否也想抓住某种过去经历主的方式，而他要带我进入新的关系？多马说「我的主！我的神！」今天我可以怎样不只用口，也用生活来这样承认他？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 20 covers the day of resurrection, from early morning to evening, and then eight days later. The empty tomb (vv. 1–10): Mary, Peter and the other disciple come to the tomb one after another. Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene (vv. 11–18): "Mary." "Rabboni!" He appears to the disciples (vv. 19–23): "Peace be with you." "Receive the Holy Spirit." Thomas (vv. 24–29): "My Lord and my God!" The purpose of the book (vv. 30–31).

The chapter follows a clear pattern: each person moves from unbelief or incomprehension to faith. Mary thinks someone has taken the Lord's body, then recognizes him; the other disciple "saw and believed"; the disciples behind locked doors move from fear to joy; Thomas moves from "I will never believe" to the book's highest confession of faith. And at the end John turns to the reader: you have not seen, but you can believe.

Going Deeper: 20:1–10 The Empty Tomb and the Cloths Left Behind

1. While it was still dark. "Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark" (John 20:1). John notes that it was still dark. In this book darkness often carries symbolic weight (John 1:5; John 13:30). The new day, the new creation, begins while the darkness has not yet fully lifted.

2. A woman as the first witness. In Jewish society at the time, a woman's testimony was often not accepted in court. If the resurrection story had been invented later, it would hardly have made women the first witnesses. All four Gospels record that women were the first to find the tomb empty, which is one piece of evidence for the truthfulness of the resurrection accounts.

3. The linen cloths and the face cloth. Peter went into the tomb and "saw the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself" (John 20:6–7). Someone stealing a body wouldn't stop to unwrap the grave clothes and fold the face cloth to one side. Contrast Lazarus (John 11:44): he came out still wrapped and needed to be unbound; Jesus left the wrappings of death behind.

4. "He saw and believed." "Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed; for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead" (John 20:8–9). What did he believe? The most natural reading is that he believed Jesus had risen, even though he couldn't yet explain it from Scripture. Sometimes faith runs ahead of understanding.

Going Deeper: 20:11–18 "Mary"

1. Supposing him to be the gardener. Mary is weeping outside the tomb. She turns and sees Jesus standing there but doesn't know it's Jesus, "supposing him to be the gardener" (John 20:15). Many readers see an irony here: she takes him for the gardener, and he is indeed the one at work in the garden of the new creation (cf. John 19:41; Gen 2:8, 15).

2. One name. "Jesus said to her, 'Mary.' She turned and said to him in Aramaic, 'Rabboni!'" (John 20:16). She recognizes him not because she sees his face clearly but because he calls her by name. This is exactly John 10:3: "The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out."

3. "Do not cling to me." "Jesus said to her, 'Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father'" (John 20:17). The Chinese Union Version, like the King James ("Touch me not"), reads "Do not touch me," but the Greek is a present imperative (mē mou haptou), closer to "stop holding on to me." Mary wants to hold on to the Lord she has just found again, as if to return to the old relationship. Jesus says a new relationship is about to begin, not by holding on physically but through the Spirit he will give after his ascension.

4. "My Father and your Father." "Go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God'" (John 20:17). In John's Gospel this is the first time Jesus calls the disciples "my brothers." Through the cross and resurrection his Father has become their Father. Yet he doesn't say "our Father" but "my Father and your Father": he is God's Son by nature; they become God's children through him (John 1:12).

5. The first to announce the resurrection. "Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, 'I have seen the Lord'" (John 20:18). She became the first to proclaim the resurrection.

Going Deeper: 20:19–23 "As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you"

1. Locked doors. "On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them" (John 20:19). His risen body is a real body (he shows them his hands and side), yet no longer bound by its former limits.

2. "Peace be with you." Twice Jesus says, "Peace be with you" (John 20:19, 21). It was an ordinary greeting (shalom), but at this moment it carries new weight: the peace promised in John 14:27 has been won through the cross. He shows them his hands and side; the peace rests on those wounds: he bore our sins there, so he can give us peace.

3. Sent. "As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you" (John 20:21). John's Gospel repeatedly calls the Father "him who sent me." Now the one who was sent sends his disciples. Their mission continues his (cf. John 17:18).

4. He breathed on them. "And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit'" (John 20:22). "Breathed" (emphysaō) occurs only here in the New Testament. The Septuagint uses it in Genesis 2:7, where God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life," and in Ezekiel 37:9 ("Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live"). John seems to be saying that the risen Lord is carrying out a new creation.

5. How does this relate to Pentecost? Interpreters hold several views. Some think this is John's version of Pentecost; some think it is an initial gift of the Spirit, with Pentecost the fuller outpouring; others (Carson among them) see an acted prophecy anticipating what would happen at Pentecost. The question must be weighed with John 7:39, John 16:7 and Acts 1:4–5 (the Spirit is given after Jesus is glorified and goes away; the disciples are told to wait in Jerusalem), which is why most evangelicals favor the second or third view.

6. The authority to forgive. "If you forgive the sins of anyone, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld" (John 20:23). "You" is plural, spoken to the gathered disciples. This doesn't mean the disciples have power of their own to forgive sins. In the evangelical understanding, it refers to the authority the church carries in proclaiming the gospel: whoever believes the gospel proclaimed can be sure their sins are forgiven; whoever rejects it remains in their sin (cf. John 3:18, 36).

Going Deeper: 20:24–29 "My Lord and my God!"

1. Thomas's conditions. "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe" (John 20:25). Thomas wants very specific evidence, and it's about the wounds. He wants to be sure the risen one is the one who was crucified.

2. Jesus knows what he said. Eight days later Jesus comes again and speaks directly to Thomas: "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe" (John 20:27). Jesus answers Thomas with his own words. His rebuke is gentle, and he first meets Thomas's need. "Do not disbelieve, but believe" is literally "do not become unbelieving, but believing."

3. The summit of the book. "Thomas answered him, 'My Lord and my God!'" (John 20:28). The text doesn't say Thomas actually reached out to touch. Seeing was enough. His confession is the high point of the whole book: the Prologue opened with "the Word was God" (John 1:1), and here a disciple calls Jesus "my God," the two forming bookends. The Greek is ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou, and the text says Thomas "answered him," so this isn't an exclamation of surprise but a confession addressed to Jesus. Some scholars note that the emperor Domitian styled himself "our Lord and God" (his official letters used the title). If John's readers met these words in Domitian's day, they would feel their weight: the one who truly deserves that title isn't Caesar but the risen Jesus.

4. Blessed are those who have not seen. "Jesus said to him, 'Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed'" (John 20:29). The words are spoken to Thomas, but even more to every later reader. We haven't seen as Thomas did, but we aren't at a disadvantage: Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing.

The point: John's Gospel begins with "the Word was God" and reaches its summit in Thomas's "My Lord and my God!" The road the whole book invites readers to walk is the road Thomas walked: from doubt to worship.
Going Deeper: 20:30–31 The Purpose of the Book

"Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (John 20:30–31). Right after Thomas's confession, John turns to the reader and states the purpose of the whole book. The introduction discussed the details: "believe" may mean "come to believe" or "go on believing," and Carson reads the sentence as "that you may believe that the Christ, the Son of God, is Jesus." Either way, by saying this right after Thomas, John is inviting us: Thomas believed because he saw; you can believe because of the testimony written in this book.

Meditation

Reflect: The risen Lord called Mary by name and came with his wounds to meet Thomas's doubt. What doubt can I bring to him as honestly as Thomas did? Jesus told Mary to stop clinging to him. Am I holding on to some past way of experiencing the Lord, when he wants to lead me into a new relationship? Thomas said, "My Lord and my God!" How can I confess him that way today, not only with my mouth but with my life?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第二十章以写书的目的作结，看起来全书已经完结了，第二十一章却像一段尾声。提比哩亚海边的捕鱼（1-14节）：整夜一无所获，耶稣叫他们把网撒在船的右边，网满了一百五十三条大鱼。恢复彼得（15-19节）：耶稣三次问「你爱我吗」。那门徒的结局（20-23节）：「与你何干？你跟从我吧！」结语（24-25节）：这门徒的见证是真的。

学者对这一章是原本就有，还是后来补上的，有不同看法。但现存所有的希腊文抄本都有第二十一章，它和全书的语言、主题都紧密相连：炭火、羊、「跟从我」、那门徒的见证。第二十章说复活的主对世界的意义（差遣、赦罪、多马的告白）；第二十一章说复活的主怎样对待一个失败的门徒。

深读 21:1-14 一百五十三条鱼

1. 回到加利利。 「西门彼得对他们说：『我打鱼去。』他们说：『我们也和你同去。』」（约21:3）有人认为彼得这是放弃了，回到旧行业；也有人认为他们只是在等候主的时候，做他们熟悉的事。经文没有评断。但「那一夜并没有打着什么」，直到主开口。

2. 似曾相识的一幕。 耶稣在岸上说：「你们把网撒在船的右边，就必得着。」（约21:6）路加福音5章记载，耶稣最初呼召彼得时，也有一次整夜徒劳、照着他的话撒网就网满了鱼的经历。复活的主用同样的方式，提醒彼得他最初是怎样被呼召的。

3. 「是主！」 那门徒先认出来：「是主！」彼得「就束上一件外衣，跳在海里」（约21:7）。两个门徒，两种性格：一个先看见，一个先行动。

4. 一百五十三条。 「那网满了大鱼，共一百五十三条；鱼虽这样多，网却没有破。」（约21:11）这个数字引起了很多解释。耶柔米说当时的希腊动物学家认为世上有一百五十三种鱼，象征福音要临到万族，但现存的古代资料并不支持这个说法；奥古斯丁注意到153是从1加到17的和，作了一些数字上的推想。最简单的解释是：这是一个目击者的细节，当时有人真的数了。约翰特别注明「网却没有破」，与路加福音约5:6网险些裂开形成对比，许多解经家在这里看见一个象征：无论有多少人被带进来，主的网都容得下。

5. 主预备的早饭。 「他们上了岸，就看见那里有炭火，上面有鱼，又有饼。」（约21:9）他们还没有把鱼拿上岸，耶稣已经预备好了。他又说：「把刚才打的鱼拿几条来。」（约21:10）主不需要他们的鱼，却邀请他们把劳力的成果带来。

深读 21:15-17「你爱我吗？」

1. 又是炭火。 「炭火」（anthrakia）这个字在新约里只出现两次：约18:18和约21:9。彼得在大祭司院子里的炭火旁三次不认主；现在，在另一堆炭火旁，耶稣三次问他「你爱我吗」。主没有回避彼得的失败，而是在相似的场景中，温柔地医治了他的伤痛。

2. 「约翰的儿子西门」。 耶稣三次都称他「约翰的儿子西门」，而不是「彼得」（磐石）。这是约1:42耶稣第一次见他时所用的称呼：「你是约翰的儿子西门，你要称为矶法。」耶稣好像带他回到起点，重新开始。

3. 「比这些更深吗？」 第一次的问题是：「你爱我比这些更深吗？」（约21:15）「这些」可以指其他门徒（你爱我比他们爱我更深吗？），也可以指船、网、鱼这些东西。许多解经家倾向第一种：彼得曾经说过「我愿意为你舍命」（约13:37），马可福音还记载他说「众人虽然跌倒，我总不能」（可14:29）。耶稣在问：你还认为自己比别人更爱我吗？彼得的回答没有再和别人比较，只说：「主啊，是的，你知道我爱你。」

4. 两个「爱」字。 前两次耶稣问「你爱我吗」用的是 agapaō，彼得三次回答用的都是 phileō；第三次耶稣也改用 phileō。有人认为这里有深意：agapaō 是更高的、舍己的爱，彼得不敢说他有，只敢说 phileō（朋友的爱），而耶稣第三次就「降到」彼得的层次来问他。但许多解经家（如卡森）认为这是约翰惯用的同义词交替：约翰在约3:35用 agapaō、在约5:20用 phileō，同样说「父爱子」；这段经文里的「喂养／牧养」、「小羊／羊」、「知道」（两个不同的希腊字）也都在交替。较稳妥的读法是：重点不在两个字的差别，而在问题被问了三次。

5. 「就忧愁」。 「彼得因为耶稣第三次对他说『你爱我吗』，就忧愁。」（约21:17）第三次的问题碰到了他最痛的地方：三次不认主。他的回答也从「你知道我爱你」变成了「主啊，你是无所不知的；你知道我爱你」。他不再倚靠自己的表白，而是投靠主的全知：你知道我所有的失败，你也知道我真的爱你。

6. 「你喂养我的羊」。 每一次彼得回答，耶稣就给他一个托付：「你喂养我的小羊」、「你牧养我的羊」、「你喂养我的羊」。不认主的人，被托付去牧养主的羊。好牧人（约10:11）把他的羊交给一个被恢复的罪人去照顾。彼得后来在彼得前书5:1-4劝勉众长老「牧养在你们中间神的群羊」，并称耶稣为「牧长」。注意耶稣说的是「我的羊」：羊始终属于主。

要点：耶稣恢复彼得，不是叫他忘记失败，而是在失败的地方重新问他「你爱我吗」，然后把羊交给他。服事的资格，不是从不失败，而是被主饶恕、并且爱他。
深读 21:18-19 伸出手来

1. 预言彼得的死。 「你年少的时候，自己束上带子，随意往来；但年老的时候，你要伸出手来，别人要把你束上，带你到不愿意去的地方。」（约21:18）约翰解释：「耶稣说这话是指着彼得要怎样死，荣耀神。」（约21:19）在古代文献中，「伸出手来」有时用来指钉十字架。革利免一书（约主后96年）已提到彼得殉道；后来特土良明说他在尼禄时期于罗马被钉十字架，优西比乌引俄利根说他是倒钉的。

2. 实现了他的话。 彼得曾说「我愿意为你舍命」（约13:37），那时他做不到。现在耶稣告诉他：你将来真的会为我舍命，而且你的死要「荣耀神」，这正是约翰福音对耶稣自己的死的描写（约12:23；约13:31）；「要怎样死」这个说法，也正是约12:33、约18:32说耶稣自己的死所用的话。

3. 「你跟从我吧！」 这是耶稣对彼得最早的呼召（可1:17），也是他最后的命令；它也成就了约13:36的应许：「后来却要跟我去」。从起点到终点，门徒的道路就是「跟从我」这三个字。

深读 21:20-25「与你何干？你跟从我吧！」

1. 比较的试探。 彼得转过来，看见那门徒跟着，就问：「主啊，这人将来如何？」（约21:21）刚刚被恢复，他就开始和别人比较。

2. 耶稣的回答。 「我若要他等到我来的时候，与你何干？你跟从我吧！」（约21:22）希腊文在最后一句加了一个强调的「你」（sy）：「你，跟从我！」每个门徒有各自的道路，彼得走向殉道，那门徒也许活到很老。主对每个人的安排不同，我们的责任不是比较，而是跟从。

3. 更正一个谣言。 「于是这话传在弟兄中间，说那门徒不死。其实，耶稣不是说他不死。」（约21:23）这节经文显示，约翰写作的时候，早期教会中流传着那门徒会活到主再来的说法。约翰更正它：耶稣只是说「若我要他等……」。许多学者认为，这暗示那门徒年纪很大，或者已经去世，所以需要澄清。

4. 见证是真的。 「为这些事作见证，并且记载这些事的就是这门徒；我们也知道他的见证是真的。」（约21:24）「我们」可能是那门徒所在的教会群体，为他的见证作保证。全书以见证开始（约1:7，施洗约翰「为光作见证」），也以见证结束。

5. 世界也容不下。 「耶稣所行的事还有许多，若是一一地都写出来，我想，所写的书就是世界也容不下了。」（约21:25）约翰福音以宇宙的尺度开始：「太初有道」；也以宇宙的尺度结束：这位道成肉身的主所做的，全世界的书都写不完。我们读完的这二十一章，只是他的一小部分，却足以叫我们信，并因信得生命。

默想

默想： 彼得在一堆炭火旁失败，又在另一堆炭火旁被恢复。我有没有一个「炭火」的地方，一个我失败、一直不敢再去面对的地方？主今天可能正在那里，问我「你爱我吗」。我是否常常像彼得一样，问「这人将来如何？」耶稣对我说：「与你何干？你跟从我吧！」读完约翰福音，我要怎样回应这位「太初有道」、又为我舍命复活的主？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 20 ended with the book's statement of purpose, as if the Gospel were finished, but chapter 21 follows like an epilogue. Fishing by the Sea of Tiberias (vv. 1–14): after a night of catching nothing, Jesus tells them to cast the net on the right side of the boat, and it fills with 153 large fish. Peter restored (vv. 15–19): Jesus asks three times, "Do you love me?" What about the other disciple? (vv. 20–23): "What is that to you? You follow me!" The conclusion (vv. 24–25): this disciple's testimony is true.

Scholars differ on whether this chapter was part of the original book or added later. But every surviving Greek manuscript includes chapter 21, and it is closely tied to the language and themes of the whole Gospel: the charcoal fire, the sheep, "follow me," the beloved disciple's witness. Chapter 20 shows what the risen Lord means for the world (sending, forgiveness, Thomas's confession); chapter 21 shows how the risen Lord treats a disciple who failed.

Going Deeper: 21:1–14 One Hundred Fifty-Three Fish

1. Back in Galilee. "Simon Peter said to them, 'I am going fishing.' They said to him, 'We will go with you'" (John 21:3). Some think Peter was giving up and going back to his old trade; others think they were simply doing what they knew while waiting for the Lord. The text doesn't judge. But "that night they caught nothing," until the Lord spoke.

2. A familiar scene. From the shore Jesus says, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some" (John 21:6). Luke 5 records that when Jesus first called Peter, there was also a fruitless night followed by a net filled with fish at his word. The risen Lord does the same thing again, reminding Peter how he was first called.

3. "It is the Lord!" The beloved disciple recognizes him first: "It is the Lord!" Peter "put on his outer garment... and threw himself into the sea" (John 21:7). Two disciples, two temperaments: one sees first, one acts first.

4. One hundred fifty-three. "Full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn" (John 21:11). The number has drawn many interpretations. Jerome claimed Greek zoologists counted 153 kinds of fish, symbolizing the gospel reaching every people, but the surviving ancient sources don't support this. Augustine noted that 153 is the sum of the numbers 1 to 17 and built speculations on it. The simplest explanation is that it's an eyewitness detail: someone actually counted. John notes that "the net was not torn," in contrast to Luke 5:6, where the nets were breaking, and many interpreters see a symbol here: however many are brought in, the Lord's net holds.

5. Breakfast the Lord prepared. "When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread" (John 21:9). Before they brought any of their catch ashore, Jesus had breakfast ready. Then he says, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught" (John 21:10). The Lord doesn't need their fish, but he invites them to bring the fruit of their labor.

Going Deeper: 21:15–17 "Do you love me?"

1. Another charcoal fire. "Charcoal fire" (anthrakia) appears only twice in the New Testament: John 18:18 and John 21:9. Beside the charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard Peter denied the Lord three times; now, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus asks him three times, "Do you love me?" The Lord doesn't avoid Peter's failure; in a similar setting he gently heals it.

2. "Simon, son of John." All three times Jesus calls him "Simon, son of John," not "Peter" (the rock). It's what Jesus called him at their first meeting: "So you are Simon the son of John? You shall be called Cephas" (John 1:42). It's as if Jesus takes him back to the beginning to start again.

3. "More than these?" The first question is, "do you love me more than these?" (John 21:15). "These" could mean the other disciples (do you love me more than they do?) or the boat, nets and fish. Many interpreters favor the first: Peter had said, "I will lay down my life for you" (John 13:37), and Mark records him saying, "Even though they all fall away, I will not" (Mark 14:29). Jesus is asking: do you still think you love me more than the others? Peter's answer makes no comparison now: "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you."

4. Two words for "love." The first two times Jesus asks "do you love me," he uses agapaō; Peter answers all three times with phileō; the third time Jesus also switches to phileō. Some see deep meaning here: agapaō is the higher, self-giving love that Peter dares not claim, so he says only phileō (the love of friends), and the third time Jesus comes down to Peter's level. But many interpreters (Carson among them) see John's habit of alternating synonyms: John uses agapaō in John 3:35 and phileō in John 5:20 to say the same thing, "the Father loves the Son," and this passage also alternates "feed/tend," "lambs/sheep" and two Greek words for "know." The safer reading is that the point lies not in the difference between the two words but in the question being asked three times.

5. "Peter was grieved." "Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, 'Do you love me?'" (John 21:17). The third question touched his deepest wound: three denials. His answer changes from "you know that I love you" to "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." He no longer relies on his own declaration; he entrusts himself to the Lord's knowledge: you know all my failures, and you also know I truly love you.

6. "Feed my sheep." Each time Peter answers, Jesus gives him a charge: "Feed my lambs," "Tend my sheep," "Feed my sheep." The man who denied the Lord is entrusted with shepherding the Lord's sheep. The good shepherd (John 10:11) hands his flock to a restored sinner. Peter later urged the elders to "shepherd the flock of God that is among you" and called Jesus "the chief Shepherd" (1 Pet 5:1–4). Note that Jesus says "my sheep": the sheep always belong to the Lord.

The point: Jesus doesn't restore Peter by making him forget his failure but by asking, in the very place of failure, "Do you love me?" and then entrusting him with the sheep. The qualification for service isn't never failing; it is being forgiven by the Lord and loving him.
Going Deeper: 21:18–19 "You will stretch out your hands"

1. Peter's death foretold. "When you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go" (John 21:18). John explains: "This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God" (John 21:19). In ancient writings, "stretching out the hands" was sometimes used of crucifixion. 1 Clement (c. AD 96) already refers to Peter's martyrdom; Tertullian later states he was crucified at Rome under Nero, and Eusebius, citing Origen, says he was crucified head-down.

2. His words fulfilled. Peter once said, "I will lay down my life for you" (John 13:37), and at the time he couldn't. Now Jesus tells him that one day he truly will, and that his death will "glorify God," the very way John describes Jesus' own death (John 12:23; John 13:31), and "by what kind of death" repeats the wording used of Jesus' own death in John 12:33 and John 18:32.

3. "Follow me." This was Jesus' first call to Peter (Mark 1:17), and it is his last command; it also fulfills the promise of John 13:36: "you will follow afterward." From beginning to end, the disciple's road is these two words.

Going Deeper: 21:20–25 "What is that to you? You follow me!"

1. The temptation to compare. Peter turns, sees the beloved disciple following and asks, "Lord, what about this man?" (John 21:21). Just restored, he starts comparing himself with someone else.

2. Jesus' answer. "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!" (John 21:22). The Greek adds an emphatic "you" (sy): "You, follow me!" Each disciple has a road of their own. Peter's leads to martyrdom; the other disciple's perhaps to old age. The Lord's plan for each is different. Our task isn't to compare but to follow.

3. Correcting a rumor. "So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die" (John 21:23). This verse shows that when John wrote, a rumor circulated in the early church that the beloved disciple would live until the Lord returned. John corrects it: Jesus only said "if it is my will that he remain..." Many scholars think this suggests the disciple was very old, or had already died, so the rumor needed clearing up.

4. The testimony is true. "This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true" (John 21:24). "We" may be the church community around the beloved disciple, vouching for his testimony. The book begins with witness (John 1:7, John the Baptist "came as a witness, to bear witness about the light") and ends with witness.

5. The world could not contain them. "Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written" (John 21:25). John's Gospel began on a cosmic scale, "In the beginning was the Word," and ends on one: all the books in the world could not record everything this incarnate Lord has done. The twenty-one chapters we've read are only a small part of it, yet enough for us to believe and, believing, to have life.

Meditation

Reflect: Peter failed beside one charcoal fire and was restored beside another. Do I have a "charcoal fire," a place where I failed and have never dared to face again? The Lord may be there today, asking, "Do you love me?" Am I often like Peter, asking "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus says to me, "What is that to you? You follow me!" Having read John's Gospel, how will I respond to the Lord who was in the beginning and who died and rose for me?

entries.verse_text: 但圣灵降临在你们身上，你们就必得着能力，并要在耶路撒冷、犹太全地，和撒马利亚，直到地极，作我的见证。」
entries.content:
这卷书在讲什么

使徒行传的书名是后来加上的，书中其实不只记使徒的事，主角也不是使徒。作者一开头就说：「我已经作了前书，论到耶稣开头一切所行所教训的。」（徒1:1）许多解经家认为，「开头」这两个字是全书的钥匙：路加福音记的是耶稣「开头」所做的；使徒行传记的，是复活升天的耶稣借着圣灵、借着他的教会继续做的。就算「开头」只是一种惯用说法，使徒行传本身也清楚显明，升天的耶稣仍在作工（徒2:33；徒9:5；徒16:7）。所以有人说，这卷书更合适的名字是「圣灵行传」，或「复活的主行传」。

作者与写作背景

使徒行传和路加福音是同一位作者写给同一个人的上下两卷。两卷都是写给「提阿非罗」（路1:3；徒1:1），名字的意思是「蒙神爱的」或「神的朋友」；路加福音称他「大人」，他很可能是一位有身份、资助这部著作的人。早期教会一致认为作者是路加，就是保罗所说的「所亲爱的医生路加」（西4:14）和同工（门24；提后4:11）。书中有几段忽然从「他们」变成「我们」（徒16:10-17；徒20:5–21:18；徒27:1–28:16），最自然的解释是：作者在这些时候亲身同行。

路加在福音书开头说，他「从起头都详细考察了」，「要按着次序」写，「使你知道所学之道都是确实的」（路1:3-4）。他是一位细心的史家：书中提到的官职、地名、头衔，许多都已被考古和古代文献证实。

成书年代有两种主要看法。一种认为在主后62年左右：全书在保罗于罗马软禁两年时结束（徒28:30），没有提到保罗受审的结果、尼禄对基督徒的大逼迫（64年）或圣殿被毁（70年）。另一种认为在主后70至80年代。两种看法在福音派学者中都有人支持。

钥匙经文：1:8

1. 一节经文就是全书的目录。 「但圣灵降临在你们身上，你们就必得着能力，并要在耶路撒冷、犹太全地，和撒马利亚，直到地极，作我的见证。」福音的路线图就在这里： - 耶路撒冷（1–7章）：圣灵降临，教会诞生，司提反殉道。 - 犹太全地和撒玛利亚（8–12章）：逼迫使信徒分散，腓利到撒玛利亚，扫罗归主，彼得到外邦人哥尼流家。 - 直到地极（13–28章）：保罗三次宣教旅程，最后被押解到帝国的中心罗马。

2. 能力从哪里来。 门徒不是靠自己的勇气或口才出去的。「圣灵降临在你们身上，你们就必得着能力。」这卷书提到圣灵的次数，远多于新约其他书卷。每一次突破，无论是福音传到撒玛利亚人，还是传到外邦人，都是圣灵带领的。

3. 「作我的见证」。 门徒的任务不是推广一套理念，而是为一个人作见证：复活的耶稣。「见证」这个词贯穿全书（徒1:22；徒2:32；徒3:15；徒10:39-41；徒22:15；徒26:16）。

怎样读这卷书

1. 留意「道兴旺」的进展报告。 路加在书中几次停下来作总结，像路标一样标出福音的进展：「神的道兴旺起来」（徒6:7），「教会……都得平安，被建立」（徒9:31），「神的道日见兴旺，越发广传」（徒12:24），「众教会信心越发坚固，人数天天加增」（徒16:5），「主的道大大兴旺，而且得胜」（徒19:20）。最后一节以保罗在罗马「放胆传讲神国的道……并没有人禁止」作结（徒28:31）。「没有人禁止」在原文只是一个词（akōlytōs），也正是全书的最后一个词。保罗被锁着，神的道却没有被捆绑。

2. 叙事与教导的分别。 使徒行传大部分是叙事：记载当时发生了什么。路加记下的事，并不都是要今天的教会照着做的。例如，门徒用摇签选出马提亚（徒1:26），初期教会凡物公用（徒2:44），圣灵降临的方式在不同场合各不相同（2章；8章；10章；19章）。读的时候要问：路加记这件事，是要我们效法，还是要我们看见神在救恩历史中独特的一步？最可靠的方法，是把叙事和新约书信中清楚的教导一起读。

3. 留意讲道。 书中的讲道（彼得、司提反、保罗）约占全书的三分之一。这些讲道一再回到同一个核心：耶稣被钉、神叫他复活、旧约在他身上应验、人要悔改信他。读这些讲道，就是在学习使徒怎样传福音。

4. 一个未完的结尾。 使徒行传没有交代保罗最后的结局。这也许是有意的：福音的故事还没有结束。复活的主还在写这个故事，而且他把每一个世代的教会，连同今天的我们，都写进去了。

默想

默想： 使徒行传说，耶稣「开头」所行的，复活以后借着圣灵继续在做。我是把耶稣的工作看成已经过去的历史，还是相信他今天仍借着圣灵、借着他的教会在作工？那些带着福音出去的人，几十天前还都弃主逃走了；差他们出去的，是赦免了他们的主。我心里认定「不可能信主」的那个人是谁？拦着我的，是害怕、成见，还是忘了我自己也是这样蒙恩的？
entries.content_en:
What This Book Is About

The title "Acts of the Apostles" was added later. The book isn't only about the apostles, and they aren't its main character. The author opens, "In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach" (Acts 1:1). Many interpreters see "began" as the key to the whole book (and even if it is only an idiom, Acts plainly shows the ascended Jesus still acting: Acts 2:33; Acts 9:5; Acts 16:7). The Gospel of Luke recorded what Jesus began to do; Acts records what the risen, ascended Jesus continues to do through the Spirit and through his church. That's why some have said a better title would be "the Acts of the Holy Spirit," or "the Acts of the Risen Lord."

Author and Setting

Acts and the Gospel of Luke are two volumes by the same author to the same person. Both are addressed to "Theophilus" (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1), whose name means "loved by God" or "friend of God." Luke calls him "most excellent," so he was likely a patron who sponsored the work. The early church agreed that the author was Luke, "the beloved physician" (Col 4:14) and Paul's fellow worker (Philem 24; 2 Tim 4:11). In several passages the narrative suddenly switches from "they" to "we" (Acts 16:10–17; Acts 20:5–21:18; Acts 27:1–28:16); the most natural explanation is that the author was traveling with Paul at those times.

At the start of his Gospel, Luke says he has "followed all things closely," to write "an orderly account... that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught" (Luke 1:3–4). He is a careful historian: many of the officials, places and titles he mentions have been confirmed by archaeology and ancient sources.

There are two main views on the date. One places it around AD 62: the book ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30) and says nothing of the outcome of his trial, Nero's persecution of Christians (64) or the destruction of the temple (70). The other places it in the 70s or 80s. Both views have evangelical support.

The Key Verse: 1:8

1. One verse is the book's table of contents. "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." The gospel's route map is here: - Jerusalem (chs. 1–7): the Spirit comes, the church is born, Stephen is martyred. - All Judea and Samaria (chs. 8–12): persecution scatters the believers, Philip goes to Samaria, Saul is converted, Peter goes to the Gentile Cornelius. - The end of the earth (chs. 13–28): Paul's three missionary journeys, and finally his transfer under guard to Rome, the heart of the empire.

2. Where the power comes from. The disciples didn't go out on their own courage or eloquence. "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you." Acts mentions the Spirit far more often than any other New Testament book, and every breakthrough, as the gospel reaches Samaritans and then Gentiles, is led by the Spirit.

3. "My witnesses." The disciples' task isn't to promote an idea but to bear witness to a person: the risen Jesus. "Witness" runs through the whole book (Acts 1:22; Acts 2:32; Acts 3:15; Acts 10:39–41; Acts 22:15; Acts 26:16).

How to Read This Book

1. Watch for the progress reports. Several times Luke pauses to sum up, like signposts marking the gospel's advance: "the word of God continued to increase" (Acts 6:7); "the church... had peace and was being built up" (Acts 9:31); "the word of God increased and multiplied" (Acts 12:24); "the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily" (Acts 16:5); "the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily" (Acts 19:20). The book closes with Paul in Rome "proclaiming the kingdom of God... with all boldness and without hindrance" (Acts 28:31). "Without hindrance" is the very last word of the book in Greek. Paul is in chains, but the word of God is not bound.

2. The difference between narrative and teaching. Most of Acts is narrative: a record of what happened. Not everything it records is meant for the church to repeat today. For example, the disciples chose Matthias by casting lots (Acts 1:26), the early church held everything in common (Acts 2:44), and the way the Spirit came differed from one occasion to another (chs. 2, 8, 10, 19). As you read, ask: is Luke recording this for us to imitate, or to show a unique step in God's plan of salvation? The safest approach is to read the narrative alongside the clear teaching of the New Testament letters.

3. Watch the sermons. The speeches in Acts (Peter's, Stephen's, Paul's) make up about a third of the book. They return again and again to the same core: Jesus was crucified, God raised him, the Old Testament is fulfilled in him, and people must repent and believe in him. Reading these sermons is learning how the apostles preached the gospel.

4. An unfinished ending. Acts doesn't tell us how Paul's story finally ends. That may be deliberate: the gospel story isn't over. The risen Lord is still writing this story, and he has written the church of every generation, including us, into it.

Meditation

Reflect: Acts says that what Jesus "began" to do, he continues to do after his resurrection through the Spirit. Do I see Jesus' work as past history, or do I believe he is still at work today through the Spirit and through his church? The people who carried the gospel out had, a few weeks earlier, all deserted Jesus; the Lord who sent them was the Lord who had forgiven them. Who is the person I've quietly decided will never believe? What holds me back: fear, prejudice, or forgetting that I too was reached by grace?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第一章是一座桥，连接路加福音的结尾和教会的开始。序言（1-5节）：复活的耶稣四十天向使徒显现，吩咐他们等候父的应许。最后的问题与托付（6-8节）：「主啊，你复兴以色列国就在这时候吗？」升天（9-11节）：一朵云彩把他接去，两个穿白衣的人说他「还要怎样来」。楼房里的祷告（12-14节）。补选马提亚（15-26节）：十二使徒的数目恢复。

这一章里，门徒什么大事都还没有做。他们在等候、在祷告。教会的历史，不是从行动开始，而是从等候神的应许开始。

深读 1:1-5「耶稣开头一切所行所教训的」

1. 「开头」。 「提阿非罗啊，我已经作了前书，论到耶稣开头一切所行所教训的。」（徒1:1）路加没有说「耶稣一切所行所教训的」，而是「开头」所行所教训的。许多解经家这样理解：耶稣的工作没有在升天时结束，使徒行传要记的，就是他继续在做的事。

2. 四十天。 「他受害之后，用许多的凭据将自己活活地显给使徒看，四十天之久向他们显现，讲说神国的事。」（徒1:3）「许多的凭据」这几个字，显出路加是一位重视证据的作者（路1:1-4）。四十天也让人想起以色列在旷野四十年、耶稣在旷野受试探四十天：一段预备的时间。

3. 「受圣灵的洗」。 「约翰是用水施洗，但不多几日，你们要受圣灵的洗。」（徒1:5）施洗约翰在路加福音徒3:16早就预言：「他要用圣灵与火给你们施洗。」现在耶稣说，这应许「不多几日」就要成就。第二章的五旬节，就是这个应许的实现。

深读 1:6-8「你复兴以色列国就在这时候吗？」

1. 门徒的问题。 「主啊，你复兴以色列国就在这时候吗？」（徒1:6）听了四十天关于「神国」的教导，门徒想的仍是以色列国的复兴。这个问题不全是错的：旧约先知确实应许神要复兴以色列（如结37章；摩9:11-15）。问题在于：他们关心的是时间（「就在这时候吗？」），眼光也只局限于以色列。

2. 耶稣的回答。 「父凭着自己的权柄所定的时候、日期，不是你们可以知道的。」（徒1:7）耶稣没有说以色列的盼望是错的，而是把门徒的目光从「什么时候」转向「现在要做什么」。

3. 范围的扩大。 「但圣灵降临在你们身上，你们就必得着能力，并要在耶路撒冷、犹太全地，和撒马利亚，直到地极，作我的见证。」（徒1:8）门徒问的是以色列，耶稣的回答是「直到地极」。以赛亚书49:6说，神的仆人不只要复兴雅各众支派，还要「作外邦人的光，叫你施行我的救恩，直到地极」。神复兴他子民的方式，是把福音带到万国。保罗后来在安提阿就引用了这节以赛亚书（徒13:47）。

要点：门徒想知道时间表，耶稣给他们一个使命和一份能力。基督徒对末世的盼望，不是让我们猜日期，而是推动我们去作见证。
深读 1:9-11「他还要怎样来」

1. 云彩。 「他就被取上升，有一朵云彩把他接去，便看不见他了。」（徒1:9）在圣经里，云彩常是神同在的记号：旷野的云柱、会幕上的云、登山变像时的云（路9:34-35）。但以理书7:13更说，有一位「像人子的，驾着天云而来，被领到亘古常在者面前」，得着权柄、荣耀和国度。耶稣升天，就是这位人子被领到父面前、坐上宝座。

2. 升天的意义。 升天不只是离开，更是登基。使徒行传接下来一再说，他被高举在神的右边（徒2:33-36；徒5:31；徒7:55-56）。正因为他坐在宝座上，他才能把圣灵浇灌下来（徒2:33）。

3. 「为什么站着望天呢？」 两个穿白衣的人说：「加利利人哪，你们为什么站着望天呢？这离开你们被接升天的耶稣，你们见他怎样往天上去，他还要怎样来。」（徒1:11）这句话有安慰，也有提醒：安慰是，同一位耶稣，会以同样可见的方式再来；提醒是，不要只站着望天，回到耶路撒冷去，等候圣灵，然后去作见证。路加在福音书结尾说，门徒「大大地欢喜，回耶路撒冷去」（路24:52）。主离开了，他们反而欢喜，因为他们明白：他不是走了，而是登基了。

深读 1:12-14「同心合意地恒切祷告」

1. 楼房里的人。 十一位使徒，「同着几个妇人和耶稣的母亲马利亚，并耶稣的弟兄，都同心合意地恒切祷告」（徒1:14）。路加特别提到妇女，这与他福音书一贯的关注一致。耶稣的弟兄们也在其中。约翰福音徒7:5说他们还不信他，如今他们却和众人一同祷告。复活改变了他们（复活的主曾向雅各显现，林前15:7）。

2. 「同心合意」。 这个词（homothymadon）在使徒行传里一再出现（徒2:46；徒4:24；徒5:12），在这里形容初期教会的合一。他们等候的方式，是一起祷告。

3. 等候不是消极的。 耶稣叫他们等候，他们就祷告。等候神的应许，不是什么都不做，而是在祷告中谦卑、敞开地预备领受。

深读 1:15-26 补选马提亚

1. 为什么要补足十二个？ 耶稣拣选十二个使徒，对应以色列的十二支派（路22:30）。犹大的位置空了，彼得说必须补足（徒1:21-22）。在圣灵降临、福音传给以色列之前，这个代表新以色列的核心群体要先完整。

2. 犹大的死。 路加说犹大「身子仆倒，肚腹崩裂」（徒1:18），马太福音说他「出去吊死了」（太27:5）。马太说祭司长用那钱买了一块田（太27:7），路加说「这人用他作恶的工价买了一块田」。解经家常见的解释是：两处记的是同一件事的不同方面，祭司长用犹大的钱买了田，所以可以说是犹大买的；他吊死以后，身体坠落破裂。犹大跟随耶稣三年，亲眼见过神迹，最后却出卖了主。这是严肃的警告：靠近耶稣不等于属于耶稣。

3. 使徒的资格。 被选的人必须是「从约翰施洗起，直到主离开我们被接上升的日子为止」一直与使徒同在的人，并且要「与我们同作耶稣复活的见证」（徒1:21-22）。使徒的核心身份，是复活的亲眼见证人。这也说明为什么使徒的职分是独特、不能延续的：之后的世代，没有人能再满足这个条件。后来蒙召的保罗，也是亲眼见过复活之主的（林前9:1；林前15:8），他说主「末了也显给我看」。

4. 摇签。 「于是众人为他们摇签，摇出马提亚来。」（徒1:26）这是圣经里最后一次记载用摇签来寻求神的旨意（参箴16:33「签放在怀里，定事由耶和华」）。彼得也是先根据圣经（徒1:20引诗69:25；诗109:8）说明必须补选，才摇签的。五旬节以后，使徒行传里再没有出现摇签：圣灵降临以后，教会在祷告、圣经和众人的商议中寻求神的引导（如徒15:28「圣灵和我们定意」）。这是叙事记载，不是要今天的教会照着做的方法。

5. 两个辜负主的人。 站起来讲论犹大的，正是不久前三次不认主的彼得。两个人都辜负了主；一个在绝望中「往自己的地方去了」，一个被复活的主寻回、重新托付（参路22:32）。分别不在于谁的罪比较小，而在于谁回到了主面前。

默想

默想： 门徒问「什么时候」，耶稣没有给他们时间表，却应许把他自己的灵赐给他们。我在为什么事焦急地问「什么时候」？如果那位坐在宝座上的主已经应许与我同在，我能不能在等候中先享受他，而不是只等那件事？像楼房里的门徒那样，我是在焦躁中等候，还是在祷告中等候他的应许？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 1 is a bridge between the end of Luke's Gospel and the beginning of the church. The prologue (vv. 1–5): for forty days the risen Jesus appears to the apostles and tells them to wait for the Father's promise. The last question and the charge (vv. 6–8): "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" The ascension (vv. 9–11): a cloud takes him, and two men in white say he "will come in the same way." Prayer in the upper room (vv. 12–14). Matthias chosen (vv. 15–26): the number of the Twelve is restored.

In this chapter the disciples haven't yet done anything great. They are waiting and praying. The church's history begins not with action but with waiting for God's promise.

Going Deeper: 1:1–5 "All that Jesus began to do and teach"

1. "Began." "In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach" (Acts 1:1). Luke doesn't say "all that Jesus did and taught" but all he began to do and teach. Many interpreters take the implication to be that Jesus' work didn't end at the ascension, and Acts records what he goes on doing.

2. Forty days. "He presented himself alive after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God" (Acts 1:3). "Many proofs": Luke is an author who cares about evidence (Luke 1:1–4). Forty days also recalls Israel's forty years in the wilderness and Jesus' forty days of temptation, a time of preparation.

3. "Baptized with the Holy Spirit." "For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now" (Acts 1:5). John the Baptist had foretold it in Luke 3:16: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." Now Jesus says the promise will be fulfilled "not many days from now." Pentecost in chapter 2 is its fulfillment.

Going Deeper: 1:6–8 "Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?"

1. The disciples' question. "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). After forty days of teaching about "the kingdom of God," the disciples are still thinking of Israel's restoration. The question isn't entirely wrong: the prophets did promise that God would restore Israel (e.g., Ezek 37; Amos 9:11–15). The problem lies in their focus on timing ("at this time?") and scope (Israel only).

2. Jesus' answer. "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority" (Acts 1:7). Jesus doesn't say Israel's hope is mistaken; he turns the disciples' eyes from "when?" to "what now?"

3. A wider scope. "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8). The disciples asked about Israel; Jesus answers, "to the end of the earth." Isaiah 49:6 says God's servant will not only raise up the tribes of Jacob but be "a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth." God restores his people by carrying the gospel to the nations. Paul later quotes this very verse of Isaiah at Antioch (Acts 13:47).

The point: The disciples wanted a timetable; Jesus gave them a mission and the power for it. Christian hope about the last things isn't meant to set us guessing dates but to send us out as witnesses.
Going Deeper: 1:9–11 "He will come in the same way"

1. The cloud. "He was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight" (Acts 1:9). In Scripture a cloud is often a sign of God's presence: the pillar of cloud in the wilderness, the cloud over the tabernacle, the cloud at the transfiguration (Luke 9:34–35). Daniel 7:13 describes "one like a son of man" coming "with the clouds of heaven" and presented before the Ancient of Days, to receive dominion, glory and a kingdom. Jesus' ascension is this Son of Man being brought before the Father and taking his throne.

2. What the ascension means. The ascension isn't only a departure; it is his enthronement. Acts repeatedly says he is exalted at the right hand of God (Acts 2:33–36; Acts 5:31; Acts 7:55–56). It is precisely because he sits on the throne that he can pour out the Spirit (Acts 2:33).

3. "Why do you stand looking into heaven?" The two men in white say, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11). These words bring comfort and a nudge. The comfort: the same Jesus will return in the same visible way. The nudge: don't just stand gazing at the sky; go back to Jerusalem, wait for the Spirit, then bear witness. Luke's Gospel ends by saying the disciples "returned to Jerusalem with great joy" (Luke 24:52). Their Lord had gone, yet they rejoiced, because they understood he hadn't simply left; he had been crowned.

Going Deeper: 1:12–14 "With one accord... devoting themselves to prayer"

1. Who was in the upper room. The eleven apostles, "with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers" (Acts 1:14). Luke mentions the women, consistent with his concern throughout his Gospel. Jesus' brothers are here too. In John 7:5 they didn't yet believe; now they are among those praying. The resurrection changed them (the risen Christ appeared to James, 1 Cor 15:7).

2. "With one accord." This word (homothymadon) recurs in Acts (Acts 2:46; Acts 4:24; Acts 5:12), here describing the unity of the early church. They waited by praying together.

3. Waiting isn't passive. Jesus told them to wait, so they prayed. Waiting for God's promise isn't doing nothing; it's putting yourself in a posture to receive.

Going Deeper: 1:15–26 Matthias Chosen

1. Why restore the Twelve? Jesus chose twelve apostles to correspond to Israel's twelve tribes (Luke 22:30). Judas's place was empty, and Peter says it must be filled (Acts 1:21–22). Before the Spirit comes and the gospel goes to Israel, this core group representing the new Israel needs to be complete.

2. Judas's death. Luke says that "falling headlong he burst open in the middle" (Acts 1:18); Matthew says he "went and hanged himself" (Matt 27:5). Matthew says the chief priests bought a field with the money (Matt 27:7); Luke says Judas "bought a field with the reward of his wickedness." A common explanation is that these are two sides of the same event: the chief priests bought the field with Judas's money, so it could be called his purchase, and after he hanged himself his body fell and burst open. Judas followed Jesus for three years and saw his miracles, yet in the end betrayed him. It is a solemn warning: being near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.

3. The qualification for an apostle. The one chosen had to be someone who had been with the apostles "beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us," and who would "become with us a witness to his resurrection" (Acts 1:21–22). The core of an apostle's identity was being an eyewitness of the resurrection. This also explains why the apostolic office was unique and couldn't continue: no later generation could meet that condition. Paul, called later, was likewise an eyewitness of the risen Lord (1 Cor 9:1; 1 Cor 15:8): "Last of all... he appeared also to me."

4. Casting lots. "And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias" (Acts 1:26). This is the last time Scripture records casting lots to seek God's will (cf. Prov 16:33, "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD"). Peter first grounded the need for a replacement in Scripture (Acts 1:20, quoting Ps 69:25; Ps 109:8), and only then were lots cast. After Pentecost, lots never appear again in Acts. Once the Spirit has come, the church seeks God's guidance through prayer, Scripture and shared deliberation (e.g., Acts 15:28, "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"). This is narrative, recording what happened, not a method for the church today.

5. Two men who failed their Lord. The one who stands up to speak of Judas is Peter, who had denied Jesus three times weeks before. Both men failed their Lord; one went in despair "to his own place," the other was sought out by the risen Christ and given his charge again (cf. Luke 22:32). The difference wasn't the size of their sin but whether they came back to him.

Meditation

Reflect: The disciples asked "when?" Jesus gave them no timetable, but promised them his own Spirit. What am I anxiously asking "when?" about? If the enthroned Lord has promised to be with me, can I enjoy him in the waiting, rather than only waiting for the thing? Like the disciples in the upper room, am I waiting anxiously, or waiting in prayer for his promise?
