entries.content:
本章脉络

第十三章是使徒行传的第二个起点。从这里开始，故事的中心从耶路撒冷转到安提阿，焦点从彼得转到保罗；福音也开始有计划地向「地极」推进。

本章有四段：安提阿的差遣（1-3节），圣灵在敬拜中说话，教会差出巴拿巴和扫罗；塞浦路斯（4-12节），行法术的以吕马瞎了眼，罗马方伯信了主；彼西底的安提阿（13-41节），保罗在会堂里的第一篇长篇讲道，以「称义」作为高峰；两种回应（42-52节），外邦人欢喜，犹太人嫉妒，使徒被赶出境外，门徒却「满心喜乐」。

深读 13:1-3 在敬拜中被差遣

1. 一个多元的领袖群体。 「在安提阿的教会中，有几位先知和教师，就是巴拿巴和称呼尼结的西面、古利奈人路求，与分封之王希律同养的马念，并扫罗。」（徒13:1）巴拿巴来自塞浦路斯；「尼结」是拉丁文「黑」的意思，西面可能来自非洲；路求来自北非的古利奈；马念是和分封之王希律安提帕一同长大的人（原文这个词也可指宫廷近臣）；扫罗是大数的法利赛人。安提阿教会的领袖，本身就是福音拆毁隔断之墙的见证。

2. 事奉主、禁食的时候。 「他们事奉主、禁食的时候，圣灵说：『要为我分派巴拿巴和扫罗，去做我召他们所做的工。』」（徒13:2）教会历史上第一次有计划的宣教差遣，不是从策略会议开始的，而是从敬拜和禁食中开始的。「事奉主」原文是 leitourgeō，常用来指圣殿里的敬拜事奉。

3. 「为我」分派。 圣灵说「要为我分派」：宣教士首先是属于神的，然后才是属于教会的。「我召他们」：呼召来自圣灵。可是圣灵把这个呼召交给教会去确认、去差遣：「于是禁食祷告，按手在他们头上，就打发他们去了。」（徒13:3）第4节说：「他们既被圣灵差遣。」差遣的，是圣灵，也是教会；两者不冲突。

4. 差出最好的。 安提阿教会差出的，不是闲着没事的人，而是他们最有恩赐的两位教师。神先把他最好的，就是他的独生子，赐给了我们；真正明白这福音的教会，也会甘心把最好的献出去。

要点：宣教不是教会的一项活动，而是圣灵的工作；教会在敬拜中聆听，又甘心把最好的人交给神。
深读 13:4-12 塞浦路斯：方伯与行法术的人

1. 先到会堂。 他们到了撒拉米，「就在犹太人各会堂里传讲神的道」（徒13:5）。这是保罗一贯的做法：先向犹太人，再向外邦人（参罗1:16）。

2. 方伯士求·保罗。 在帕弗，他们遇见罗马方伯士求·保罗，「是个通达人」，「要听神的道」（徒13:7）。罗马帝国的高官，愿意听两位犹太巡回传道人讲道。

3. 以吕马的敌挡。 行法术的巴·耶稣（又名以吕马）「敌挡使徒，要叫方伯不信真道」（徒13:8）。保罗「被圣灵充满，定睛看他」，说：「你这充满各样诡诈奸恶，魔鬼的儿子……你混乱主的正道还不止住吗？」（徒13:9-10）「巴·耶稣」意思是「耶稣（约书亚）的儿子」，保罗却称他为「魔鬼的儿子」。「混乱主的正道」原文是「把主笔直的道路弄弯」，呼应以赛亚书「在沙漠地修平我们神的道」（赛40:3）。

4. 暂且瞎眼。 「现在主的手加在你身上，你要瞎眼，暂且不见日光。」（徒13:11）保罗自己也曾在大马士革路上瞎眼三天，后来眼睛得开、归向主。以吕马的瞎眼是审判；但「暂且」二字，或许也给他留下了悔改的余地。

5. 「很希奇主的道」。 「方伯看见所做的事，很希奇主的道，就信了。」（徒13:12）路加说得很细：方伯看见的是神迹，希奇的却是「主的道」。神迹的作用，是叫人注意神的话。

6. 扫罗又名保罗。 「扫罗又名保罗。」（徒13:9）从这里开始，除了保罗自己讲述归主经历的地方（徒22:7，13；徒26:14），路加都称他为「保罗」。扫罗是他的希伯来名字，保罗是他的罗马名字。保罗开始向外邦人传福音，路加也就改用外邦人熟悉的这个名字。「巴拿巴和扫罗」也渐渐变成了「保罗和他的同人」（徒13:13）。

深读 13:13-41 保罗在会堂里的讲道

1. 约翰马可离开。 「约翰就离开他们，回耶路撒冷去。」（徒13:13）路加没有说原因。这件事后来在保罗和巴拿巴之间引起了一场严重的争执（徒15:37-39）。

2. 「若有什么劝勉众人的话」。 在彼西底的安提阿，管会堂的读完律法和先知书以后，请他们说话（徒13:15）。保罗「站起来，举手」（徒13:16），这是路加记下的第一篇保罗讲道。他的听众有两种人：「以色列人和一切敬畏神的人」，也就是犹太人和像哥尼流那样敬畏神的外邦人。

3. 从出埃及到大卫。 保罗先回顾以色列的历史：神拣选列祖，领他们出埃及，在旷野容忍他们，赐他们迦南地，兴起士师和扫罗王，然后「选立大卫作他们的王」（徒13:17-22）。他引用神的话：「我寻得耶西的儿子大卫，他是合我心意的人。」（徒13:22；参诗89:20；撒上13:14）

4. 从大卫到耶稣。 「从这人的后裔中，神已经照着所应许的，为以色列人立了一位救主，就是耶稣。」（徒13:23）整段历史都指向这一位。和司提反一样，保罗讲历史，是要讲基督；不同的是，司提反的重点是「你们弃绝了他」，保罗的重点是「神应验了应许」。

5. 不认识他，却应验了预言。 「耶路撒冷居住的人和他们的官长，因为不认识基督，也不明白每安息日所读众先知的书，就把基督定了死罪，正应了先知的预言。」（徒13:27）他们每个安息日都读先知书，却没有认出先知书所讲的那一位；而他们定他的罪，正好应验了他们所读的经文。

6. 三处经文证明复活。 保罗用三处经文讲耶稣的复活： - 「你是我的儿子，我今日生你」（徒13:33；诗2:7）。这里的「生」不是指耶稣的起源，他本是永远的神子；而是指神藉着复活，公开宣告并高举他为有能力的神子、受膏的王（参罗1:4「以大能显明是神的儿子」）。 - 「我必将所应许大卫那圣洁、可靠的恩典赐给你们」（徒13:34；赛55:3）。神给大卫的应许是永远的，只有一位永远活着的大卫子孙，才能使这应许「可靠」。 - 「你必不叫你的圣者见朽坏」（徒13:35；诗16:10）。在七十士译本里，「圣洁……的恩典」（ta hosia）和「你的圣者」（ton hosion sou）是同一个字，所以保罗把这两处经文放在一起读。保罗的论证和彼得在五旬节的论证一样（徒2:25-31）：大卫「已见朽坏」，「惟独神所复活的，他并未见朽坏」（徒13:36-37）。

7. 讲道的高峰：称义。 「所以，弟兄们，你们当晓得：赦罪的道是由这人传给你们的。你们靠摩西的律法，在一切不得称义的事上信靠这人，就都得称义了。」（徒13:38-39）整卷使徒行传，只有这里用到保罗书信的核心词「称义」（dikaioō）。和合本这一句不容易读，意思是：凡靠摩西的律法在一切事上都不能称义的，信靠这人就都得称义了。这不是说律法能使人在某些事上称义、耶稣补足其余的；而是说律法在任何事上都不能使人称义，耶稣却使信他的人在一切事上称义。这正是保罗在加拉太书和罗马书里要详细阐明的福音。

8. 警告。 保罗最后引用哈巴谷书：「你们这轻慢的人要观看，要惊奇，要灭亡；因为在你们的时候，我行一件事，虽有人告诉你们，你们总是不信。」（徒13:41；哈1:5）哈巴谷当年说的「一件事」，是神要兴起巴比伦来审判犹大；现在神行的「一件事」，是在耶稣里施行拯救。（保罗的引文跟随七十士译本「你们这轻慢的人」；希伯来文本作「你们要向列国中观看」。）轻慢这救恩，比当年轻慢审判的警告更危险。

要点：保罗讲以色列的整段历史，是为了讲一个人：大卫的子孙耶稣。他的死应验了经文，他的复活证明了神的应许；律法不能叫人称义，他却叫一切信靠他的人「都得称义了」。
深读 13:42-52 欢喜与嫉妒

1. 合城的人几乎都来了。 「到下安息日，合城的人几乎都来聚集，要听神的道。」（徒13:44）福音向所有人敞开，这消息一传开，几乎全城的人都来了。

2. 满心嫉妒。 「但犹太人看见人这样多，就满心嫉妒，硬驳保罗所说的话，并且毁谤。」（徒13:45）他们嫉妒的，或许不只是人数，更是这些外邦人不必先成为犹太人，就可以直接蒙神接纳。

3. 「断定自己不配得永生」。 「神的道先讲给你们原是应当的；只因你们弃绝这道，断定自己不配得永生，我们就转向外邦人去。」（徒13:46）路加强调的是他们自己的责任：他们弃绝了道，就是「断定自己不配得永生」。

4. 外邦人的光。 「因为主曾这样吩咐我们说：我已经立你作外邦人的光，叫你施行救恩，直到地极。」（徒13:47；赛49:6）以赛亚书这句话原是讲「耶和华的仆人」，耶稣就是那位仆人（参路2:32，圣殿里的老人西面称耶稣为「照亮外邦人的光」）。现在保罗和巴拿巴说，这是主「吩咐我们」的：他们跟随那位仆人，也一同承担仆人的使命。

5. 「凡预定得永生的人都信了」。 「外邦人听见这话，就欢喜了，赞美神的道；凡预定得永生的人都信了。」（徒13:48）把这节和第46节放在一起读，就看见圣经的两面：人弃绝福音，要为自己负责（46节）；人相信福音，是因为神的预定和恩典（48节）。神的拣选不叫人骄傲，因为信心本身就是恩典；也不叫人灰心，因为福音仍然向每一个人宣讲。

6. 跺下脚上的尘土。 他们被赶出境外，「二人对着众人跺下脚上的尘土，就往以哥念去了」（徒13:51）。这是照着耶稣的吩咐（路9:5），表示「我们已经尽了责任，后果由你们自己承担」。

7. 满心喜乐。 「门徒满心喜乐，又被圣灵充满。」（徒13:52）使徒被赶走了，留下来的初信者却满心喜乐。他们的喜乐不倚靠传道人在不在，而倚靠那位住在他们里面的圣灵。

要点：同一篇讲道，有人嫉妒，有人欢喜。弃绝福音的人，是自己断定自己不配；相信福音的人，却只能把功劳归给神的预定和恩典。
默想

默想： 圣灵在安提阿说话，不是在一场「求带领」的会议上，而是在教会「事奉主、禁食」的时候。他们不是把敬拜当作得到答案的手段，而是在寻求主自己；差遣正是在这样的敬拜中临到的。我来到神面前，是不是常常只为要一个答案：这份工作接不接，这段关系要不要继续？这一周，我能不能找一段时间，先不急着求什么，单单为他是谁而敬拜他，相信他会在他的时候说话？保罗说，律法在一切事上都不能叫人称义，凡信靠耶稣的，却「就都得称义了」。我心里有没有一件事，是我觉得这个「都」盖不过去的：一次堕胎、一段不能告人的关系、一句伤透家人的话？我也许已经认过很多次罪，心里却还觉得要再多做一点，才算真的被赦免。可是称义不是神慢慢消气，而是一次宣判：在基督里，「无罪」。今天我可以把那件事带到十字架前，不是为了说服他赦免我，而是相信他已经这样宣告了。最后，使徒被赶出城，初信的门徒却「满心喜乐，又被圣灵充满」。如果我所依靠的牧者、带我信主的弟兄姊妹离开了，我的喜乐还在吗？人会离开；那位住在我里面的圣灵却从来没有离开，他一直把我指向那位称我为义的主。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 13 is Acts' second starting point. From here the story's center moves from Jerusalem to Antioch, its focus from Peter to Paul, and the gospel begins a deliberate advance toward "the end of the earth."

The chapter has four parts: sending from Antioch (vv. 1–3), where the Spirit speaks in worship and the church sends out Barnabas and Saul; Cyprus (vv. 4–12), where the magician Elymas is blinded and a Roman proconsul believes; Pisidian Antioch (vv. 13–41), Paul's first long synagogue sermon, which peaks in "justification"; and two responses (vv. 42–52): Gentiles rejoice, Jews are jealous, the apostles are driven out, and the disciples are "filled with joy."

Going Deeper: 13:1–3 Sent Out in Worship

1. A diverse leadership. "Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a member of the court of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul" (Acts 13:1). Barnabas was from Cyprus; "Niger" is Latin for "black," and Simeon may have come from Africa; Lucius was from Cyrene in North Africa; Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas (the word can also mean a close member of his court); Saul was a Pharisee from Tarsus. The leadership of the Antioch church was itself a witness to the gospel breaking down dividing walls.

2. While they were worshiping and fasting. "While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them'" (Acts 13:2). The first planned missionary sending in church history didn't begin in a strategy meeting; it began in worship and fasting. "Worshiping" is leitourgeō, a word often used for the worship service of the temple.

3. Set apart "for me." The Spirit says "set apart for me": missionaries belong first to God, and only then to the church. "I have called them": the call comes from the Spirit. Yet the Spirit gives the church the task of confirming and sending: "Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off" (Acts 13:3). Verse 4 says they were "sent out by the Holy Spirit." The sending is the Spirit's and the church's; the two don't conflict.

4. Sending their best. The Antioch church didn't send people who had nothing else to do; it sent its two most gifted teachers. God first gave us his best, his only Son; a church that has understood that gospel will gladly give away its best.

The point: Mission isn't one of the church's programs; it is the Spirit's work. The church listens in worship and gladly hands its best people to God.
Going Deeper: 13:4–12 Cyprus: The Proconsul and the Magician

1. Synagogues first. At Salamis "they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews" (Acts 13:5). This was Paul's consistent pattern: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (cf. Rom 1:16).

2. The proconsul Sergius Paulus. At Paphos they met the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus, "a man of intelligence," who "sought to hear the word of God" (Acts 13:7). A high Roman official was willing to listen to two traveling Jewish preachers.

3. Elymas's opposition. The magician Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas, "opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith" (Acts 13:8). Paul, "filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, 'You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?'" (Acts 13:9–10). "Bar-Jesus" means "son of Jesus (Joshua)," but Paul calls him "son of the devil." "Making crooked the straight paths" echoes Isaiah's "make straight in the desert a highway for our God" (Isa 40:3).

4. Blind for a time. "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time" (Acts 13:11). Paul himself had been blinded for three days on the Damascus road before his eyes were opened. Elymas's blindness was judgment, but "for a time" may also leave room for repentance.

5. Astonished at the teaching. "Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord" (Acts 13:12). Luke is careful: the proconsul saw a miracle, but what astonished him was "the teaching of the Lord." Miracles serve to draw attention to God's word.

6. Saul, also called Paul. "But Saul, who was also called Paul" (Acts 13:9). From here on Luke calls him "Paul," except where Paul retells his conversion (Acts 22:7, 13; Acts 26:14). Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul his Roman name; as he begins taking the gospel into the Gentile world, Luke uses the name that world knew. "Barnabas and Saul" also gradually becomes "Paul and his companions" (Acts 13:13).

Going Deeper: 13:13–41 Paul's Synagogue Sermon

1. John Mark leaves. "And John left them and returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13). Luke gives no reason. Later this would cause a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39).

2. "Any word of exhortation." At Pisidian Antioch, after the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue rulers invited them to speak (Acts 13:15). Paul "stood up, and motioning with his hand" (Acts 13:16), began the first sermon of Paul's that Luke records for us. He addressed two groups: "Men of Israel and you who fear God," that is, Jews and God-fearing Gentiles like Cornelius.

3. From the exodus to David. Paul first reviews Israel's history: God chose the fathers, led them out of Egypt, put up with them in the wilderness, gave them Canaan, raised up judges and King Saul, and then "raised up David to be their king" (Acts 13:17–22). He quotes God's word: "I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart" (Acts 13:22; cf. Ps 89:20; 1 Sam 13:14).

4. From David to Jesus. "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised" (Acts 13:23). The whole history points to this one person. Like Stephen, Paul tells history to tell of Christ; but where Stephen's emphasis was "you rejected him," Paul's is "God has kept his promise."

5. Not recognizing him, yet fulfilling the prophets. "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him" (Acts 13:27). They read the prophets every Sabbath but didn't recognize the one the prophets spoke of; and by condemning him they fulfilled the very Scriptures they read.

6. Three Scriptures for the resurrection. Paul uses three texts to speak of Jesus' resurrection: - "You are my Son, today I have begotten you" (Acts 13:33; Ps 2:7). "Begotten" here doesn't refer to Jesus' origin, for he is the eternal Son. It refers to God publicly declaring and enthroning him, through the resurrection, as the messianic King, "the Son of God in power" (Rom 1:4). - "I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David" (Acts 13:34; Isa 55:3). God's promise to David was everlasting; only a Son of David who lives forever can make those blessings "sure." - "You will not let your Holy One see corruption" (Acts 13:35; Ps 16:10). In the Septuagint, "holy [blessings]" (ta hosia) and "your Holy One" (ton hosion sou) share one word, which is why Paul reads the two texts together. Paul's argument is the same as Peter's at Pentecost (Acts 2:25–31): David "saw corruption," "but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (Acts 13:36–37).

7. The sermon's peak: justification. "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses" (Acts 13:38–39). "Freed" here translates dikaioō, "justify," the key word of Paul's letters, and the only place it appears in Acts. Luke is not saying the law justifies in some matters and Jesus completes the rest; the law could justify from nothing, and Jesus justifies the believer from everything. This is the gospel Paul will unfold in detail in Galatians and Romans.

8. A warning. Paul closes with Habakkuk: "Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you" (Acts 13:41; Hab 1:5). The "work" in Habakkuk's day was God raising up Babylon to judge Judah (Paul's wording, "you scoffers," follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads "Look among the nations"); the "work" God is doing now is salvation in Jesus. Scorning this salvation is more dangerous than scorning that warning of judgment.

The point: Paul tells Israel's whole history to speak of one person: Jesus, the Son of David. His death fulfilled the Scriptures, his resurrection proved God's promises, and for everyone who believes in him he has done what the law could not: they are justified.
Going Deeper: 13:42–52 Joy and Jealousy

1. Almost the whole city came. "The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord" (Acts 13:44). The news that the gospel was open to all drew the entire city.

2. Filled with jealousy. "But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him" (Acts 13:45). What provoked their jealousy may not have been only the crowd's size but the fact that these Gentiles could be accepted by God without first becoming Jews.

3. "Judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life." "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles" (Acts 13:46). Luke puts the weight on their own responsibility: by thrusting the word aside, they "judge themselves unworthy of eternal life."

4. A light for the Gentiles. "For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth'" (Acts 13:47; Isa 49:6). In Isaiah these words are spoken of "the Servant of the LORD," and Jesus is that Servant (cf. Luke 2:32, where Simeon calls Jesus "a light for revelation to the Gentiles"). Now Paul and Barnabas say the Lord has "commanded us": following the Servant, they share in the Servant's mission.

5. "As many as were appointed to eternal life believed." "And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed" (Acts 13:48). Read alongside verse 46, this shows both sides of Scripture: those who reject the gospel are responsible for doing so (v. 46); those who believe it do so because of God's appointment and grace (v. 48). God's choosing doesn't make anyone proud, since faith itself is grace; nor does it make anyone despair, since the gospel is still proclaimed to everyone.

6. Shaking off the dust. Driven out of the district, "they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium" (Acts 13:51). This followed Jesus' instruction (Luke 9:5) and meant, "We have done our duty; you bear the consequences."

7. Filled with joy. "And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit" (Acts 13:52). The apostles were driven away, yet the new believers left behind were full of joy. Their joy didn't depend on whether the preachers stayed but on the Spirit who lived in them.

The point: The same sermon drew jealousy from some and joy from others. Those who reject the gospel judge themselves unworthy; those who believe can credit only God's appointment and grace.
Meditation

Reflect: The Spirit spoke at Antioch not at a meeting called to seek guidance, but while the church was "worshiping the Lord and fasting." They weren't using worship to get an answer; they were seeking the Lord himself, and the sending came in the middle of that worship. When I come to God, is it often only to get an answer: should I take this job, should this relationship go on? This week, could I set aside some time to ask for nothing at first, and simply worship him for who he is, trusting him to speak in his time? Paul said that everyone who believes in Jesus is freed from everything the law could never free them from. Is there one thing in my heart that I feel this "everything" can't cover: an abortion, a relationship I've never told anyone about, words that wounded my family? I may have confessed it many times and still feel I must do a little more before I'm really forgiven. But justification isn't God slowly cooling down; it is a verdict, once for all: in Christ, "not guilty." Today I can bring that thing to the cross, not to persuade him to forgive me, but to believe that he has already said so. Finally, the apostles were driven out of town, yet the new disciples were "filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit." If the pastor I rely on, or the believers who led me to faith, were to leave, would my joy still be there? People leave; the Spirit who lives in me never has, and he keeps pointing me to the Lord who declared me righteous.

entries.verse_text: 「诸君，为什么做这事呢？我们也是人，性情和你们一样。我们传福音给你们，是叫你们离弃这些虚妄，归向那创造天、地、海，和其中万物的永生神。坚固门徒的心，劝他们恒守所信的道；又说：「我们进入神的国，必须经历许多艰难。」
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十四章完成了第一次宣教旅程。以哥念（1-7节）：许多人信了，城里却分了党，使徒被迫逃走。路司得（8-20节）：一个生来瘸腿的人得医治，众人把巴拿巴和保罗当作希腊的神明，要向他们献祭；没过多久，同一群人却用石头打保罗，以为他死了。回程（21-28节）：他们回到刚刚逼迫过他们的城，坚固门徒，选立长老，然后回到差派他们的安提阿，述说「神怎样为外邦人开了信道的门」。

这一章有一个强烈的对比：人一会儿要拜他们，一会儿要杀他们。一个人（尤其是传道人）若把信心建立在人的反应上，很快就会垮掉；保罗和巴拿巴所倚靠的，是那位「证明他的恩道」的主（徒14:3）。

深读 14:1-7 以哥念：恩道与分裂

1. 犹太人和希腊人信的很多。 「二人在以哥念同进犹太人的会堂，在那里讲的，叫犹太人和希腊人信的很多。」（徒14:1）福音一传开，就同时得着犹太人和外邦人。

2. 他的恩道。 「二人在那里住了多日，倚靠主放胆讲道，主藉他们的手施行神迹奇事，证明他的恩道。」（徒14:3）路加称福音为「他的恩道」，这个名字很美：就是关于神恩典的道。神迹在这里的作用，是「证明」这恩典的话是真的。

3. 城里的人分了党。 「城里的众人就分了党，有附从犹太人的，有附从使徒的。」（徒14:4）耶稣曾说，他来是要叫人「纷争」（路12:51）。福音带来平安，也带来分别。

4. 逃走，然后继续传。 有人要「用石头打他们」，「使徒知道了，就逃往吕高尼的路司得、特庇两个城和周围地方去，在那里传福音」（徒14:5-7）。逃避逼迫不是不忠心（参太10:23）；他们离开一个地方，只是为了在另一个地方继续传福音。

深读 14:8-18 路司得：「我们也是人」

1. 有信心可得痊愈。 路司得有一个人「生来是瘸腿的，从来没有走过」。「他听保罗讲道，保罗定睛看他，见他有信心，可得痊愈，就大声说：『你起来，两脚站直！』那人就跳起来，而且行走。」（徒14:8-10）这件事和彼得在圣殿美门口医治瘸腿的人十分相似（徒3:1-10）。路加有意让我们看见：在外邦人中工作的保罗，和在犹太人中工作的彼得，是同一位主所用的。

2. 神藉着人形降临。 众人用本地的吕高尼话大喊：「有神藉着人形降临在我们中间了。」（徒14:11）他们称巴拿巴为宙斯，称保罗为希耳米，「因为他说话领首」（徒14:12）。罗马诗人奥维德记载过一个传说：宙斯和希耳米化成人形来到邻近的弗吕家，无人接待，只有一对贫穷的老夫妇款待了他们，其余的人都遭了灾。当地也出土过同时敬拜这两位神明的碑文。路司得人也许知道类似的传说，不想再犯同样的错误。

3. 撕开衣裳。 宙斯庙的祭司牵着牛、拿着花圈要献祭，「巴拿巴、保罗二使徒听见，就撕开衣裳，跳进众人中间」（徒14:13-14）。撕开衣裳，是犹太人听见亵渎神的话时的反应。对他们来说，被人当作神来敬拜，不是荣耀，而是可怕的亵渎。

4. 「我们也是人，性情和你们一样。」 「诸君，为什么做这事呢？我们也是人，性情和你们一样。我们传福音给你们，是叫你们离弃这些虚妄，归向那创造天、地、海，和其中万物的永生神。」（徒14:15）面对这些不认识旧约的外邦人，保罗不是从摩西和大卫讲起，而是从创造主讲起。这是书中第一次记载向没有圣经背景的人传福音，到第十七章雅典的讲道会更完整。

5. 神为自己留下的证据。 「他在从前的世代，任凭万国各行其道；然而为自己未尝不显出证据来，就如常施恩惠，从天降雨，赏赐丰年，叫你们饮食饱足，满心喜乐。」（徒14:16-17）神学上称为「普遍恩典」：神赐雨水和丰收给所有人，不论他们是否认识他。保罗在罗马书说，神的永能和神性「藉着所造之物就可以晓得，叫人无可推诿」（罗1:20）。每一碗饭、每一场雨，都在为神作见证。这样的见证足以叫人无可推诿，却不足以叫人得救；所以保罗还要传福音，叫他们「离弃这些虚妄，归向」永生神（徒14:15）。

6. 好不容易才拦住。 「二人说了这些话，仅仅地拦住众人不献祭与他们。」（徒14:18）人心多么容易拜偶像：就在使徒面前，他们还几乎要把使徒当成偶像。

要点：路司得人不认识真神，就把行神迹的人当作神。保罗不肯接受这份荣耀，却把他们指向那位一直藉着雨水和丰收向他们施恩的创造主。
深读 14:19-20 被石头打，又起来

1. 同一群人。 「但有些犹太人从安提阿和以哥念来，挑唆众人，就用石头打保罗，以为他是死了，便拖到城外。」（徒14:19）不久前还要向他献祭的人，现在要用石头打死他。人的赞美和人的愤怒，常常只有一步之遥。

2. 保罗记得这件事。 保罗后来说：「被石头打了一次。」（林后11:25）他也写信给提摩太，提到「我在安提阿、以哥念、路司得所遭遇的逼迫、苦难」，又说「从这一切苦难中，主都把我救出来了」（提后3:11）。提摩太就是路司得人（徒16:1）；他很可能亲眼看见了这件事。

3. 他就起来，走进城去。 「门徒正围着他，他就起来，走进城去。第二天，同巴拿巴往特庇去。」（徒14:20）路加没有说这是神迹，但这一幕令人震撼：被石头打得像死了一样的人，站起来，走回打他的那座城。

深读 14:21-28 回程：坚固、劝勉、交托

1. 原路回去。 在特庇传福音以后，他们「就回路司得、以哥念、安提阿去」（徒14:21）。解经家常指出，若从特庇继续往东，经过保罗的家乡大数，是回叙利亚安提阿最近的路；他们却原路折返，回到刚刚逼迫他们的城。为什么？为了那些初信的门徒。

2. 「必须经历许多艰难」。 他们「坚固门徒的心，劝他们恒守所信的道；又说：『我们进入神的国，必须经历许多艰难。』」（徒14:22）这句话很诚实。保罗没有对初信的人说「信了主，一切都会顺利」，而是说艰难是「必须」的。「必须」这个字（dei），路加常用来讲神的计划（参路24:26，和合本译作「应当」：「基督这样受害，又进入他的荣耀，岂不是应当的吗？」）。艰难是进国的路，不是进国的代价；门徒所走的路，是他们的主先走过的路。

3. 选立长老。 「二人在各教会中选立了长老，又禁食祷告，就把他们交托所信的主。」（徒14:23）这些教会成立不久，保罗和巴拿巴就为他们选立领袖。他们相信，即使没有使徒在场，主也能保守他的教会。

4. 交托所信的主。 「就把他们交托所信的主」：他们没有把这些教会当作自己的产业；尽了责任，就放手，把他们交在主的手里。

5. 神为外邦人开了信道的门。 回到叙利亚的安提阿，「就述说神藉他们所行的一切事，并神怎样为外邦人开了信道的门」（徒14:27）。请留意是谁开的门：不是「我们为外邦人开了门」，而是「神」。他们所报告的，是神的作为。

要点：进国的路要经过许多艰难，这是主自己先走过的路。所以保罗和巴拿巴不必隐瞒艰难，也不必把初信的人抓在自己手里；他们说出实话，选立长老，然后把一切交托给那位保守他教会的主。
默想

默想： 路司得人先要把保罗当神来拜，没过多久却用石头打他。人心常常这样：先把一个人捧上神坛，等他叫我们失望了，又把他推下来。我有没有这样对待过一位牧者、一位属灵长辈，甚至我的配偶或父母，期待他给我只有神才给得了的东西：永远不让我失望，永远懂我？保罗撕开衣裳说「我们也是人」，是把那份不属于他的重担放下来。只有一位，真正「藉着人形降临」在我们中间，又为我舍了自己，他从不叫信靠他的人失望。保罗又说，神「从天降雨，赏赐丰年，叫你们饮食饱足，满心喜乐」。今天的一碗饭、一场雨，都是那位赐恩者的签名；连雨水都不吝惜的父，更是连自己的儿子也没有爱惜（罗8:32）。许多华人遇到好事会说「谢天谢地」；今天在饭桌上，我能不能带着喜乐，说出那位赐恩者的名字？最后，保罗对初信的人说：「我们进入神的国，必须经历许多艰难。」有没有人对我说过「信了主就一切顺利」，以致艰难临到时，我以为神离开了我？艰难不是神不在的证据，而是我正走在主先走过的路上。我牵挂的那个人，一个将要离家的孩子，一位刚信主的朋友，也要走这条路；我已经尽了我能尽的，今天可以把他交托给那位比我更爱他、也亲自走过这条路的主。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 14 completes the first missionary journey. Iconium (vv. 1–7): many believe, but the city is divided and the apostles have to flee. Lystra (vv. 8–20): a man crippled from birth is healed, and the crowds take Barnabas and Paul for Greek gods and try to offer sacrifices to them; soon after, the same crowds stone Paul and leave him for dead. The journey home (vv. 21–28): they go back to the very cities that had just persecuted them, strengthen the disciples, appoint elders, and return to Antioch, which had sent them, to report "how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles."

The chapter turns on a sharp contrast: one moment people want to worship them, the next they want to kill them. Anyone, and especially a preacher, who builds confidence on people's reactions will soon collapse; Paul and Barnabas relied on the Lord "who bore witness to the word of his grace" (Acts 14:3).

Going Deeper: 14:1–7 Iconium: The Word of Grace and Division

1. Many Jews and Greeks believed. "Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed" (Acts 14:1). As soon as the gospel spread, it won both Jews and Gentiles.

2. The word of his grace. "So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands" (Acts 14:3). Luke gives the gospel a beautiful name: "the word of his grace," the message about God's grace. The signs here serve to "bear witness" that this word of grace is true.

3. The city was divided. "But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles" (Acts 14:4). Jesus had said he came to bring "division" (Luke 12:51). The gospel brings peace, and it also divides.

4. Fleeing, and preaching on. When there was an attempt "to mistreat them and to stone them, they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel" (Acts 14:5–7). Escaping persecution isn't unfaithfulness (cf. Matt 10:23); they left one place only to keep preaching in another.

Going Deeper: 14:8–18 Lystra: "We Also Are Men"

1. Faith to be made well. At Lystra there was a man "crippled from birth" who "had never walked." "He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, said in a loud voice, 'Stand upright on your feet.' And he sprang up and began walking" (Acts 14:8–10). It closely mirrors Peter healing the lame man at the temple's Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1–10). Luke wants us to see that Paul among the Gentiles and Peter among the Jews are used by the same Lord.

2. Gods in the likeness of men. The crowds shouted in their local Lycaonian language, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" (Acts 14:11). They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, "because he was the chief speaker" (Acts 14:12). The Roman poet Ovid preserves a legend (Baucis and Philemon) in which Zeus and Hermes visited neighboring Phrygia in human form; no one welcomed them except a poor elderly couple, and the rest were destroyed. Inscriptions from the area also link the two gods. The Lystrans may have known a similar story and not wanted to make the same mistake.

3. Tearing their garments. The priest of Zeus brought oxen and garlands to offer sacrifice, but "when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd" (Acts 14:13–14). Tearing one's garments was the Jewish response to hearing blasphemy. To them, being worshiped as gods was no honor but a dreadful blasphemy.

4. "We also are men, of like nature with you." "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them" (Acts 14:15). For these Gentiles who didn't know the Old Testament, Paul doesn't start with Moses and David but with the Creator. This is the first example of preaching to people with no biblical background; the Athens sermon in chapter 17 will develop it more fully.

5. The witness God left himself. "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness" (Acts 14:16–17). Theologians call this "common grace": God gives rain and harvest to everyone, whether or not they know him. In Romans Paul says God's eternal power and divine nature "have been clearly perceived... in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse" (Rom 1:20). Every bowl of rice and every rainfall bears witness to God. This witness leaves people without excuse, but it cannot save them; that is why Paul still brings "good news" calling them to "turn... to a living God" (Acts 14:15).

6. Scarcely restrained. "Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them" (Acts 14:18). How easily the human heart turns to idols: right in front of the apostles, they nearly made the apostles themselves into idols.

The point: Not knowing the true God, the people of Lystra took the miracle-workers for gods. Paul refused that glory and pointed them instead to the Creator who had been showing them kindness all along through rain and harvest.
Going Deeper: 14:19–20 Stoned, and Rising Again

1. The same crowd. "But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead" (Acts 14:19). The people who had wanted to sacrifice to him now wanted to stone him to death. Human praise and human rage are often only a short step apart.

2. Paul remembered. Paul later wrote, "Once I was stoned" (2 Cor 11:25). He also wrote to Timothy of "my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra," adding, "yet from them all the Lord rescued me" (2 Tim 3:11). Timothy was from Lystra (Acts 16:1); he may well have seen it happen.

3. He rose up and entered the city. "But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe" (Acts 14:20). Luke doesn't call it a miracle, but the picture is powerful: a man stoned until he looked dead stands up and walks back into the city that stoned him.

Going Deeper: 14:21–28 The Return: Strengthening, Encouraging, Entrusting

1. Back the way they came. After preaching in Derbe, "they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch" (Acts 14:21). Commentators often note that from Derbe the shortest way home lay east, through Paul's hometown of Tarsus; instead they went back, to the very cities that had just persecuted them. Why? For the sake of the new disciples.

2. "Through many tribulations." They were "strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22). This is honest. Paul didn't tell new believers, "Believe in the Lord and everything will go well"; he said hardship "must" come. Luke often uses this "must" for God's plan (dei; cf. Luke 24:26, "Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?"). Tribulation is the road into the kingdom, not its price; the disciples' road is the road their Lord walked first.

3. Appointing elders. "And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed" (Acts 14:23). These churches were young, yet Paul and Barnabas appointed leaders for them. They trusted that the Lord could keep his church even without an apostle present.

4. Committed to the Lord. "They committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed": They didn't treat these churches as their own. They did their part, then let go and placed them in the Lord's hands.

5. God opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. Back in Syrian Antioch, "they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles" (Acts 14:27). Notice who opened the door: not "we opened a door for the Gentiles" but "God." What they reported was God's work.

The point: The road into the kingdom runs through many tribulations, and it is the road the Lord walked first. So Paul and Barnabas had no need to hide the hardships or to keep the new believers in their own grip. They told the truth, appointed elders, and entrusted everything to the Lord who keeps his church.
Meditation

Reflect: The people of Lystra first wanted to worship Paul as a god; soon after, they stoned him. The heart often works this way: we lift someone onto a pedestal, and when they disappoint us, we pull them down. Have I done this to a pastor, a spiritual mentor, even my spouse or parents, expecting them to give me what only God can give: never to let me down, always to understand me? When Paul tore his clothes and said, "We also are men," he was laying down a weight that was never his to carry. Only one has truly come among us "in the likeness of men" and given himself for me, and he never puts to shame those who trust him. Paul also said that God gives "rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Today's bowl of rice and today's rain are the Giver's signature; and the Father who doesn't hold back the rain did not spare even his own Son (Rom 8:32). Many Chinese people say "thank heaven and earth" when things go well; at my table today, could I gladly name the Giver himself? Finally, Paul told the new believers, "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." Has someone told me that "once you believe, everything will go well," so that when hardship came I thought God had left me? Hardship isn't proof that God is absent; it means I'm on the road my Lord walked first. The one I carry on my heart, a child about to leave home or a friend newly come to faith, will walk this road too. I have done what I can; today I can entrust them to the Lord who loves them more than I do and has walked this road himself.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十五章接近使徒行传的中间，许多人认为这是全书神学上最关键的一章。外邦人大量归主以后，一个问题再也回避不了：外邦人要得救，是否必须先受割礼、遵守摩西的律法？换句话说：人得救，是靠「耶稣加上别的」，还是单单靠耶稣的恩典？

本章有四段：争论的起因（1-5节）；耶路撒冷会议（6-21节），彼得、巴拿巴和保罗、雅各先后发言；会议的书信（22-35节），外邦教会读了信「就欢喜了」；保罗和巴拿巴分开（36-41节），两位同工因为马可的事起了争论，各自出发。这一章既有教会最清楚的教义决定，也有同工之间最真实的冲突。

深读 15:1-5 「若不受割礼，不能得救」

1. 从犹太下来的人。 「有几个人从犹太下来，教训弟兄们说：『你们若不按摩西的规条受割礼，不能得救。』」（徒15:1）他们不是说「受割礼会更好」，而是说「不受割礼，不能得救」。这就把割礼变成了得救的条件。

2. 大大地纷争辩论。 「保罗、巴拿巴与他们大大地纷争辩论。」（徒15:2）保罗没有为了表面的和睦而让步；若在这里让步，福音就不再是福音了。保罗在加拉太书中，也把类似的争论称为「福音的真理」的问题（加2:5）。加拉太书第2章所记的耶路撒冷之行，究竟是指这次会议，还是指徒11:30的赈灾之行，福音派学者看法不一；但两处的立场完全一致：外邦人不必受割礼，单凭恩典称义。

3. 法利赛教门的信徒。 在耶路撒冷，「有几个信徒是法利赛教门的人，起来说：『必须给外邦人行割礼，吩咐他们遵守摩西的律法。』」（徒15:5）请注意，他们是「信徒」。这场争论不是教会和外人的争论，而是教会内部的争论。

要点：问题不在于割礼本身，而在于把任何东西加在基督身上，当作得救的条件。「耶稣加上别的」，就不再是福音。
深读 15:6-12 彼得：「我们得救乃是因主耶稣的恩」

1. 辩论已经多了。 「使徒和长老聚会商议这事。辩论已经多了，彼得就起来。」（徒15:6-7）教会没有回避辩论；有分歧的时候，他们聚在一起，公开讨论。

2. 神并不分他们我们。 彼得提醒大家哥尼流家里发生的事：「知道人心的神也为他们作了见证，赐圣灵给他们，正如给我们一样；又藉着信洁净了他们的心，并不分他们我们。」（徒15:8-9）神已经用行动作了决定：外邦人的心是「藉着信」洁净的，不是藉着割礼。

3. 不能负的轭。 「现在为什么试探神，要把我们祖宗和我们所不能负的轭放在门徒的颈项上呢？」（徒15:10）彼得身为犹太人，在这里坦白承认：律法本身是圣洁的（罗7:12），但人若要靠它得救，它就成了「我们祖宗和我们所不能负的轭」。没有人能靠遵守律法站在神面前。耶稣却说：「我的轭是容易的，我的担子是轻省的。」（太11:30）

4. 「和他们一样」。 「我们得救乃是因主耶稣的恩，和他们一样，这是我们所信的。」（徒15:11）请注意彼得的说法。他没有说「外邦人得救是因恩典，和我们一样」，而是倒过来说：「我们（犹太人）得救是因恩典，和他们（外邦人）一样。」犹太人并没有比外邦人多一条得救的路。在恩典面前，人人站在同一个地方。

5. 众人都默默无声。 「众人都默默无声，听巴拿巴和保罗述说神藉他们在外邦人中所行的神迹奇事。」（徒15:12）巴拿巴和保罗没有提出新的论证，只是述说神的作为。

要点：犹太人和外邦人得救，都是「因主耶稣的恩」，没有第二条路。律法是人所不能负的轭；恩典却是神白白的礼物。
深读 15:13-21 雅各：经文与智慧

1. 主的兄弟雅各。 「他们住了声，雅各就说：『诸位弟兄，请听我的话。』」（徒15:13）这位雅各是耶稣的兄弟，耶路撒冷教会的领袖，按教会传统，他一生严守律法。由他来作总结，分量特别重。

2. 阿摩司书的预言。 雅各引用阿摩司书：「此后，我要回来，重新修造大卫倒塌的帐幕……叫余剩的人，就是凡称为我名下的外邦人，都寻求主。」（徒15:16-17；摩9:11-12）神应许要恢复大卫的国度，而外邦人归向神，正是这恢复的一部分。雅各的引文跟随希腊文的七十士译本；希伯来文本作「使以色列人得以东所余剩的和所有称为我名下的国」。两种文本都指向同一件事：大卫的国度恢复的时候，列国要归入神的名下。

3. 「不可难为」。 「所以据我的意见，不可难为那归服神的外邦人。」（徒15:19）结论很清楚：外邦人不必受割礼，不必成为犹太人。

4. 四件事。 「只要写信，吩咐他们禁戒偶像的污秽和奸淫，并勒死的牲畜和血。」（徒15:20）这四件事不是得救的条件（第11节已经说清楚了）；其中关于饮食的几件，是为了让外邦信徒和犹太信徒能够在一起生活、一同吃饭。这几件事大多是犹太人最敏感的地方，有些也和利未记17-18章对「寄居的外人」的要求相似。雅各接着说：「因为从古以来，摩西的书在各城有人传讲。」（徒15:21）意思是：各城都有犹太人，外邦信徒要顾及他们的良心。

5. 奸淫为什么也在其中？ 其他几件主要和饮食、祭祀有关，奸淫却直接是道德问题。这里的「奸淫」（porneia）很可能包括利未记18章所禁止的各样性关系；在外邦世界，这类事极为普遍，也常和拜偶像的宴席连在一起。前三件是为了体贴犹太弟兄的良心；禁戒奸淫却是神对一切信徒永不改变的命令（林前6:18；帖前4:3）。

要点：耶路撒冷会议守住了三件事：在得救的事上，单单靠恩典，绝不妥协；在可以自由的事上，为了爱弟兄，甘心放下自己的自由；在神的道德命令上，则一同顺服。
深读 15:22-35 「圣灵和我们」

1. 一封信和两位使者。 「使徒和长老并全教会定意」，差派犹大和西拉，带着书信同保罗、巴拿巴往安提阿去（徒15:22-23）。他们不只寄一封信，还差人亲自去解释。

2. 「圣灵和我们定意」。 「因为圣灵和我们定意不将别的重担放在你们身上，惟有几件事是不可少的。」（徒15:28）这句话很特别：教会经过讨论，听了神作为的见证，又查考了经文，然后作出决定；他们相信，这也是圣灵的意思。这是使徒时代的决定，已经成为圣经的一部分；今天教会的决定却会出错，必须时时用圣经来检验。教会若谦卑顺服神的话、彼此商议，就可以信靠圣灵的带领。

3. 就欢喜了。 「众人念了，因为信上安慰的话就欢喜了。」（徒15:31）外邦信徒最怕听到的，是「你还不够」；他们收到的信，却告诉他们：在基督里，你已经完全被接纳了。

深读 15:36-41 保罗和巴拿巴分开

1. 为马可起争论。 保罗提议回去看望各城的弟兄，「巴拿巴有意要带称呼马可的约翰同去；但保罗因为马可从前在旁非利亚离开他们，不和他们同去做工，就以为不可带他去」（徒15:37-38）。两人都有道理：保罗看重工作的需要，巴拿巴看重马可这个人。巴拿巴是马可的表兄（西4:10），自然更愿意再给他一次机会。

2. 「甚至彼此分开」。 「于是二人起了争论，甚至彼此分开。」（徒15:39）「争论」原文是很强烈的字，指激烈的冲突。圣经没有替任何一方掩饰：刚刚帮助教会解决了最大分歧的两个人，自己却因为人选的问题分开了。

3. 神仍然掌权。 结果，一个宣教队变成了两个：「巴拿巴带着马可，坐船往塞浦路斯去；保罗拣选了西拉，也出去，蒙弟兄们把他交于主的恩中。」（徒15:39-40）神没有因为他们的冲突而停止工作。这不是说冲突是好事，而是说神的恩典比人的软弱更大。

4. 后来的和好。 多年以后，保罗在书信中提到马可，吩咐教会「接待他」（西4:10），又说「他在传道的事上于我有益处」（提后4:11）。曾经半途离开的马可，后来成了保罗的同工。早期教父帕皮亚说，马可记下了彼得的讲道；教会传统也认为，他就是马可福音的作者。巴拿巴给马可的第二次机会，并没有白费。

要点：同一章里，教会在教义上达成了合一，两位领袖却在人事上分开了。圣经不掩饰神仆人的软弱；但神的工作没有停，马可也没有被放弃；分开的两队人，都被「交于主的恩中」。
默想

默想： 「你们若不受割礼，不能得救。」今天很少人这样说；可是我心里会不会有别的「若不」：若不像我们这样受洗，若不用我们习惯的方式敬拜，若不守我们教会的那些规矩，他就不算「真正」的基督徒？彼得说：「我们得救乃是因主耶稣的恩，和他们一样。」在十字架下，我和我最看不上的那位信徒站在同一块地上，手里都是空的。这不是叫我放下信念，而是叫我放下那份暗暗的「我比较好」，和他一同为同一份恩典惊奇。会议也提醒我：在得救的事上不能让步，在可以自由的事上，却可以为爱让步。比如在婚宴或应酬上喝一杯酒，我在神面前也许有这个自由；可是身边若有一位刚戒酒的弟兄，或一位良心敏感的初信者，我愿意为他放下吗？基督「不求自己的喜悦」（罗15:3），我也可以为了弟兄放下一点自己的权利。最后，刚刚帮教会化解了最大分歧的保罗和巴拿巴，自己却「起了争论，甚至彼此分开」。我有没有一位曾经一起服事、后来不欢而散的同工？我不必急着判定谁对谁错；我可以像安提阿的弟兄们那样，把他和我一同「交于主的恩中」（徒15:40），今天为他的事工祷告，也把那扇门留着。多年以后，保罗说马可「在传道的事上于我有益处」；恩典能走的路，常常比我想的更远。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 15 stands near the center of Acts, and many regard it as the book's most important chapter theologically. Once Gentiles were coming to faith in large numbers, one question could no longer be avoided: must Gentiles first be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved? In other words, are people saved by "Jesus plus something else," or by the grace of Jesus alone?

The chapter has four parts: the dispute arises (vv. 1–5); the Jerusalem council (vv. 6–21), where Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James speak in turn; the council's letter (vv. 22–35), which the Gentile church reads and "rejoiced"; and Paul and Barnabas part ways (vv. 36–41), as the two co-workers clash over Mark and set out separately. The chapter holds both the church's clearest doctrinal decision and its most honest conflict between co-workers.

Going Deeper: 15:1–5 "Unless You Are Circumcised, You Cannot Be Saved"

1. Men from Judea. "But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved'" (Acts 15:1). They weren't saying circumcision would be better; they were saying that without it you cannot be saved. That turns circumcision into a condition of salvation.

2. No small dissension. "Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them" (Acts 15:2). Paul didn't give way for the sake of surface harmony; give way here, and the gospel would no longer be the gospel. In Galatians Paul calls a similar dispute a matter of "the truth of the gospel" (Gal 2:5). Evangelical scholars differ on whether the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 2 is this council or the famine visit of Acts 11:30, but the stance is the same in both: Gentiles need not be circumcised; justification is by grace alone.

3. Believers from the Pharisees. In Jerusalem, "some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses'" (Acts 15:5). Notice they were "believers." This wasn't a dispute between the church and outsiders but within the church.

The point: The issue isn't circumcision itself; it is adding anything to Christ as a condition of salvation. "Jesus plus something" is no longer the gospel.
Going Deeper: 15:6–12 Peter: "We Will Be Saved Through the Grace of the Lord Jesus"

1. Much debate. "The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up" (Acts 15:6–7). The church didn't avoid debate; when they disagreed, they met and discussed it openly.

2. No distinction between us and them. Peter reminded them of what happened in Cornelius's house: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith" (Acts 15:8–9). God had already decided by his actions: Gentile hearts were cleansed "by faith," not by circumcision.

3. A yoke we could not bear. "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?" (Acts 15:10). This is a strikingly honest admission from a Jewish apostle: the law itself is holy (Rom 7:12), but as a way to stand before God it is a yoke "neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear." No one can stand before God by keeping the law. But Jesus said, "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Matt 11:30).

4. "Just as they will." "But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will" (Acts 15:11). Notice how Peter puts it. He doesn't say, "Gentiles are saved by grace, just as we are," but the reverse: "We (Jews) are saved by grace, just as they (Gentiles) are." Jews have no second road to salvation. Before grace, everyone stands in the same place.

5. All fell silent. "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles" (Acts 15:12). Barnabas and Paul offered no new argument; they simply told what God had done.

The point: Jews and Gentiles alike are saved "through the grace of the Lord Jesus"; there is no other road. The law is a yoke no one can bear; grace is God's free gift.
Going Deeper: 15:13–21 James: Scripture and Wisdom

1. James the Lord's brother. "After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me'" (Acts 15:13). This James was Jesus' brother, leader of the Jerusalem church, remembered in later tradition for his strict observance of the law. A summary from him carried special weight.

2. Amos's prophecy. James quotes Amos: "After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen... that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name" (Acts 15:16–17; Amos 9:11–12). God promised to restore David's kingdom, and that restoration includes the Gentiles turning to God. James's quotation follows the Greek Septuagint; the Hebrew text reads "that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name." Both point to the same thing: when David's kingdom is restored, the nations will come under God's name.

3. "We should not trouble them." "Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God" (Acts 15:19). The conclusion is clear: Gentiles need not be circumcised or become Jews.

4. Four things. "But should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood" (Acts 15:20). These four aren't conditions of salvation (verse 11 has settled that); the food rules among them are so that Gentile and Jewish believers can live together and share meals. Most of them touched Jewish sensitivities most deeply, and several resemble what Leviticus 17–18 required of "the stranger who sojourns" among Israel. James adds, "For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him" (Acts 15:21): there are Jews in every city, and Gentile believers should be mindful of their consciences.

5. Why sexual immorality? The others mainly concern food and sacrifice, but sexual immorality is directly a moral matter. Porneia here probably covers the sexual relations forbidden in Leviticus 18, which were common in the Gentile world and often tied to idol feasts. The food rules served a brother's conscience; abstaining from sexual immorality is God's unchanging command for every believer (1 Cor 6:18; 1 Thess 4:3).

The point: The Jerusalem council held three things together: on salvation, grace alone, with no compromise; in matters of freedom, a willingness to set it aside out of love; in God's moral commands, shared obedience.
Going Deeper: 15:22–35 "The Holy Spirit and Us"

1. A letter and two messengers. "It seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church," to send Judas and Silas with a letter, along with Paul and Barnabas, to Antioch (Acts 15:22–23). They didn't only send a letter; they sent people to explain it in person.

2. "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." "For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements" (Acts 15:28). This is remarkable: a decision reached after debate, testimony to God's work and the Scriptures, they believed was also the Spirit's will. This apostolic decision is now part of Scripture. Church decisions today can err and must be tested by Scripture; yet when a church humbly submits to God's word and confers together, it may trust the Spirit's leading.

3. They rejoiced. "And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement" (Acts 15:31). What Gentile believers most feared to hear was "You're not enough yet"; the letter they received told them that in Christ they were fully accepted.

Going Deeper: 15:36–41 Paul and Barnabas Part Ways

1. A dispute over Mark. Paul proposed revisiting the brothers in each city. "Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work" (Acts 15:37–38). Both had a point: Paul weighed the needs of the work, Barnabas weighed Mark as a person. Barnabas was Mark's cousin (Col 4:10), and naturally more willing to give him another chance.

2. "So that they separated." "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other" (Acts 15:39). "Sharp disagreement" is a strong word for a heated conflict. Scripture covers for neither side: the two men who had just helped the church settle its greatest dispute parted ways over a personnel question.

3. God still reigns. The result was that one mission team became two: "Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord" (Acts 15:39–40). God didn't stop working because of their conflict. That doesn't make conflict good; it means God's grace is greater than human weakness.

4. Reconciliation later. Years later Paul mentions Mark in his letters, telling a church to "welcome him" (Col 4:10) and saying "he is very useful to me for ministry" (2 Tim 4:11). The Mark who once turned back became Paul's co-worker, and the early church father Papias says he recorded Peter's preaching; tradition holds he wrote the Gospel of Mark. The second chance Barnabas gave him was not wasted.

The point: In the same chapter the church reached unity on doctrine, while two leaders parted over people. Scripture doesn't hide the weakness of God's servants; but God's work didn't stop, Mark wasn't given up on, and both teams were commended to the grace of the Lord.
Meditation

Reflect: "Unless you are circumcised, you cannot be saved." Few people say that today; but is there another "unless" in my heart: unless they're baptized the way we do it, unless they worship the way we're used to, unless they keep our church's rules, they aren't "real" Christians? Peter said, "We will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will." At the foot of the cross I stand on the same ground as the believer I think least of, with the same empty hands. This doesn't ask me to give up my convictions; it asks me to give up my quiet sense that "I'm better," and to wonder at the same grace alongside them. The council also reminds me that I can't give way on salvation, yet in matters of freedom I can give way out of love. A glass of wine at a wedding banquet or a business dinner may be a freedom I have before God; but if a brother beside me has just stopped drinking, or a new believer has a tender conscience, am I willing to set it aside for him? Christ "did not please himself" (Rom 15:3); I can lay down a little of my own right for a brother's sake. Finally, Paul and Barnabas, who had just helped the church settle its greatest dispute, "had a sharp disagreement, so that they separated." Is there a co-worker I once served beside and parted from badly? I don't have to rush to decide who was right. Like the believers at Antioch, I can commend both of us "to the grace of the Lord" (Acts 15:40), pray for their ministry today, and leave the door open. Years later Paul called Mark "very useful to me for ministry"; grace often goes further than I imagine.

verse_parts.text: 有一个卖紫色布疋的妇人，名叫吕底亚，是推雅推喇城的人，素来敬拜神。她听见了，主就开导她的心，叫她留心听保罗所讲的话。

entries.verse_text: 有一个卖紫色布疋的妇人，名叫吕底亚，是推雅推喇城的人，素来敬拜神。她听见了，主就开导她的心，叫她留心听保罗所讲的话。他们说：「当信主耶稣，你和你一家都必得救。」
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十六章记载保罗第二次宣教旅程（始于徒15:36）的头一段，也是福音第一次进入欧洲。提摩太加入（1-5节）；关闭的门与马其顿的异象（6-10节），圣灵两次「禁止」「不许」，然后在夜间异象中呼召他们过到马其顿；腓立比（11-40节），福音临到三个截然不同的人：卖紫色布疋的富商吕底亚、被巫鬼所附的使女、看守监牢的禁卒。吕底亚和禁卒信了主；使女得了释放（路加没有记载她后来是否信主）。

从第10节开始，叙述忽然从「他们」变成「我们」。许多学者认为，这表示作者路加本人在特罗亚加入了保罗的同工团队。

深读 16:1-5 提摩太加入

1. 一个混合家庭的青年。 在路司得，有一个门徒名叫提摩太，「是信主之犹太妇人的儿子，他父亲却是希腊人」（徒16:1）。保罗后来写信给他，提到他的信心「是先在你外祖母罗以和你母亲友妮基心里的」（提后1:5）。一个家庭里母亲和外祖母的信心，栽培出了一位日后的教会领袖。

2. 为什么给他行割礼？ 「保罗要带他同去，只因那些地方的犹太人都知道他父亲是希腊人，就给他行了割礼。」（徒16:3）这看起来好像和第十五章的决定矛盾。其实不然：耶路撒冷会议决定的是，割礼不是得救的条件；保罗也曾坚持不让希腊人提多受割礼（加2:3），因为那时有人要把割礼当作得救的条件。提摩太的情况不同。他母亲是犹太人，当地犹太人很可能把他看作犹太人，只是一个没有受割礼的犹太人，因为「那些地方的犹太人都知道他父亲是希腊人」。保罗给他行割礼，是免得传福音时，在犹太人面前造成不必要的拦阻。保罗说：「向犹太人，我就作犹太人，为要得犹太人。」（林前9:20）

3. 坚固与加增。 他们把耶路撒冷会议的决定交给各城的门徒，「于是众教会信心越发坚固，人数天天加增」（徒16:5）。这是使徒行传的又一个「进展报告」。

要点：在得救的事上，保罗绝不让步；在传福音的方法上，他却甘心让步。同一个保罗，不让提多受割礼，却让提摩太受割礼，因为他看重的是福音的真理和福音的传开。
深读 16:6-10 关闭的门与马其顿的异象

1. 两次被拦阻。 「圣灵既然禁止他们在亚细亚讲道」，他们想往庇推尼去，「耶稣的灵却不许」（徒16:6-7）。亚细亚和庇推尼都是人口稠密、需要福音的地方，保罗的计划并没有错。可是圣灵关上了门。路加没有告诉我们圣灵是怎样禁止的，也许是借着环境、疾病，或先知的话。

2. 「耶稣的灵」。 新约只有这里用「耶稣的灵」这个说法（参腓1:19；罗8:9）。第6节说「圣灵」，第7节说「耶稣的灵」：圣灵是升天的主所差来的（徒2:33），带领宣教的，是父、子、圣灵一同作工的三一真神。

3. 马其顿人的呼声。 他们来到特罗亚，「在夜间有异象现与保罗。有一个马其顿人站着求他说：『请你过到马其顿来帮助我们。』」（徒16:9）两扇门关了，一扇新的门开了。「保罗既看见这异象，我们随即想要往马其顿去，以为神召我们传福音给那里的人听。」（徒16:10）「以为」原文有「把几件事合起来推断」的意思：他们把关闭的门和夜间的异象放在一起，彼此商量，得出了结论。

要点：神的带领不只是开门，也包括关门。圣灵两次说「不」，是要把他们引到一个意想不到的方向：福音要进入欧洲。
深读 16:11-15 吕底亚：主开导她的心

1. 河边的祷告处。 腓立比是罗马的殖民城，也是马其顿那一带的重要城市。那里似乎连一个会堂也没有（按后来拉比文献的记载，某些公众崇拜须有十个男子在场；若当时已有这规矩，可见那里犹太男人很少）。「当安息日，我们出城门，到了河边，知道那里有一个祷告的地方，我们就坐下对那聚会的妇女讲道。」（徒16:13）福音在欧洲的第一场聚会，是在河边向几个妇女讲道。

2. 「主就开导她的心」。 「有一个卖紫色布疋的妇人，名叫吕底亚，是推雅推喇城的人，素来敬拜神。她听见了，主就开导她的心，叫她留心听保罗所讲的话。」（徒16:14）紫色布料是贵重的货品，吕底亚很可能是一位富裕的商人。路加说得很清楚：保罗讲道，但开她心的是主。人能明白、相信福音，是神的工作。

3. 打开的心，打开的家。 「她和她一家既领了洗，便求我们说：『你们若以为我是真信主的，请到我家里来住』；于是强留我们。」（徒16:15）主打开了她的心，她就打开了她的家。后来弟兄们就聚在她家（徒16:40）。腓立比教会也一直慷慨地支持保罗的事工（腓4:15）。

深读 16:16-24 使女的释放与代价

1. 被巫鬼所附的使女。 有一个使女「被巫鬼所附，用法术，叫她主人们大得财利」（徒16:16）。「巫鬼」原文是「皮同的灵」，皮同是希腊神话中守护德尔斐神谕的巨蛇；人们相信被这灵附着的人能说预言。她是一个被双重捆绑的人：被鬼捆绑，又被主人当作摇钱树。今天华人社会中的算命、问神、观落阴，同样是借灵界的事来赚钱，福音却叫人从这一切捆绑中得释放。

2. 话虽不假，出处却错了。 她一连多日跟着喊：「这些人是至高神的仆人，对你们传说救人的道。」（徒16:17）她说的话是真的，可是福音不需要鬼来作见证。保罗「转身对那鬼说：『我奉耶稣基督的名，吩咐你从她身上出来！』那鬼当时就出来了」（徒16:18）。

3. 失去财利的愤怒。 「使女的主人们见得利的指望没有了」（徒16:19），就揪住保罗和西拉，诬告他们「骚扰我们的城」。他们真正的问题不是宗教，而是钱。一个女孩得了自由，她的主人只看见收入断了。官长吩咐把他们剥了衣裳，用棍打，下在内监，两脚上了木狗（徒16:22-24）。

要点：福音释放人，也会触动靠捆绑人得利的势力。使女的主人看重钱过于看重人；主人把她当作赚钱的工具，福音却看她是一个人，一个值得得释放的人。
深读 16:25-40 半夜的诗歌与禁卒一家

1. 半夜唱诗。 「约在半夜，保罗和西拉祷告，唱诗赞美神，众囚犯也侧耳而听。」（徒16:25）他们的背被打得皮开肉绽，脚被木狗锁着，却在黑暗中唱诗。多年以后，保罗从另一座监牢写信给腓立比教会：「你们要靠主常常喜乐。」（腓4:4）腓立比人知道，这不是一句空话。

2. 地震与「我们都在这里」。 忽然地大震动，监门全开，锁链都松开了。禁卒以为囚犯都逃走了，按罗马的规矩他要替逃犯受死（参徒12:19；徒27:42），就拔刀要自杀。「保罗大声呼叫说：『不要伤害自己！我们都在这里。』」（徒16:28）他们本可以逃走，却留了下来；他们顾的不是自己能否脱身，而是这个刚把他们锁进内监之人的性命。

3. 「我当怎样行才可以得救？」 禁卒战战兢兢地俯伏在保罗、西拉面前，问：「二位先生，我当怎样行才可以得救？」他们说：「当信主耶稣，你和你一家都必得救。」（徒16:30-31）这是新约中最简洁的福音宣告之一。不是「你要做什么」，而是「当信主耶稣」。「你和你一家」不是说一个人信了，全家就自动得救，而是说这应许也同样向他的全家敞开；接着他们「就把主的道讲给他和他全家的人听」（徒16:32）。

4. 洗伤，受洗。 「当夜，就在那时候，禁卒把他们带去，洗他们的伤；他和属乎他的人立时都受了洗。」（徒16:33）同一个夜晚，禁卒洗了他们的伤，自己也受了洗；这洗礼是他因信而罪得洗净的记号。一个刚刚用木狗锁住他们的人，现在为他们摆上饭，「他和全家，因为信了神，都很喜乐」（徒16:34）。

5. 「我们是罗马人」。 天亮以后，官长要私下释放他们。保罗却说：「我们是罗马人，并没有定罪，他们就在众人面前打了我们……叫他们自己来领我们出去吧！」（徒16:37）他不是为了报复，而很可能是为了保护腓立比初生的教会：让官长公开承认他们无罪，以后的信徒就不容易被随意欺压。

要点：福音在腓立比临到的三个人，一个是富有的商人，一个是被奴役的女孩，一个是罗马殖民城的禁卒。福音没有因为身份、地位或民族而改变它的内容，对三个人都是同一句「当信主耶稣」；也没有一个人是这位主的大能救不了的。
默想

默想： 圣灵两次关上了保罗想走的门，而保罗的计划本身并没有错。我生命中有没有一扇我很想进去、却被关上的门：一份没有得到的工作，一个落空的计划，一段始终没有开始的关系？神并没有应许，每一扇关上的门后面，都会有我想要的另一扇；他给保罗的「是」，是福音进入欧洲，不是保罗自己的方便。我能不能把这个「不」带到他面前，诚实地说出我的失望，也相信这位关门的主所看重的，比我的计划更大，而他自己就是我最好的福分？在腓立比，使女的主人只看见「得利的指望没有了」。我是否也在不知不觉中，把人当作工具：只看员工的业绩、孩子的分数、家里帮佣的用处，或教会里谁比较「有用」？主耶稣曾被人用三十块钱估价，那正是旧约里一个奴仆的身价（出21:32；太26:15）；他甘愿被当作可以买卖的人，好叫被当作工具的人得着自由。最后，保罗和西拉在半夜、在伤痛和锁链中「祷告，唱诗赞美神」。如果我现在正在自己的「半夜」，我的诗也许只是一声叹息，一句诗篇里的呼求；但我仍可以开口，因为那位为我受鞭打的主，就在这内监里与我同在。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 16 follows the opening stage of Paul's second missionary journey (begun in Acts 15:36) and brings the gospel into Europe for the first time. Timothy joins (vv. 1–5); closed doors and the Macedonian vision (vv. 6–10), where the Spirit twice "forbids" and "does not allow," then calls them in a night vision to cross into Macedonia; and Philippi (vv. 11–40), where the gospel reaches three very different people: Lydia, a wealthy seller of purple goods; a slave girl with a spirit of divination; and the jailer of the prison. Lydia and the jailer believe; the slave girl is set free (Luke does not tell us whether she later believed).

From verse 10 the narrative suddenly shifts from "they" to "we." Many scholars take this to mean that Luke, the author, joined Paul's team at Troas.

Going Deeper: 16:1–5 Timothy Joins

1. A young man from a mixed family. At Lystra was a disciple named Timothy, "the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek" (Acts 16:1). Paul later wrote to him of his faith, which "dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (2 Tim 1:5). The faith of a mother and grandmother in one household raised up a future church leader.

2. Why circumcise him? "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek" (Acts 16:3). This might seem to contradict chapter 15. It doesn't: the Jerusalem council decided that circumcision is not a condition of salvation, and Paul had insisted that Titus, a Greek, not be circumcised (Gal 2:3), because some wanted to make it a condition of salvation. Timothy's case was different: his mother was Jewish, so local Jews would likely have regarded him as a Jew, but an uncircumcised one (the text says "they all knew that his father was a Greek"); Paul had him circumcised so as not to put an unnecessary obstacle before Jews when preaching the gospel. As Paul said, "To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews" (1 Cor 9:20).

3. Strengthened and growing. They delivered the Jerusalem decisions to the disciples in each city, "so the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily" (Acts 16:5). This is another of Acts' "progress reports."

The point: On salvation Paul would not give an inch; in how he preached the gospel, he gladly gave way. The same Paul refused to circumcise Titus but circumcised Timothy, because what he cared about was the truth of the gospel and its spread.
Going Deeper: 16:6–10 Closed Doors and the Macedonian Vision

1. Blocked twice. They had been "forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia," and when they tried to go into Bithynia, "the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them" (Acts 16:6–7). Asia and Bithynia were populous regions that needed the gospel; Paul's plan wasn't wrong. But the Spirit shut the door. Luke doesn't say how the Spirit forbade them; perhaps through circumstances, illness or a prophetic word.

2. "The Spirit of Jesus." Only here does the New Testament use exactly the phrase "the Spirit of Jesus" (cf. Phil 1:19; Rom 8:9). The "Holy Spirit" of v. 6 is called "the Spirit of Jesus" in v. 7: the Spirit is sent by the ascended Lord (Acts 2:33), so the mission is directed by Father, Son and Spirit together.

3. The Macedonian call. They came to Troas, "and a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, 'Come over to Macedonia and help us'" (Acts 16:9). Two doors closed; a new one opened. "And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them" (Acts 16:10). "Concluding" means putting things together: they weighed the closed doors, the vision and their discussion together and reached a conclusion.

The point: God's guidance includes closing doors as well as opening them. The Spirit said "no" twice to lead them to a "yes" they hadn't imagined: the gospel was to enter Europe.
Going Deeper: 16:11–15 Lydia: The Lord Opened Her Heart

1. A place of prayer by the river. Philippi was a Roman colony and a leading city of that part of Macedonia. It seems to have had no synagogue (later rabbinic sources require ten men for certain communal prayers; if that applied then, there were few Jewish men there). "On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together" (Acts 16:13). The first gospel meeting in Europe was a talk with a few women by a river.

2. "The Lord opened her heart." "One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul" (Acts 16:14). Purple cloth was a luxury good; Lydia was probably a wealthy businesswoman. Luke is clear: Paul preached, but the Lord opened her heart. That anyone understands and believes the gospel is God's work.

3. An open heart, an open home. "And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, 'If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.' And she prevailed upon us" (Acts 16:15). The Lord opened her heart, and she opened her home. At Acts 16:40 the brothers were gathered at her house, and the Philippians went on supporting Paul's ministry generously (Phil 4:15).

Going Deeper: 16:16–24 The Slave Girl Set Free, and the Cost

1. A girl with a spirit of divination. A slave girl "had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling" (Acts 16:16). The phrase is literally "a python spirit," after the serpent of Greek myth that guarded the oracle at Delphi; people believed those possessed by it could foretell the future. She was doubly enslaved: bound by a spirit and used by her owners to make money. Fortune-telling and consulting spirits still make money today, in Chinese communities as elsewhere; the gospel sets people free from all such bondage.

2. True words from the wrong source. For many days she followed them, crying, "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation" (Acts 16:17). What she said was true, but the gospel needs no testimony from demons. Paul "turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour" (Acts 16:18).

3. Anger at lost income. "When her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone" (Acts 16:19), they seized Paul and Silas and accused them of "disturbing our city." Their real problem wasn't religion but money. A girl had been set free; her owners saw only that their income had stopped. The magistrates had them stripped and beaten with rods, thrown into the inner prison, and their feet fastened in the stocks (Acts 16:22–24).

The point: The gospel sets people free, and it also disturbs those who profit from others' bondage. The girl's owners valued money above a person; the gospel treated a girl used as a tool as a person worth setting free.
Going Deeper: 16:25–40 Midnight Hymns and the Jailer's Household

1. Singing at midnight. "About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them" (Acts 16:25). Their backs were torn open, their feet locked in stocks, yet they sang in the dark. Years later Paul wrote to the Philippian church from another prison: "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Phil 4:4). The Philippians knew those weren't empty words.

2. An earthquake, and "we are all here." Suddenly a great earthquake shook the prison, the doors opened and everyone's bonds came loose. The jailer, thinking the prisoners had escaped, and knowing that under Roman practice he would answer with his life (cf. Acts 12:19; Acts 27:42), drew his sword to kill himself. "But Paul cried with a loud voice, 'Do not harm yourself, for we are all here'" (Acts 16:28). They could have fled, but stayed; what they cared about was not their own freedom but the life of the man who had just locked them up.

3. "What must I do to be saved?" Trembling, the jailer fell down before Paul and Silas and asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" They said, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household" (Acts 16:30–31). This is one of the simplest gospel statements in the New Testament. Not "here is what you must do," but "believe in the Lord Jesus." "You and your household" doesn't mean that one person's faith automatically saves a family, but that the same promise is open to his whole household; and so "they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house" (Acts 16:32), and the whole household heard the word.

4. Washing wounds, washed in baptism. "And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family" (Acts 16:33). That same night the jailer washed their wounds and himself received baptism, the sign of the cleansing he had received through faith. The man who had just locked them in the stocks now set food before them, "and he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God" (Acts 16:34).

5. "We are Roman citizens." At daybreak the magistrates wanted to release them quietly. But Paul said, "They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens... Let them come themselves and take us out" (Acts 16:37). This wasn't revenge but, most likely, protection for the newborn Philippian church: with the magistrates publicly acknowledging their innocence, believers there would be harder to mistreat at will.

The point: The three people the gospel reached at Philippi were a wealthy merchant, an enslaved girl and a Roman jailer. The gospel did not change its message for anyone's status, rank or nation; to all three it was the same "Believe in the Lord Jesus," and no one stood outside his power.
Meditation

Reflect: Twice the Spirit closed a door Paul wanted to go through, and Paul's plan wasn't wrong. Is there a door in my life I badly wanted to enter that has been shut: a job I didn't get, a plan that fell through, a relationship that never began? God hasn't promised that behind every closed door is another one leading to what I wanted; the "yes" he gave Paul was the gospel entering Europe, not Paul's convenience. Can I bring this "no" to him, tell him honestly how disappointed I am, and trust that the Lord who closed it cares about more than my plans, and that he himself is my best portion? In Philippi the girl's owners saw only that "their hope of gain was gone." Do I quietly treat people as tools: an employee as numbers, a child as grades, a domestic helper as usefulness, a church member as whether they're "useful"? The Lord Jesus was priced at thirty pieces of silver, the Old Testament price of a slave (Exod 21:32; Matt 26:15); he let himself be valued as something bought and sold, so that people treated as tools could go free. Finally, Paul and Silas were "praying and singing hymns to God" at midnight, in pain and in chains. If I am in my own "midnight" now, my song may be no more than a sigh, a psalm's cry for help; but I can still open my mouth, because the Lord who was flogged for me is with me in this inner prison.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十七章记载了三座城、三种回应。帖撒罗尼迦（1-9节）：保罗在会堂讲解基督必须受害、复活，有人信了，也有人嫉妒，掀起暴动，指控他们是「那搅乱天下的」。庇哩亚（10-15节）：这里的人「甘心领受这道，天天考查圣经」。雅典（16-34节）：在哲学与偶像之城，保罗站在亚略·巴古当中，向从未读过旧约的听众讲论那位「未识之神」。

雅典的讲论和第十四章在路司得的简短讲话一样，是向没有圣经背景的人传福音；只是这一次，保罗面对的是当时希腊世界最有学问的听众之一。

深读 17:1-9 帖撒罗尼迦：另有一个王耶稣

1. 本着圣经辩论。 「保罗照他素常的规矩进去，一连三个安息日，本着圣经与他们辩论，讲解陈明基督必须受害，从死里复活；又说：『我所传与你们的这位耶稣就是基督。』」（徒17:2-3）在会堂里，保罗的方法是从犹太人自己的圣经出发。许多犹太人等候的是一位得胜的弥赛亚；保罗要证明，弥赛亚「必须」先受害，然后复活。「必须」（dei）是神计划中的必然，是圣经早已写明的（路24:26，44-46；赛53章）。

2. 「那搅乱天下的」。 不信的犹太人心里嫉妒，招聚市井匪类，闯进收留保罗的耶孙家，找不着保罗，就把耶孙拉到地方官那里，喊叫说：「那搅乱天下的也到这里来了。」（徒17:6）这是敌人的控诉，却无意中说出了真相：福音确实在翻转整个世界。

3. 「另有一个王耶稣」。 他们又说：「这些人都违背凯撒的命令，说另有一个王耶稣。」（徒17:7）这个指控在政治上是诬告，在属灵上却是真的：基督徒确实承认耶稣是万王之王。这不是说基督徒要推翻地上的政权（参罗13:1-7），而是说一切地上的权柄，都在那位万王之王的权柄之下。

要点：福音不只是给个人的安慰，也是一个宣告：耶稣是王。这宣告会搅乱一切以为自己是最高权柄的势力。
深读 17:10-15 庇哩亚：天天考查圣经

1. 贤于帖撒罗尼迦的人。 弟兄们连夜送保罗和西拉往庇哩亚去。「这地方的人贤于帖撒罗尼迦的人，甘心领受这道，天天考查圣经，要晓得这道是与不是。」（徒17:11）「贤」原文是「高贵」：不是出身高贵，而是心志高贵。

2. 两样并存。 庇哩亚人可贵之处，在于两样兼备：「甘心领受」，也「天天考查」。他们不是多疑、挑剔的人，也不是什么都照单全收的人。他们愿意听，又用圣经来检验所听的，连使徒保罗的话也不例外。

3. 结果。 「所以他们中间多有相信的。」（徒17:12）认真考查圣经，没有叫他们远离信心，反而带领他们相信。可是帖撒罗尼迦的犹太人又追到庇哩亚来挑唆，弟兄们只好把保罗送到雅典。

要点：庇哩亚人既敞开心领受，又认真用圣经检验。真正的信心不怕查考；神的话经得起最仔细的考查。
深读 17:16-21 满城都是偶像

1. 心里着急。 「保罗在雅典等候他们的时候，看见满城都是偶像，就心里着急。」（徒17:16）雅典是希腊文化的中心，有宏伟的神庙和艺术品；游客看见的是美，保罗看见的却是偶像。「着急」原文是很强烈的字，在七十士译本中用来形容神对偶像崇拜的「激怒」（参申9:18）。保罗的心与神的心一同被激动。

2. 在会堂，也在市场。 他「在会堂里与犹太人和虔敬的人，并每日在市上所遇见的人，辩论」（徒17:17）。保罗没有只待在宗教的场所，他也走进雅典人每天讨论哲学和新闻的市场。

3. 「胡言乱语的」。 伊壁鸠鲁和斯多亚两派的学士与他争论。有人说：「这胡言乱语的要说什么？」（徒17:18）「胡言乱语的」原文是「捡种子的」，指在地上啄食零星种子的鸟，后来用来讥笑东拼西凑、学问肤浅的人。还有人以为他在传「外邦鬼神」，「这话是因保罗传讲耶稣与复活的道」：「复活」一词在希腊人听来像一位女神的名字，他们也许以为「耶稣」和「复活」是一男一女两位新的神明。

深读 17:22-34 亚略·巴古的讲论

1. 从「未识之神」讲起。 「众位雅典人哪，我看你们凡事很敬畏鬼神。我游行的时候……遇见一座坛，上面写着『未识之神』。你们所不认识而敬拜的，我现在告诉你们。」（徒17:22-23）保罗从他们自己的处境开始，不是为了肯定他们的宗教，而是要指出：你们承认有一位你们不认识的神，我要告诉你们他是谁。

2. 创造主不住人手所造的殿。 「创造宇宙和其中万物的神，既是天地的主，就不住人手所造的殿，也不用人手服事，好像缺少什么；自己倒将生命、气息、万物，赐给万人。」（徒17:24-25）这几句话推翻了雅典人的整个宗教：神不需要我们的神庙、祭物和服事，是我们需要他。这也呼应司提反的话（徒7:48）。

3. 「他离我们各人不远」。 「他从一本造出万族的人」，定准他们的年限和疆界，「要叫他们寻求神，或者可以揣摩而得，其实他离我们各人不远」（徒17:26-27）。人类都出于一个祖先，没有哪个民族天生比别人高贵。神安排人的历史，是为了叫人寻求他。

4. 引用他们的诗人。 「我们生活、动作、存留，都在乎他。就如你们作诗的，有人说：『我们也是他所生的。』」（徒17:28）前一句常被认为出自克里特诗人伊庇米尼底（这说法来自较晚的注释传统），后一句出自基利家诗人亚拉图。保罗借用异教诗人的话，却把这些话放进圣经的真理里来讲。借用不等于认同：今天华人传道人引用孔孟老庄，也当如此。我们是神所造的，所以不当以为神像人手所雕刻的金、银、石（徒17:29）。

5. 悔改与审判。 讲论的高峰是：「世人蒙昧无知的时候，神并不监察，如今却吩咐各处的人都要悔改。因为他已经定了日子，要藉着他所设立的人按公义审判天下，并且叫他从死里复活，给万人作可信的凭据。」（徒17:30-31）「不监察」不是说无知就无罪（参徒17:29；罗1:18-21），而是神在忍耐中暂缓了最后的审判（参徒14:16；罗3:25）；如今基督已经来了，人当以悔改来回应神的忍耐。保罗没有停在哲学讨论上，而是讲到悔改、审判和复活。耶稣的复活，是神给全人类的「凭据」。

6. 三种回应。 「众人听见从死里复活的话，就有讥诮他的；又有人说：『我们再听你讲这个吧！』」（徒17:32）但也「有几个人贴近他，信了主」，其中有亚略·巴古的官丢尼修和一个名叫大马哩的妇人（徒17:34）。讥笑、拖延、相信：今天人听福音，仍不外这三种回应。

要点：保罗从雅典人熟悉的东西开始，却没有停在他们熟悉的地方。他讲创造、讲人人都出于一本，最后讲悔改、审判和那位复活的人。路加记下保罗在雅典讲到复活和审判；保罗后来写信回顾初到哥林多的时候，说他「定了主意，在你们中间不知道别的，只知道耶稣基督并他钉十字架」（林前2:2）。福音可以从任何地方开始，却总要走到那位为罪人死而复活的基督。
默想

默想： 庇哩亚人「甘心领受这道，天天考查圣经」。我听讲道、读属灵书籍、刷网上的短视频时，是什么都照单全收，还是习惯性地挑毛病？我打开圣经查考，是为了证明别人错了，还是因为我渴望听见神自己的声音？保罗看见雅典满城的偶像，就「心里着急」。我所生活的城市也有它的偶像：成功、名校、房子、健康、安全感。在批评别人之前，我可以先问：这些当中，哪一样在我心里也有一座庙？偶像总是向人要：要我的时间、睡眠、家庭，要孩子的童年去为它拼命。保罗所传的神却「不用人手服事，好像缺少什么；自己倒将生命、气息、万物，赐给万人」。偶像靠我的供奉而「活」，我却是靠他的赐予而活；而且他「离我们各人不远」。最后，有人听了复活的道，说：「我们再听你讲这个吧！」我是否也一直在说「以后再说」：来教会好几年，还在「再想想」要不要信、要不要受洗；或是知道有一件事该悔改，却总想等一个更好的时机？神「如今却吩咐各处的人都要悔改」，并且叫耶稣从死里复活，给万人作可信的凭据。那位要审判的，正是为我死而复活的主；我不必等到自己准备好了才转向他，他早已为我预备好了赦免。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 17 records three cities and three responses. Thessalonica (vv. 1–9): Paul explains in the synagogue that the Christ had to suffer and rise; some believe, others become jealous and stir up a riot, accusing them of being men "who have turned the world upside down." Berea (vv. 10–15): here the people "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily." Athens (vv. 16–34): in the city of philosophy and idols, Paul stands in the midst of the Areopagus and speaks to an audience that has never read the Old Testament about the "unknown god."

Like his brief words at Lystra in chapter 14, the Athens speech is preaching to people with no biblical background; but this time Paul faces one of the most learned audiences of the Greek world.

Going Deeper: 17:1–9 Thessalonica: Another King, Jesus

1. Reasoning from the Scriptures. "And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ'" (Acts 17:2–3). In the synagogue, Paul starts from the Jews' own Scriptures. Many expected a conquering Messiah; Paul shows that the Messiah "had to" suffer first and then rise. "Had to" (dei) expresses the necessity of God's plan, already written in Scripture (Luke 24:26, 44–46; Isa 53).

2. "These men who have turned the world upside down." The unbelieving Jews, jealous, gathered a mob and attacked the house of Jason, who had taken Paul in. Not finding Paul, they dragged Jason before the city authorities, shouting, "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also" (Acts 17:6). It was an enemy's charge, yet it unwittingly told the truth: the gospel really was overturning the world.

3. "Another king, Jesus." They added, "They are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus" (Acts 17:7). Politically the charge was false; spiritually it was true: Christians do confess Jesus as King of kings. This doesn't mean Christians aim to overthrow earthly governments (cf. Rom 13:1–7), but that every earthly authority stands under that higher King.

The point: The gospel is not only comfort for individuals; it is an announcement that Jesus is King. That announcement unsettles every power that thinks itself the highest authority.
Going Deeper: 17:10–15 Berea: Examining the Scriptures Daily

1. More noble than those in Thessalonica. The brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea by night. "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so" (Acts 17:11). "Noble" here describes not their birth but their attitude.

2. Two things together. The Bereans' nobility lay in holding two things together: they "received with all eagerness" and they "examined daily." They were neither suspicious and fault-finding nor ready to swallow anything. They were willing to listen, and they tested what they heard by Scripture, even the words of the apostle Paul.

3. The result. "Many of them therefore believed" (Acts 17:12). Careful study of Scripture didn't lead them away from faith; it led them to it. But Jews from Thessalonica came to Berea to stir up the crowds, and the brothers sent Paul on to Athens.

The point: The Bereans opened their hearts to receive and searched the Scriptures to test. Real faith is not afraid of investigation; God's word stands up to the most careful examination.
Going Deeper: 17:16–21 A City Full of Idols

1. Provoked within. "Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16). Athens was the center of Greek culture, full of magnificent temples and art; tourists saw beauty, Paul saw idols. "Provoked" is a strong word; in the Septuagint it describes God being provoked by idolatry (cf. Deut 9:18). Paul's heart was stirred along with God's.

2. In the synagogue, and in the marketplace. He "reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there" (Acts 17:17). Paul didn't stay in religious settings; he went into the marketplace where Athenians discussed philosophy and news every day.

3. "This babbler." Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him. Some said, "What does this babbler wish to say?" (Acts 17:18). "Babbler" is literally "seed-picker," a bird pecking at scattered seeds, used to mock someone who picks up scraps of learning. Others thought he was proclaiming "foreign divinities," "because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection": they may have thought "Jesus" and "Resurrection" (Anastasis) were a new pair of gods, male and female.

Going Deeper: 17:22–34 The Areopagus Speech

1. Beginning with the "unknown god." "Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription, 'To the unknown god.' What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you" (Acts 17:22–23). Paul begins where they are, not to affirm their religion, but to point out that they admit there is a God they don't know, and he will tell them who he is.

2. The Creator does not live in temples made by hands. "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything" (Acts 17:24–25). These sentences overturn the whole of Athenian religion: God doesn't need our temples, sacrifices or service; we need him. It also echoes Stephen (Acts 7:48).

3. "Not far from each one of us." "He made from one man every nation of mankind," determining their times and boundaries, "that they should seek God, in the hope that they might feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us" (Acts 17:26–27). All humanity comes from one ancestor; no people is innately nobler than another. God orders human history so that people will seek him.

4. Quoting their poets. "'In him we live and move and have our being'; as even some of your own poets have said, 'For we are indeed his offspring'" (Acts 17:28). The first line is often attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides (an attribution resting on a later commentary tradition), the second to the Cilician poet Aratus. Paul borrows pagan poets' words but sets them within biblical truth. Quoting is not endorsing; the same holds when Chinese preachers quote Confucius or Laozi. we are God's creatures, so we shouldn't think God is like an image of gold, silver or stone made by human hands (Acts 17:29).

5. Repentance and judgment. The speech peaks here: "The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:30–31). "Overlooked" does not mean ignorance was innocent (cf. Acts 17:29; Rom 1:18–21), but that God in forbearance held back final judgment (cf. Acts 14:16; Rom 3:25). Now that Christ has come, that patience calls for repentance. Paul doesn't stop at philosophical discussion; he moves on to repentance, judgment and resurrection. Jesus' resurrection is God's "assurance" to all humanity.

6. Three responses. "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this'" (Acts 17:32). But "some men joined him and believed," among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:34). Mockery, delay, belief: the three responses are the same today.

The point: Paul began with what the Athenians knew, but didn't stay there. He spoke of creation and of all people coming from one man, and finally of repentance, judgment and the man God raised. Luke records Paul in Athens reaching the resurrection and judgment; later, writing back about his arrival in Corinth, Paul said he "decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified" (1 Cor 2:2). The gospel can begin anywhere, but it always arrives at the Christ who died for sinners and was raised.
Meditation

Reflect: The Bereans "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily." When I listen to sermons, read Christian books or scroll through short videos online, do I swallow everything, or habitually find fault? And when I open my Bible to check, is it to prove someone wrong, or because I long to hear God himself? Seeing Athens full of idols, Paul's "spirit was provoked within him." My city has its idols too: success, top schools, property, health, security. Before I criticize anyone else, I can ask: which of these has a temple in my own heart? Idols keep asking: for my time, my sleep, my family, my children's childhood. The God Paul preached "is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything." Idols live off my offerings; I live off his gifts, and "he is actually not far from each one of us." Finally, some heard of the resurrection and said, "We will hear you again about this." Have I been saying "later" too: coming to church for years while still "thinking about" believing or being baptized, or knowing there is something to repent of but waiting for a better time? God "now commands all people everywhere to repent," and he has given assurance by raising Jesus from the dead. The coming Judge is the one who died and rose for me; I don't have to wait until I feel ready to turn to him, because he has already made forgiveness ready.
