entries.verse_text: 惟有不做工的，只信称罪人为义的神，他的信就算为义。
entries.content:
本章脉络

罗3:28说：「人称义是因着信，不在乎遵行律法。」犹太读者一定会问：那么亚伯拉罕呢？犹太人的祖宗，岂不是因为顺服神才蒙悦纳的吗？第四章就用亚伯拉罕作例证，证明因信称义不是保罗的新发明，而是律法书本身的见证（罗3:21，31）。

本章分四段。不是因行为（1-8节）：「亚伯拉罕信神，这就算为他的义」（罗4:3，引创15:6）；大卫也称「主不算为有罪的」人是有福的。不是因割礼（9-12节）：亚伯拉罕称义在受割礼以前，所以他是一切信之人的父，不论受割礼与否。不是因律法（13-17节）：应许是「因信而得的义」，所以「就属乎恩」。信心的样式（17-25节）：亚伯拉罕所信的，是「那叫死人复活、使无变为有的神」；我们所信的，是使耶稣从死里复活的神。

深读 4:1-8 算为义

1. 亚伯拉罕有可夸的吗？ 「倘若亚伯拉罕是因行为称义，就有可夸的；只是在神面前并无可夸。」（罗4:2）当时一些犹太教导，强调亚伯拉罕的顺服，特别是献以撒（创22章），认为他因此蒙神悦纳。保罗却回到更早的一节经文。（雅各书2:21-23也引用了这些经文，雅各讲的是用行为证明信心是真的，而不是称义的根据。）

2. 「算为他的义」。 「经上说什么呢？说：『亚伯拉罕信神，这就算为他的义。』」（罗4:3；引创15:6）「算」（原文 logizomai）可以用在记账上（如罗4:4），意思是记在某人的账上；七十士译本在创15:6就用这个字。这个字在第四章出现十一次。亚伯拉罕的义，不是他自己挣来的，而是神「算」给他的。要留意：信心本身不是一种代替行为的功劳；保罗说神是「在行为以外」把「义」算给人（罗4:6，11）。信心只是空手，领受神所算给的义。

3. 工价与恩典。 「做工的得工价，不算恩典，乃是该得的；惟有不做工的，只信称罪人为义的神，他的信就算为义。」（罗4:4-5）这是本章最令人惊讶的一句话。「称罪人为义」，原文是「称不敬虔的人为义」。旧约要求审判官不可「定恶人为义」（箴17:15），神自己也说：「我必不以恶人为义」（出23:7）。那么，神怎能「称不敬虔的人为义」，而不违背自己的公义呢？答案在罗3:25-26：神设立耶稣作挽回祭，基督在十字架上担当了他们罪的刑罚，所以神称信的人为义，「使人知道他自己为义」。神不是对罪视而不见，而是在基督身上审判了罪。神所称为义的，不是已经变好的人，而是「不敬虔的人」。这就是福音的好消息：我们不需要先把自己变好，才能来到神面前。

4. 大卫的见证。 「得赦免其过、遮盖其罪的，这人是有福的。主不算为有罪的，这人是有福的。」（罗4:7-8；引诗32:1-2）大卫犯了奸淫和谋杀，正是一个「不敬虔的人」，却经历了神的赦免。这里有一个美丽的对照：神把义「算」给信的人，却不把罪「算」在他们身上。

要点：神所称为义的，是「不敬虔的人」。称义不是工价，而是恩典：我们不必先变好才能来到神面前，而是空着手来，领受神白白算给我们的义。
深读 4:9-12 割礼以前

1. 时间的先后。 「是怎么算的呢？是在他受割礼的时候呢？是在他未受割礼的时候呢？不是在受割礼的时候，乃是在未受割礼的时候。」（罗4:10）创世记十五章亚伯拉罕因信称义，到十七章他才受割礼，中间相隔至少十三年（参创16:16；创17:24）。

2. 记号与印证。 「并且他受了割礼的记号，作他未受割礼的时候因信称义的印证。」（罗4:11）割礼不是称义的原因，而是称义的「印证」，像盖在文件上的印章，证明里面所写的是真实的。许多信徒（特别是改革宗传统）从这里看到圣礼的意义（参西2:11-12）：洗礼和圣餐是主所命定的恩典的记号和印证，用来坚固我们的信心；它们是必须遵守的，却不是我们称义的根据。

3. 一切信之人的父。 这样，亚伯拉罕就「作一切未受割礼而信之人的父」，也「作受割礼之人的父」，就是那些「按我们的祖宗亚伯拉罕未受割礼而信之踪迹去行的人」（罗4:11-12）。在神的家里，血统不能叫人成为亚伯拉罕的儿女，只有信才能。

要点：亚伯拉罕在受割礼以前就已经称义，所以宗教的仪式不能叫人称义；它只是印证神已经藉着信所赐下的义。
深读 4:13-17 本乎信，属乎恩

1. 承受世界。 「因为神应许亚伯拉罕和他后裔，必得承受世界，不是因律法，乃是因信而得的义。」（罗4:13）神原来应许亚伯拉罕的是迦南地（创12:7；创15:18），也应许地上的万族要因他得福（创12:3）。这应许从一开始就是普世的：亚伯拉罕要「作多国的父」（创17:4-6），他的后裔要得着仇敌的城门（创22:17-18），诗篇也盼望那位王「执掌权柄，从这海直到那海」（诗72:8）。这应许在基督，就是那「一个子孙」，以及一切属基督的人身上得着应验（加3:16，29）；神的应许最终是要更新整个受造界（参罗8:19-21）。

2. 律法惹动忿怒。 「若是属乎律法的人才得为后嗣，信就归于虚空，应许也就废弃了。因为律法是惹动忿怒的。」（罗4:14-15）如果应许要靠遵守律法才能得着，没有人能得着，因为人人都违背了律法。

3. 「本乎信，因此就属乎恩」。 「所以人得为后嗣是本乎信，因此就属乎恩，叫应许定然归给一切后裔。」（罗4:16）信和恩典是连在一起的：正因为是靠信，所以是恩典；正因为是恩典，应许才「定然」，也就是确定、稳固。如果应许要靠我们，它就永远不会稳固；正因为它靠的是神，所以它是确定的。

要点：应许若靠我们的表现，就永远不会稳固；正因为它本乎信、属乎恩，靠的是神的信实，所以它是确定的。
深读 4:17-25 叫死人复活的神

1. 亚伯拉罕所信的神。 「亚伯拉罕所信的，是那叫死人复活、使无变为有的神。」（罗4:17）信心的力量，不在于信心本身，而在于所信的对象。亚伯拉罕的信心之所以伟大，是因为他所信的神，能从无中创造，能从死里带出生命。

2. 无可指望中的指望。 「他在无可指望的时候，因信仍有指望。」（罗4:18）这句话原文很有力：「在指望以外，仍在指望中相信。」按人的眼光，一切都已经没有指望；可是亚伯拉罕把眼光放在神的应许上。

3. 正视事实的信心。 「他将近百岁的时候，虽然想到自己的身体如同已死，撒拉的生育已经断绝，他的信心还是不软弱。」（罗4:19）信心不是闭上眼睛不看现实。亚伯拉罕很清楚地「想到」自己的身体如同已死，他没有假装事情不是这样；他只是相信，神比这个事实更大。

4. 将荣耀归给神。 「并且仰望神的应许，总没有因不信心里起疑惑，反倒因信心里得坚固，将荣耀归给神，且满心相信神所应许的必能做成。」（罗4:20-21）这不是说亚伯拉罕从来没有软弱：他曾两次说妻子是他的妹子（创12章；20章），也曾想靠夏甲生子（创16章），甚至在神应许时「就俯伏在地喜笑」（创17:17）。保罗描写的不是一份毫无瑕疵的记录，而是他信心的总方向：从整体来看，他的信心是一直望着神的。信心本身就是「将荣耀归给神」：它承认神是信实的，神是有能力的。这和罗1:21正好相反：在那里，人「不当作神荣耀他」；在这里，信心把荣耀归给神。

5. 为我们写的。 「『算为他义』的这句话不是单为他写的，也是为我们将来得算为义之人写的，就是我们这信神使我们的主耶稣从死里复活的人。」（罗4:23-24）亚伯拉罕信神能从「如同已死」的身体中带出生命；我们信神已经使耶稣从死里复活。我们的信心，和亚伯拉罕的信心，是同一种信心，所信的是同一位神。

6. 被交与复活。 「耶稣被交给人，是为我们的过犯；复活，是为叫我们称义。」（罗4:25）这句话很可能是初期教会的一句信仰宣告，回应以赛亚书53章的受苦仆人。「被交给人」是神亲自把他交出来（参罗8:32）。耶稣的死，是替我们担当了罪的刑罚；耶稣的复活，证明神已经接纳了他的牺牲，也宣告了我们的称义。

要点：信心的力量不在信心本身，而在所信的神：他叫死人复活，使无变为有。信心正视现实，却相信神比现实更大，这样的信心就是把荣耀归给神。
默想

默想： 「惟有不做工的，只信称罪人为义的神。」我是否仍然觉得，必须先把自己的生命整理好一点，神才会接纳我？保罗说，神所称为义的，正是「不敬虔的人」。这个好消息，我是只在信主的那一天需要，还是今天、在我又一次失败以后，也同样需要？再想想亚伯拉罕：他没有假装自己的身体不是「如同已死」，却仍然相信神。在我的生命中，有没有一件事，在人看来已经「无可指望」：一段破裂的关系、一个久治不愈的病、一个还没有信主的家人？我能不能像亚伯拉罕一样，诚实地面对现实，却仍把眼光放在那位「叫死人复活、使无变为有的神」身上？我的信心可能很软弱，可是我所信的神并不软弱。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Romans 3:28 says, "one is justified by faith apart from works of the law." A Jewish reader would immediately ask: what about Abraham? Wasn't the forefather of Israel accepted by God because he obeyed? Chapter 4 uses Abraham to prove that justification by faith is not Paul's invention but the testimony of the Law itself (Romans 3:21, 31).

The chapter has four parts. Not by works (vv. 1–8): "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3, quoting Gen 15:6); David too calls blessed the one "against whom the Lord will not count his sin." Not by circumcision (vv. 9–12): Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not. Not by the law (vv. 13–17): the promise came "through the righteousness of faith," so it "rests on grace." The shape of faith (vv. 17–25): Abraham believed the God "who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist"; we believe in the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

Going Deeper: 4:1–8 Counted as Righteousness

1. Did Abraham have something to boast of? "For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God" (Romans 4:2). Some Jewish teaching of the time stressed Abraham's obedience, especially the offering of Isaac (Gen 22), as the reason God accepted him. Paul goes back to an earlier verse. (James 2:21–23 cites these texts too; James speaks of works showing that faith is genuine, not of the ground of justification.)

2. "Counted to him as righteousness." "For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness'" (Romans 4:3, quoting Gen 15:6). "Counted" (logizomai) is a word that can be used of keeping accounts (as in Romans 4:4): to credit something to someone's account; it is the Septuagint's word in Gen 15:6. It appears eleven times in chapter 4. Abraham's righteousness was not something he earned but something God "counted" to him. Note that faith is not a substitute merit that God accepts in place of works; Paul says God counts righteousness "apart from works" (Romans 4:6, 11). Faith is the empty hand that receives it.

3. Wages and grace. "Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but trusts him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness" (Romans 4:4–5). This is the most astonishing sentence in the chapter. The Old Testament forbade judges to justify the wicked (Prov 17:15), and God said of himself, "I will not acquit the wicked" (Exod 23:7). How then can God "justify the ungodly" without betraying his own justice? The answer is Romans 3:25–26: God put Christ forward as a propitiation, and Christ bore the penalty of their sin, so that God is "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus." God does not overlook sin; he has judged it in Christ. The people God justifies are not those who have already improved, but "the ungodly." This is the good news of the gospel: we don't have to make ourselves better before we can come to God.

4. David's testimony. "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" (Romans 4:7–8, quoting Ps 32:1–2). David, an adulterer and murderer, was just such an "ungodly" man, and he knew God's forgiveness. There is a beautiful contrast: God "counts" righteousness to those who believe, and does not "count" their sin against them.

The point: The people God justifies are "the ungodly." Justification is not a wage but a gift: we don't first become good and then come to God; we come with empty hands and receive the righteousness God freely credits to us.
Going Deeper: 4:9–12 Before Circumcision

1. Which came first. "How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised" (Romans 4:10). Abraham was justified by faith in Genesis 15 and circumcised only in Genesis 17, at least thirteen years later (cf. Gen 16:16; Gen 17:24).

2. Sign and seal. "He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised" (Romans 4:11). Circumcision was not the cause of his justification but its "seal," like the stamp on a document that certifies what is written in it. Many Christians, especially in the Reformed tradition, see here a pattern for the sacraments (cf. Col 2:11–12): baptism and the Lord's Supper are signs and seals of grace, commanded by Christ to strengthen faith. They are not optional, but they are not the ground of our justification.

3. Father of all who believe. So Abraham became "the father of all who believe without being circumcised," and "the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised" (Romans 4:11–12). In God's family, bloodline doesn't make anyone a child of Abraham; only faith does.

The point: Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, so religious ritual cannot justify anyone; it only seals the righteousness God has already given through faith.
Going Deeper: 4:13–17 By Faith, Resting on Grace

1. Heir of the world. "For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith" (Romans 4:13). God first promised Abraham the land of Canaan (Gen 12:7; Gen 15:18), and that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him (Gen 12:3). The promise had a worldwide horizon from the start: Abraham would be "the father of a multitude of nations" (Gen 17:4–6), his offspring would possess the gate of his enemies (Gen 22:17–18), and the Psalms look for a king who rules "from sea to sea" (Ps 72:8). It is fulfilled in Christ, the offspring, and in all who belong to him (Gal 3:16, 29), and finally in a renewed creation (cf. Romans 8:19–21).

2. The law brings wrath. "For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void. For the law brings wrath" (Romans 4:14–15). If the promise depended on keeping the law, no one would receive it, since everyone has broken the law.

3. "It depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace." "That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring" (Romans 4:16). Faith and grace belong together: because it is by faith, it is by grace; because it is by grace, the promise is "guaranteed," that is, sure and firm. If the promise depended on us, it would never be secure; because it depends on God, it is certain.

The point: A promise resting on our performance would never be secure; because it depends on faith and rests on grace, on God's faithfulness, it is certain.
Going Deeper: 4:17–25 The God Who Gives Life to the Dead

1. The God Abraham believed. Abraham believed the God "who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Romans 4:17). The power of faith lies not in faith itself but in its object. Abraham's faith was great because the God he trusted can create out of nothing and bring life out of death.

2. Hope against hope. "In hope he believed against hope" (Romans 4:18); literally, "against hope, in hope he believed." By human reckoning there was nothing left to hope for; but Abraham fixed his eyes on God's promise.

3. Faith that faces the facts. "He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:19). Faith does not close its eyes to reality. Abraham clearly "considered" that his body was as good as dead; he did not pretend otherwise. He simply believed that God was bigger than the facts.

4. Giving glory to God. "No distrust made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised" (Romans 4:20–21). This doesn't mean Abraham was never weak: twice he passed off his wife as his sister (Gen 12; 20), he tried to gain a son through Hagar (Gen 16), and he even laughed at God's promise (Gen 17:17). Paul describes not a flawless record but the settled direction of his trust: taken as a whole, his faith kept looking to God. Faith itself "gives glory to God": it confesses that God is faithful and able. It is the exact reverse of Romans 1:21: there people "did not honor him as God"; here faith gives him glory.

5. Written for us. "But the words 'it was counted to him' were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord" (Romans 4:23–24). Abraham believed God could bring life out of a body "as good as dead"; we believe God has raised Jesus from the dead. Our faith and Abraham's are the same kind of faith in the same God.

6. Delivered up and raised. "Who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification" (Romans 4:25). This may well be an early Christian confession echoing the suffering servant of Isaiah 53. "Delivered up" means that God himself handed him over (cf. Romans 8:32). Jesus' death bore the penalty of our sins; his resurrection shows that God accepted his sacrifice and declares our justification.

The point: The power of faith lies not in faith itself but in the God it trusts, who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not exist. Faith faces reality yet trusts that God is greater, and such faith gives glory to God.
Meditation

Reflect: "To the one who does not work but trusts him who justifies the ungodly." Do I still feel I need to get my life in better order before God will accept me? Paul says the very people God justifies are "the ungodly." Is this good news something I needed only on the day I first believed, or do I need it just as much today, after yet another failure? Think too of Abraham: he did not pretend his body was not "as good as dead," yet he still believed God. Is there something in my life that looks "beyond hope": a broken relationship, a long illness, a family member who has not yet believed? Can I, like Abraham, face the facts honestly and still fix my eyes on the God "who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist"? My faith may be weak, but the God I trust is not.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第五章是罗马书的第二个大段落（5–8章）的开始。前四章讲人怎样称义；从这里开始，保罗讲称义的人得着了什么，以及他们的盼望为什么是稳固的。

本章分两部分。称义的果效（1-11节）：「我们既因信称义，就藉着我们的主耶稣基督得与神相和」；我们站在恩典中，在患难中也欢喜，因为神的爱已经浇灌在我们心里，而这爱的明证，是「基督在我们还作罪人的时候为我们死」。亚当与基督（12-21节）：罪和死藉着一个人进入世界，临到众人；义和生命也藉着一个人，耶稣基督，更加丰盛地临到一切属他的人。「罪在哪里显多，恩典就更显多了。」

第五至八章有一个首尾呼应：本章以「神的爱」开始（罗5:5，8），第八章以「神的爱」结束（罗8:39）。中间的一切，都被神的爱包围着。

深读 5:1-5 称义的人得着什么

1. 与神相和。 「我们既因信称义，就藉着我们的主耶稣基督得与神相和。」（罗5:1）「相和」不只是心里感到平安，而是我们和神之间的关系改变了：从前我们是「仇敌」（罗5:10），在神的忿怒之下（罗1:18）；如今战争已经结束。这和平是一个事实，不是一种感觉；即使我们感觉不到，它也仍然是真的。（不少重要的古抄本作「让我们与神相和吧」，原文两个字只差一个字母，当时读音几乎相同；可是多数学者和译本根据上下文，认为保罗是在陈述一个已经成就的事实。）

2. 站在恩典中。 「我们又藉着他，因信得进入现在所站的这恩典中。」（罗5:2）「进入」这个词，有被引见到君王面前的意思。我们不是偶尔进入恩典，又偶尔被赶出来；我们「站」在恩典中，这是我们的位置。

3. 盼望神的荣耀。 「并且欢欢喜喜盼望神的荣耀。」（罗5:2）人「亏缺了神的荣耀」（罗3:23）；可是称义的人，盼望有一天要分享神的荣耀（罗8:18，30）。

4. 在患难中也欢喜。 「不但如此，就是在患难中也是欢欢喜喜的；因为知道患难生忍耐，忍耐生老练，老练生盼望。」（罗5:3-4）保罗不是说患难本身是快乐的，而是说我们「知道」神在患难中做什么。「老练」原文是经过试验而证明是真的，像金子经过火炼。患难不会叫信徒的盼望消失，反倒叫它更坚固。

5. 盼望不至于羞耻。 「盼望不至于羞耻，因为所赐给我们的圣灵将神的爱浇灌在我们心里。」（罗5:5）「不至于羞耻」，就是不会落空，不会叫我们失望。为什么？因为我们的盼望不是建立在我们的感觉或环境上，而是建立在神的爱上；而圣灵把这爱「浇灌」在我们心里，这正是约珥书所应许、五旬节所应验的「浇灌」（珥2:28；徒2:17，33），像大雨倾盆，不是一点一滴。

要点：称义的人与神相和，站在恩典中，盼望神的荣耀。患难不能夺去这盼望，反而使它更坚固，因为它建立在神已经浇灌在我们心里的爱上。
深读 5:6-11 神的爱就在此显明

1. 在我们还软弱的时候。 「因我们还软弱的时候，基督就按所定的日期为罪人死。」（罗5:6）保罗用了几个词来描写我们：「软弱」（罗5:6）、「罪人」（原文是「不敬虔的人」，罗5:6；参罗4:5）、「罪人」（罗5:8）、「仇敌」（罗5:10）。基督不是为好人死的，而是为这样的人死的。

2. 人间最高的爱。 「为义人死，是少有的；为仁人死，或者有敢做的。」（罗5:7）人间最高的爱，是愿意为一个好人舍命，而这样的人也是「少有的」。

3. 神的爱。 「惟有基督在我们还作罪人的时候为我们死，神的爱就在此向我们显明了。」（罗5:8）神的爱和人的爱不同：人的爱，是因为对方可爱；神的爱，是在我们一点也不可爱的时候临到我们。「显明」是现在时态：十字架不只是过去的一件事，它今天仍然在向我们证明神的爱。还要留意，保罗说是「神的爱」在基督的死上显明：十字架不是儿子说服了一位不情愿的父，而是父亲自差遣儿子（罗8:3，32），显明他自己的爱：神的爱预备了他的公义所要求的挽回祭（罗3:25）。

4. 「就更要」。 「现在我们既靠着他的血称义，就更要藉着他免去神的忿怒。因为我们作仇敌的时候，且藉着神儿子的死，得与神和好；既已和好，就更要因他的生得救了。」（罗5:9-10）这是从难到易的推论：神在我们作仇敌的时候，尚且为我们付出了最大的代价；如今我们已经成了他的朋友，他岂不更要保守我们到底吗？「因他的生得救」，是指复活的基督长远活着，为我们代求（罗8:34）。我们将来的得救，不是建立在我们的表现上，而是建立在神过去已经为我们所做的事上。

5. 以神为乐。 「不但如此，我们既藉着我主耶稣基督得与神和好，也就藉着他以神为乐。」（罗5:11）救恩的终极目的，不只是免去忿怒，也不只是得着福气，而是得着神自己。和好的最高峰，是「以神为乐」。

要点：神的爱不是因为我们可爱，而是在我们还作罪人、作仇敌的时候就临到我们。神既在那时为我们付出了儿子的生命，如今就更要保守我们到底。救恩最大的福气，是得着神自己。
深读 5:12-21 亚当与基督

1. 一人入了世界。 「这就如罪是从一人入了世界，死又是从罪来的，于是死就临到众人，因为众人都犯了罪。」（罗5:12）保罗回到创世记第三章。罪不是人类的本来面目，而是一个「入侵者」；死也是这样，它不是自然的，而是罪的结果。

2. 「因为众人都犯了罪」。 「因为」（原文 eph' hō）多数学者理解为「因为」，而不是奥古斯丁所用拉丁译本的「在他里面」。这句话怎样理解，历来有不同的看法：

  • 有人认为，意思是每个人都亲自犯了罪；可是他们犯罪，是因为从亚当承受了败坏的本性（参罗5:19「成为罪人」），所以亚当的罪仍是根源。
  • 也有许多解经家（包括许多改革宗传统的解经家）认为，意思是众人在亚当里犯了罪：亚当作为人类的代表，他的罪算在所有人身上。他们的理由是：罗5:13-14说，从亚当到摩西，死也临到那些「不与亚当犯一样罪过的」人；罗5:18-19更明说「因一次的过犯，众人都被定罪」、「因一人的悖逆，众人成为罪人」。

两种看法都同意，每个人都是罪人，都需要救恩；而保罗的重点，是要拿亚当来和基督对比。

3. 亚当是预像。 「亚当乃是那以后要来之人的预像。」（罗5:14）亚当和基督都是「代表」：亚当所做的，影响了所有在他里面的人；基督所做的，也影响了所有在他里面的人。这样的代表观念，对现代人很陌生，我们习惯以为每个人只为自己负责。可是保罗的论证正是建立在这个代表的原则上：我们若觉得「在亚当里被定罪」不公平，就要记得，我们得救的盼望也正是「在基督里被称义」，靠的是另一个人的顺从，而不是我们自己（罗5:18-19）。

4. 「何况……更加」。 保罗不只说亚当和基督相似，更说基督远远超过亚当。「只是过犯不如恩赐……何况神的恩典，与那因耶稣基督一人恩典中的赏赐，岂不更加倍地临到众人吗？」（罗5:15）亚当的一次过犯，带来了定罪；可是基督的恩赐，是「由许多过犯而称义」（罗5:16）。恩典不只是把我们带回亚当犯罪以前的光景，而是带我们去到一个更高的地方：「在生命中作王」（罗5:17）。

5. 一次的义行，一人的顺从。 「因一次的过犯，众人都被定罪；照样，因一次的义行，众人也就被称义得生命了。因一人的悖逆，众人成为罪人；照样，因一人的顺从，众人也成为义了。」（罗5:18-19）「一次的义行」，可能指基督在十字架上的死，也可能指他一生的顺服，在十字架上达到顶峰（参腓2:8）。「成为义」的「成为」，原文的意思是「被立为」「被算为」，是地位的改变：正如因亚当的悖逆，众人被定为罪人；照样，因基督的顺从，信的人被定为义人。这里的「众人」，从上下文看，是指一切属基督的人，就是那些「受洪恩又蒙所赐之义的」（罗5:17），不是说每一个人都必然得救。

6. 恩典更显多。 「律法本是外添的，叫过犯显多；只是罪在哪里显多，恩典就更显多了。」（罗5:20）律法使罪成为明知故犯的过犯，叫过犯显多（罗4:15；罗5:13；罗7:7-13）。可是无论罪有多深，恩典总是比罪更深。最后两个「作王」对比：「就如罪作王叫人死；照样，恩典也藉着义作王，叫人因我们的主耶稣基督得永生。」（罗5:21）

要点：亚当和基督都是人类的代表。在亚当里，罪和死临到众人；在基督里，恩典和生命更加丰盛地临到一切属他的人。罪无论多深，恩典总是更深。
默想

默想： 保罗说，「神的爱就在此向我们显明了」：不是在我变好的时候，而是在我「还作罪人」、甚至「作仇敌」的时候。当我怀疑神是否爱我时，我常常看的是什么：我最近的表现、我的感觉、我的环境？保罗要我回头看十字架，因为神的爱是在那里「显明」的，而那里的证据今天仍然有效。如果神在我作他仇敌的时候都愿意为我舍了他的儿子，那么在我今天的软弱、失败、患难中，他岂会撇下我？再想想第一节：「得与神相和」。我是否把这和平当作一种时有时无的感觉？其实它是一个已经成就的事实。最后，保罗说，救恩的最高峰是「以神为乐」。我是只想从神那里得着平安、福气和盼望，还是渴慕得着神自己？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 5 opens the letter's second major section (chs. 5–8). The first four chapters explained how people are justified; from here Paul explains what justified people receive, and why their hope is secure.

The chapter has two parts. The fruits of justification (vv. 1–11): "since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ"; we stand in grace, rejoice even in suffering, because God's love has been poured into our hearts, and the proof of that love is that "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Adam and Christ (vv. 12–21): sin and death entered the world through one man and spread to all; righteousness and life came through one man, Jesus Christ, abounding far more to all who belong to him. "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more."

Chapters 5–8 are framed by God's love: this chapter begins with "God's love" (Romans 5:5, 8), and chapter 8 ends with "the love of God" (Romans 8:39). Everything in between is enclosed by God's love.

Going Deeper: 5:1–5 What the Justified Receive

1. Peace with God. "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1). "Peace" is not only a feeling of calm but a changed relationship: once we were "enemies" (Romans 5:10), under God's wrath (Romans 1:18); now the war is over. This peace is a fact, not a feeling; even when we don't feel it, it remains true. (Many important early manuscripts read "let us have peace with God"; the two Greek words differ by one letter and sounded alike. But most scholars and translations judge from the context that Paul is stating an accomplished fact.)

2. Standing in grace. "Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand" (Romans 5:2). "Access" carries the sense of being introduced into a king's presence. We don't drift in and out of grace; we "stand" in it. It is where we are.

3. Hope of the glory of God. "And we rejoice in hope of the glory of God" (Romans 5:2). Humanity "falls short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23); but the justified hope one day to share in God's glory (Romans 8:18, 30).

4. Rejoicing even in suffering. "More than that, we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3–4). Paul isn't saying suffering is pleasant in itself, but that we "know" what God is doing through it. "Character" means proven genuineness, like gold tested in fire. Suffering doesn't extinguish a believer's hope; it makes it firmer.

5. Hope that does not put us to shame. "And hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" (Romans 5:5). "Not put to shame" means it won't disappoint us or come to nothing. Why? Because our hope rests not on our feelings or circumstances but on God's love, which the Spirit has "poured" into our hearts, the very word for the outpouring promised in Joel and fulfilled at Pentecost (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17, 33), like a downpour, not a trickle.

The point: The justified have peace with God, stand in grace and hope for God's glory. Suffering cannot take that hope away; it makes it firmer, because it rests on the love God has already poured into our hearts.
Going Deeper: 5:6–11 God Shows His Love

1. While we were still weak. "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). Paul uses several words for us: "weak" (Romans 5:6), "ungodly" (Romans 5:6; cf. Romans 4:5), "sinners" (Romans 5:8), "enemies" (Romans 5:10). Christ didn't die for good people but for people like this.

2. The highest human love. "For one will scarcely die for a righteous person, though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die" (Romans 5:7). The highest human love is willingness to lay down one's life for a good person, and even that is "scarce."

3. God's love. "But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). God's love differs from human love: we love because the other is lovable; God's love came to us when we were not lovable at all. "Shows" is present tense: the cross is not only a past event; it still proves God's love to us today. Notice too that Paul says it is "God's love" shown in Christ's death: the cross is not the Son persuading a reluctant Father, but the Father himself sending the Son (Romans 8:3, 32) and showing his own love: God's love provides the propitiation his justice requires (Romans 3:25).

4. "Much more." "Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life" (Romans 5:9–10). This is an argument from the harder to the easier: if God paid the highest price for us while we were his enemies, won't he much more keep us to the end now that we are his friends? "Saved by his life" refers to the risen Christ, who lives forever and intercedes for us (Romans 8:34). Our future salvation rests not on our performance but on what God has already done for us.

5. Rejoicing in God. "More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (Romans 5:11). The final goal of salvation is not only escape from wrath, nor only receiving blessings, but receiving God himself. The summit of reconciliation is "rejoicing in God."

The point: God's love did not come because we were lovable; it came to us while we were still sinners and enemies. If God gave his Son's life for us then, he will much more keep us to the end now. The greatest blessing of salvation is God himself.
Going Deeper: 5:12–21 Adam and Christ

1. Through one man. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). Paul returns to Genesis 3. Sin is not humanity's original nature but an "invader"; so too is death, which is not natural but the result of sin.

2. "Because all sinned." Most scholars take eph' hō as "because," not "in whom" as in the Latin version Augustine used. The phrase has been understood in different ways:

  • Some take it to mean that each person has personally sinned; but they sin because they have inherited a corrupt nature from Adam (cf. Romans 5:19, "made sinners"), so Adam's sin remains the root.
  • Many interpreters (including many in the Reformed tradition) take it to mean that all sinned in Adam: Adam acted as humanity's representative, and his sin is counted to all. They point out that Romans 5:13–14 says death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those "whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam," and that Romans 5:18–19 states plainly that "one trespass led to condemnation for all men" and "by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners."

Both views agree that everyone is a sinner who needs salvation; and Paul's main purpose is to set Adam alongside Christ.

3. Adam as a type. "Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come" (Romans 5:14). Adam and Christ are both "representatives": what Adam did affected all who are in him; what Christ did affects all who are in him. Such representation feels foreign to modern people, used to thinking that each of us answers only for ourselves. Yet Paul's argument rests on this very principle of representation: if being condemned "in Adam" seems unfair, remember that our only hope is being justified "in Christ," by another's obedience rather than our own (Romans 5:18–19).

4. "Much more." Paul doesn't only say that Adam and Christ are alike; he says Christ far surpasses Adam. "But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many" (Romans 5:15). Adam's one trespass brought condemnation; but Christ's gift "following many trespasses brought justification" (Romans 5:16). Grace doesn't simply return us to where Adam was before he fell; it takes us higher: to "reign in life" (Romans 5:17).

5. One act of righteousness, one man's obedience. "Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:18–19). "One act of righteousness" may refer to Christ's death on the cross, or to his whole life of obedience reaching its climax at the cross (cf. Phil 2:8). "Made" (kathistēmi) means "appointed" or "constituted," a change of status: as Adam's disobedience constituted the many sinners, so Christ's obedience constitutes believers righteous. In context, "all" and "the many" here refer to all who belong to Christ, "those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness" (Romans 5:17); Paul is not saying that every person will inevitably be saved.

6. Grace abounding. "Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more" (Romans 5:20). The law turned sin into conscious transgression and made it abound (Romans 4:15; Romans 5:13; Romans 7:7–13). But however deep sin goes, grace goes deeper still. The chapter ends with two reigns: "so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 5:21).

The point: Adam and Christ are both representatives of humanity. In Adam, sin and death came to all; in Christ, grace and life abound far more to all who belong to him. However deep sin goes, grace goes deeper.
Meditation

Reflect: Paul says, "God shows his love for us": not when I've improved, but while I was "still a sinner," even an "enemy." When I doubt that God loves me, what do I usually look at: my recent performance, my feelings, my circumstances? Paul turns me back to the cross, because that is where God's love is "shown," and that evidence still stands today. If God gave his Son for me while I was his enemy, will he abandon me now, in today's weakness, failure or suffering? Think too of verse 1: "we have peace with God." Do I treat this peace as a feeling that comes and goes? In fact it is an accomplished fact. Finally, Paul says the summit of salvation is to "rejoice in God." Do I want only peace, blessing and hope from God, or do I long for God himself?

entries.verse_text: 这样，你们向罪也当看自己是死的；向神在基督耶稣里，却当看自己是活的。
entries.content:
本章脉络

罗5:20说：「罪在哪里显多，恩典就更显多了。」这句话很容易被人误用：既然这样，我们多犯罪，岂不是叫恩典更多吗？第六章就是回答这个问题。保罗两次提出类似的问题，两次都回答「断乎不可」。

第一个问题：可以仍在罪中吗？（1-14节）保罗的回答不是「你应该更努力」，而是「你已经和基督联合了」：我们受洗归入基督的死，旧人和他同钉十字架，所以我们「在罪上死了」；我们现在就要过新生的生活，将来也要与他一同复活。所以：「你们向罪也当看自己是死的；向神在基督耶稣里，却当看自己是活的。」第二个问题：既在恩典之下，就可以犯罪吗？（15-23节）保罗用主人和奴仆的比喻：每个人都是某一位主人的奴仆，不是罪的奴仆，就是义（神）的奴仆。最后是那句著名的话：「罪的工价乃是死；惟有神的恩赐，在我们的主基督耶稣里，乃是永生。」

第三至五章主要讲称义和称义的果效：神宣告我们为义。第六章开始讲成圣：被称义的人怎样活出新的生命。两者不能分开，也不能混淆。

深读 6:1-4 受洗归入他的死

1. 一个合理的问题。 「这样，怎么说呢？我们可以仍在罪中、叫恩典显多吗？」（罗6:1）如果有人从来没有被这个问题困扰过，也许是因为他还没有真正听明白恩典。保罗所传的恩典是如此白白、如此彻底，以致人会以为它鼓励犯罪（参罗3:8）。

2. 「在罪上死了」。 「断乎不可！我们在罪上死了的人岂可仍在罪中活着呢？」（罗6:2）保罗不是说信徒不会再犯罪，也不是说罪的试探对信徒已经没有吸引力。他说的是一个身份的改变：罪曾经是我们的主人，可是我们和那个主人之间的关系已经因着死而结束了。

3. 受洗归入基督。 「岂不知我们这受洗归入基督耶稣的人是受洗归入他的死吗？所以，我们藉着洗礼归入死，和他一同埋葬，原是叫我们一举一动有新生的样式，像基督藉着父的荣耀从死里复活一样。」（罗6:3-4）在初期教会，洗礼和信主是紧紧连在一起的（参徒2:38，41）。保罗用洗礼来说明一个属灵的事实：信徒和基督「联合」了，他的死成了我们的死，他的复活也成了我们新生命的源头。洗礼不是离开信心就自动生效的仪式（参罗4:11；西2:12「因信」）；可是保罗能说我们是「藉着洗礼」与基督同埋葬，因为洗礼是神所设立的记号和印证，标明信的人已经与基督联合。叫人得救的是基督，是藉着信与他联合，而洗礼正是这联合可见的印记。

要点：恩典不是犯罪的许可证。信徒已经和基督联合，与他同死、同埋葬，所以我们和罪之间的旧关系已经结束；我们要过的，是复活的新生命。
深读 6:5-11 看自己是死的，也是活的

1. 联合。 「我们若在他死的形状上与他联合，也要在他复活的形状上与他联合。」（罗6:5）「联合」一词原文有「一同生长」「长在一起」的意思，表示一种活的、紧密的联合。「与基督联合」是保罗神学的核心之一：称义、成圣、得荣耀，都是在基督里得着的。

2. 旧人同钉十字架。 「因为知道我们的旧人和他同钉十字架，使罪身灭绝，叫我们不再作罪的奴仆。」（罗6:6）「旧人」不是指我们里面「旧的那一部分」，而是指我们在亚当里的那个旧身份（参罗5:12-21）。那个人已经死了。「罪身灭绝」的「灭绝」，原文的意思是「失去效力」，不是说我们的身体被毁灭了，而是说罪不能再藉着我们的身体辖制我们。

3. 「只有一次」。 「他死是向罪死了，只有一次；他活是向神活着。」（罗6:10）基督「向罪死」不是因为他自己有罪，而是他为我们担当了罪的刑罚，进入罪和死的权势之下，并且一次永远地胜过了它（罗8:3；林后5:21）。他的死是一次而永远有效的。他已经彻底解决了罪的问题，死不能再作他的主。我们与他联合，这也成了我们的事实。

4. 「当看自己」。 「这样，你们向罪也当看自己是死的；向神在基督耶稣里，却当看自己是活的。」（罗6:11）这是本章第一个命令。「看」（logizomai）就是第四章「算为」的那个字。神已经把基督的义算给我们；现在，我们也要照着神所说的来「算」自己。这不是自我暗示，不是假装自己不再有罪的倾向，而是相信神所宣告的事实，并且按着这个事实来生活。

要点：成圣不是从我们的努力开始，而是从相信一个事实开始：在基督里，我们向罪已经是死的，向神是活的。我们要照着神所说的来「看」自己。
深读 6:12-14 不要容罪作王

1. 从直述到命令。 「所以，不要容罪在你们必死的身上作王，使你们顺从身子的私欲。」（罗6:12）保罗先讲「你们是什么」（罗6:1-11），然后才讲「所以你们要怎样」。这是整本罗马书，也是整本新约伦理的顺序：命令建立在恩典的事实上。神不是说「你要成为新人」，而是说「你已经是新人了，所以要活出来」。

2. 献上。 「也不要将你们的肢体献给罪作不义的器具；倒要像从死里复活的人，将自己献给神，并将肢体作义的器具献给神。」（罗6:13）「器具」原文也可以译作「兵器」。我们的眼睛、舌头、手、脚，每天都在为某一方作战。成圣是很具体的：我的舌头今天要说什么？我的眼睛今天要看什么？

3. 不在律法之下，乃在恩典之下。 「罪必不能作你们的主；因你们不在律法之下，乃在恩典之下。」（罗6:14）这是一个应许，不只是命令。为什么罪不能再作主？不是因为律法更严厉了，而是因为恩典掌权了。律法能指出罪，却不能胜过罪；恩典却能。「不在律法之下」不是说信徒可以不理会神的旨意（罗6:15；罗8:4），而是说我们不再活在摩西律法那个旧的统治之下：它吩咐人，也定人的罪，却不能赐人生命（罗7:5-6；罗8:3）。如今我们在恩典的统治之下，恩典藉着基督和圣灵，真正改变人。

要点：神的命令建立在恩典的事实上：你们已经是新人，所以要活出新人的样子。罪不能再作主，不是因为律法更严，而是因为我们在恩典之下。
深读 6:15-23 两种奴仆

1. 没有中立的地带。 「岂不晓得你们献上自己作奴仆，顺从谁，就作谁的奴仆吗？或作罪的奴仆，以至于死；或作顺命的奴仆，以至成义。」（罗6:16）现代人以为自由就是不受任何人的约束。保罗说，没有人是完全「自主」的：每个人都在服侍某一位主人。问题不是要不要作奴仆，而是作谁的奴仆。

2. 从心里顺服。 「感谢神！因为你们从前虽然作罪的奴仆，现今却从心里顺服了所传给你们道理的模范。」（罗6:17）保罗为他们的改变「感谢神」，因为这是神的工作。「模范」原文就是罗5:14「预像」的那个字，可能是指一个模子：福音像一个模子，把信徒塑造成它的样式。和合本译作「所传给你们」，原文直译却是「你们被交付给它」：不只是教训交给了他们，更是他们被交给了这教训，由它来塑造。这是神亲自的作为，正与罗1:24-28神「任凭」（原文是「交给」）人相反。

3. 「照人的常话」。 保罗承认，用「奴仆」来形容与神的关系，并不完全恰当（罗6:19）。作神的奴仆，其实是真正的自由；而作罪的奴仆，看起来自由（「不被义约束」，罗6:20），结局却是死。

4. 果子与结局。 「你们现今所看为羞耻的事，当日有什么果子呢？那些事的结局就是死。但现今，你们既从罪里得了释放，作了神的奴仆，就有成圣的果子，那结局就是永生。」（罗6:21-22）罪应许我们快乐，给我们的却是羞耻和死亡。

5. 工价与恩赐。 「因为罪的工价乃是死；惟有神的恩赐，在我们的主基督耶稣里，乃是永生。」（罗6:23）「工价」原文常指士兵的粮饷，也泛指工钱，是挣来的、应得的；「恩赐」是白白的礼物。罪是一个付工钱的主人，而它付的工钱就是死。神却不是付工钱，而是白白赐给我们永生。即使在讲成圣的这一章，保罗最后一句话仍然是恩典：永生不是成圣的工价，而是神的恩赐。

要点：每个人都是某一位主人的奴仆。罪付给我们的工钱是死；神却白白地把永生赐给我们。作神的奴仆，才是真正的自由。
默想

默想： 「你们向罪也当看自己是死的；向神在基督耶稣里，却当看自己是活的。」当我又一次在同一个罪上跌倒时，我心里怎样「看」自己？我是否说：「我就是这样的人，改不了」？保罗说，那不是神眼中的我：在基督里，我和罪的旧关系已经因着死结束了。今天，有没有一个具体的「肢体」，我需要重新把它献给神：我的舌头，不再用来抱怨、批评或说谎；我的眼睛，不再停留在不洁的画面上；我的手机和时间，不再被我拿来逃避神？这不是靠意志力咬紧牙关，而是相信基督的死和复活真的改变了我，然后按着这个事实迈出一步。罪今天仍会对我说它能给我什么，可是我知道它的工价是死；而神已经白白地把永生赐给我了。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Romans 5:20 said, "where sin increased, grace abounded all the more." That sentence is easily abused: if so, shouldn't we sin more, so that there is more grace? Chapter 6 answers that question. Paul raises a similar question twice, and twice answers, "By no means!"

First question: may we continue in sin? (vv. 1–14). Paul's answer is not "you should try harder" but "you have been united with Christ": we were baptized into his death, our old self was crucified with him, so we "died to sin"; so we now walk in newness of life, and shall share in his resurrection. Therefore: "consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus." Second question: since we are under grace, may we sin? (vv. 15–23). Paul uses the picture of masters and slaves: everyone is a slave of some master, either of sin or of righteousness (God). The chapter ends with the famous words: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord."

Chapters 3–5 have dealt mainly with justification and its fruits: God declares us righteous. Chapter 6 begins to deal with sanctification: how justified people live out the new life. The two must never be separated, nor confused.

Going Deeper: 6:1–4 Baptized into His Death

1. A reasonable question. "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?" (Romans 6:1). If someone has never been troubled by this question, perhaps they haven't really heard grace yet. The grace Paul preached was so free and so complete that people thought it encouraged sin (cf. Romans 3:8).

2. "We died to sin." "By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). Paul isn't saying believers no longer sin, or that sin's temptations no longer attract them. He is speaking of a change of identity: sin was once our master, but our relationship to that master ended in a death.

3. Baptized into Christ. "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:3–4). In the early church, baptism and coming to faith were closely bound together (cf. Acts 2:38, 41). Paul uses baptism to explain a spiritual reality: believers are "united" with Christ; his death became our death, and his resurrection the source of our new life. Baptism does not work automatically apart from faith (cf. Romans 4:11; Col 2:12, "through faith"); yet Paul can say we were buried with Christ "by baptism," because baptism is God's appointed sign and seal of the union believers have with him. It is Christ who saves, through faith-union with him, and baptism is the visible mark of that union.

The point: Grace is not a license to sin. Believers have been united with Christ, dying and buried with him, so our old relationship to sin is over; the life we now live is resurrection life.
Going Deeper: 6:5–11 Consider Yourselves Dead, and Alive

1. Union. "For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his" (Romans 6:5). "United" carries the sense of "grown together," a living and intimate union. Union with Christ is at the heart of Paul's theology: justification, sanctification and glorification are all received in Christ.

2. The old self crucified. "We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin" (Romans 6:6). The "old self" is not some "old part" of us, but our old identity in Adam (cf. Romans 5:12–21). That person has died. "Brought to nothing" means "rendered powerless": not that our bodies are destroyed, but that sin can no longer rule us through our bodies.

3. "Once for all." "For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God" (Romans 6:10). Christ "died to sin" not because he had any sin of his own, but because he bore sin's penalty for us, entered the realm of sin and death, and broke its power once for all (Romans 8:3; 2 Cor 5:21). His death was once for all, effective forever. He has dealt with sin completely; death no longer rules him. Through union with him, this becomes true of us too.

4. "Consider yourselves." "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). This is the chapter's first command. "Consider" (logizomai) is the same word as "counted" in chapter 4. God has counted Christ's righteousness to us; now we too are to "count" ourselves as God says we are. This isn't autosuggestion or pretending we no longer have sinful tendencies; it is believing the fact God has declared, and living by it.

The point: Sanctification doesn't begin with our effort but with believing a fact: in Christ we are dead to sin and alive to God. We are to "consider" ourselves as God says we are.
Going Deeper: 6:12–14 Do Not Let Sin Reign

1. From statement to command. "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal bodies, to make you obey their passions" (Romans 6:12). Paul first says "what you are" (Romans 6:1–11), and only then "so this is how you must live." This is the order of all of Romans, and of New Testament ethics as a whole: commands rest on the facts of grace. God does not say "become a new person"; he says "you are a new person, so live it out."

2. Presenting. "Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness" (Romans 6:13). "Instruments" can also be translated "weapons." Our eyes, tongue, hands and feet fight for one side or the other every day. Sanctification is very concrete: what will my tongue say today? What will my eyes look at today?

3. Not under law but under grace. "For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace" (Romans 6:14). This is a promise, not only a command. Why can sin no longer rule? Not because the law has grown stricter, but because grace now reigns. The law can expose sin but cannot overcome it; grace can. "Not under law" does not mean believers may ignore God's will (Romans 6:15; Romans 8:4); it means we no longer live under the old regime of the Mosaic law, which commanded and condemned but could not give life (Romans 7:5–6; Romans 8:3). We now live under the reign of grace, which through Christ and the Spirit actually changes us.

The point: God's commands rest on the facts of grace: you are already new, so live like it. Sin can no longer rule, not because the law is stricter, but because we are under grace.
Going Deeper: 6:15–23 Two Kinds of Slavery

1. No neutral ground. "Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?" (Romans 6:16). Modern people think freedom means being bound by no one. Paul says no one is fully "self-governing": everyone serves some master. The question is not whether to be a slave, but whose.

2. Obedient from the heart. "But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed" (Romans 6:17). Paul "thanks God" for their change, because it is God's work. "Standard" is the same word as "type" in Romans 5:14, probably picturing a mold: the gospel is like a mold that shapes believers into its pattern. Notice that Paul says they were "committed to" this teaching: not that the teaching was handed to them, but that they were handed over to the teaching. This is God's own act, the reverse of Romans 1:24–28, where God "gave them up" to impurity.

3. "In human terms." Paul admits that "slavery" is not a fully fitting picture for our relationship to God (Romans 6:19). Being God's slave is in fact true freedom; being sin's slave looks like freedom ("free in regard to righteousness," Romans 6:20), but it ends in death.

4. Fruit and end. "But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? The end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life" (Romans 6:21–22). Sin promises us happiness and pays us in shame and death.

5. Wages and gift. "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). "Wages" (opsōnia) was often used of a soldier's pay or rations, and of wages generally: something earned and owed; a "free gift" is given for nothing. Sin is a master who pays wages, and its wage is death. God doesn't pay wages; he freely gives eternal life. Even in this chapter on sanctification, Paul's last word is grace: eternal life is not the wage of sanctification but the gift of God.

The point: Everyone is a slave of some master. Sin pays us in death; God freely gives us eternal life. To be God's slave is true freedom.
Meditation

Reflect: "Consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus." When I fall into the same sin yet again, how do I "consider" myself? Do I say, "That's just who I am; I can't change"? Paul says that is not who I am in God's eyes: in Christ my old relationship with sin ended in a death. Today, is there a specific "member" I need to present to God afresh: my tongue, no longer for complaining, criticizing or lying; my eyes, no longer lingering on impure images; my phone and my time, no longer used to hide from God? This is not gritting my teeth by willpower, but believing that Christ's death and resurrection have truly changed me, and taking a step on that basis. Sin will still tell me today what it can give me, but I know its wages are death; and God has already freely given me eternal life.
